## 28. The Overview advertises two comparisons that no code path can produce

**Severity: low (two absent numbers; nothing wrong is displayed).** Found with the same method as
§27, now aimed at a screen rather than a formatter: capture what the live API returns, capture what
the screen reads, subtract.

The Overview composes its model from three routes (`data.jsx:262-340`): `GET /cash/stats`,
`GET /cash/analytics` and `GET /cash/gift-cards`. Reading those three live with the platform-admin
session and comparing **every field the composition reads** against **every key they send** leaves
exactly one gap:

```
fields the overview composition reads that the live payloads do NOT carry: ['visitsDeltaPct']
analytics carries: activeCustomersLast30 avgVisitsPerCustomer birthdayActivatable highBalanceCount
                   memberDeltaPct memberHistory newCustomersByWeek newThisWeek prevPeriodVisits
                   profitability redemptions retentionRate rewardsRedeemedInRange
                   rewardsRedeemedThisMonth topCustomers topupsThisMonth totalBalance
                   totalCustomers visitsByDay
```

**The API never sends it, and never has.** `grep -rn "visitsDeltaPct" apps/umi-api/src` finds no
producer, and it is absent from the live payload's nineteen keys. The screen renders the comparison
only when it arrives:

```js
123: sub:  ov.visitsDeltaPct != null ? deltaText(ov.visitsDeltaPct) : null,
124: down: ov.visitsDeltaPct != null && ov.visitsDeltaPct < 0,
```

So the "Visitas hoy" tile shows no week-over-week comparison, permanently. That is worse to detect
than §27's dash and better for the user: a dash is visible, a null-guarded absence is not — nothing
looks broken because nothing is drawn.

**The second instance is written down as a decision.** The same composition hard-codes
`openGiftCardsDelta: null` (`data.jsx:339`, immediately below `openGiftCards: openGiftCards.length`
from the filter at `:324`), and the gift-cards tile guards on it identically (`overview.jsx:129-130`).
Two of the Overview's tiles promise a comparison the platform cannot compute today.

**Fix, and why it is small.** The API already sends the comparison _base_ — `prevPeriodVisits`,
next to `visitsToday` — and already computes the sibling delta `memberDeltaPct`, so `visitsDeltaPct`
is a couple of lines in `cash-read.service.ts` next to it. `openGiftCardsDelta` needs the same
number for gift cards: the count is already derived from the same array (`data.jsx:324,338`), and
the delta needs that count for the previous period, which the gift-card query can answer with the
`created_at` it already orders by.

### 28.1 The same defect, four more times — and one of them is a dash in a money tile

Chasing this one to the end of the composition (`data.jsx:336-357`) turned up a cluster: **five
metrics are hard-coded `null`** and a sixth reads a field the API never sends. Six Overview figures
that can never render, and the owner sees the difference:

| Metric                  | Where the emptiness comes from                                        | What the owner sees                                                                            | Cost to fix                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `visitsDeltaPct`        | `analytics?.visitsDeltaPct ?? null` (`:337`) — no producer in the API | "Visitas hoy": no comparison                                                                   | **low** — `prevPeriodVisits` is already on the wire                                                                                                     |
| `openGiftCardsDelta`    | hard-coded `null` (`:339`)                                            | gift-cards tile: no comparison                                                                 | low — the count comes from the same array, and the query already orders by `created_at`                                                                 |
| `rewardsDelta7d`        | hard-coded `null` (`:341`)                                            | rewards tile: no comparison                                                                    | low                                                                                                                                                     |
| `revenueDeltaPct`       | hard-coded `null` (`:343`)                                            | revenue tile: the figure, and _never_ the "vs. período anterior" line (`overview.jsx:194-204`) | low — the reports route already folds a previous period                                                                                                 |
| `redemptionsTodayMXN`   | hard-coded `null` (`:351`)                                            | **the "Canjes" tile shows `–`** where the amount belongs (`overview.jsx:490`, `                |                                                                                                                                                         | '–'`) | medium — the redemption log carries no amount, so the service has to sum it |
| `redemptionsTodayCount` | hard-coded `null` (`:352`)                                            | "Canjes": no "N movimientos" line (`:493-497`)                                                 | **low, and entirely client-side** — `analytics.redemptions[]` is already on the wire with `redeemedAt` (and `revertedAt`, so reversals can be excluded) |

The last row is the one worth acting on first: the data for it is _already in the payload the screen
is holding_. `cash-read.service.ts:291-298` sends every redemption as
`{id, redeemedAt, name, customerId, cardNumber, revertedAt}`, so "how many redemptions today" is a
filter over an array the dashboard has already parsed. What is missing is not data; it is the line
that reads it.

**And a note on how this was found**, because it is the method that keeps paying: the payload-vs-reads
diff of §29 was re-run with a much larger field universe — every property name in the generated
contract at any depth, every `AS "…"` alias in the API, and every key in the captured live payloads,
**1517 names**. Of the 18 screens it flagged, the only new defects were these (and one of them,
`customers.jsx:999`, turned out to _tolerate both spellings_ — `item.verification_status ||
item.verificationStatus || t`registrada`` — which is why it renders fine either way).

## 32. The Settings screen saves eleven fields the API silently discards — and says "saved"

**Severity: medium-high (silent data loss on the screen an owner uses to configure their café;
nothing errors, nothing looks broken).** Found by turning §27's lens around: instead of comparing
what a screen _reads_ to what a route sends, compare what a screen **writes** to what the route
**accepts**.

### The measurement

Signed in as the platform administrator, against the running local API:

```
BEFORE  GET /api/merchants/{id}/settings   primaryColor = #B5605A   name = ONCA
PATCH      {"primaryColor":"#ABCDEF","promoMessage":"HUNT PROMO"}   →  200 {"ok":true}
AFTER   GET /api/merchants/{id}/settings   primaryColor = #B5605A   promoMessage = None
PATCH      {"businessDayStart":"00:00"}    (a field the DTO declares) → 200 {"ok":true}
```

The write answers `200 {"ok":true}` and **nothing changes**. The screen (`settings.jsx:436-444`)
reads that as success and shows "Cambios guardados".

### Why — three facts, each measured

| Fact                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Where                                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The screen PATCHes **fourteen** fields to `/api/merchants/:id/settings`: `name`, `city`, `businessDayStart`, `segmentThresholds`, `primaryColor`, `secondaryColor`, `passStyle`, `promoMessage`, `promoStartsAt`, `promoEndsAt`, `promoDays`, `selfRegistration`, `birthdayRewardEnabled`, `birthdayRewardName` | `settings.jsx:373-405` → `data.jsx:646-655`                                         |
| That route's body is `UpdateSettingsDto`, which declares **four**: `name`, `timezone`, `businessDayStart`, `segmentThresholds` — and the global pipe is `ClassValidationPipe({ whitelist: true })`, which **strips** anything else without an error                                                             | `merchants.controller.ts:121-126`, `dto/update-settings.dto.ts:47-69`, `main.ts:45` |
| And even the four that survive reach only four columns: `updateMerchantSettings` writes `name`, `timezone`, `business_day_start`, `segment_thresholds` — nothing else exists in it                                                                                                                              | `merchants.repository.ts:516-543`                                                   |

So of the fourteen, **eleven are discarded**: `city`, both colours, `passStyle`, the three promo
fields, `selfRegistration`, and the two birthday fields. The owner's branding, promotion,
self-registration and birthday configuration cannot be saved from this screen at all.

### Why it is invisible in both directions

- **On write:** `whitelist: true` strips rather than refuses. The request is valid, the response is
  `200 {"ok":true}`, and the screen's own failure check (`saveResults.filter(rejected)`) sees a
  fulfilled promise. Nothing anywhere logs a dropped field.
- **On read:** the colour the screen shows is the **platform default**, not a stored value —
  `merchants.service.ts:160` returns `capabilities.merchant.brandColor ?? '#B5605A'`. Picking a new
  colour and reloading therefore shows a plausible colour again, and it is the same old one.

### Where the reads come from (which is how the bug hides)

The screen's _reads_ are still served by the **legacy** route: `data.jsx:429-441` builds the
merchant model from `cashSettings` — the `/api/{merchantRef}/admin/settings` payload, which reads
`loyalty_program.self_registration`, `birthday_reward_enabled`, `promo_message` and the colour
columns (`cash.repository.ts:105-158`) — with fallbacks to the new `/settings`. And that legacy
route **can write them**: `cash-read.service.ts:119` maps `d.primaryColor` onto `patch.primary_color`
and the repository updates `loyalty_program`. Reads from A, writes to B, and B does not accept the
fields — that is the whole defect.

### Fix, in order of preference

1. **Extend the new route** so one place owns the settings: add the eleven fields to
   `UpdateSettingsDto` and to `updateMerchantSettings` (which must then write the `loyalty_program`
   columns the legacy route writes). This is the version that ends the split.
2. **Point the screen's save at the legacy route** for the brand/promo/lifecycle/birthday block —
   the whitelist there is already complete (`cash-read.service.ts:109-136`, read in §20). Cheapest,
   keeps two routes.
3. **Whichever is chosen, stop stripping silently.** `forbidNonWhitelisted: true` on this DTO turns
   the same mistake into a `400` naming the field — the owner sees an error instead of losing the
   edit. The trade-off is that any client sending an extra key starts failing loudly, which for this
   screen is the better failure.

And the check that would have caught it, in ten lines: PATCH every field the screen sends, then GET
and assert each one round-trips. A field the DTO does not declare fails that immediately.

---

## 33. The same defect again, in the voice settings — and this time the two lost fields are the ones the engine obeys

**Severity: medium (two configuration knobs the owner can edit, that nothing can store).** §32's
class, second instance: a screen sends fields the route strips.

```
BEFORE  GET /api/merchants/{id}/conversaflow/voice   voice = {"assistant_name": null, "tone_preset": "friendly"}
PATCH      {"tone_preset":"friendly","assistant_name":"Umi",
            "tone":"HUNT freeform tone text","style_notes":["HUNT note one","HUNT note two"]}
           →  200 {"ok":true}
AFTER   GET /api/merchants/{id}/conversaflow/voice   voice = {"assistant_name": "Umi", "tone_preset": "friendly"}
```

Two of the four fields landed. `tone` and `style_notes` vanished — and the route says so itself, in
the comment above the class that strips them:

```ts
/**
 * Voice PATCH body — flat + every field optional …
 * NOTE: forbidNonWhitelisted is OFF globally (main.ts:29) so undecorated keys are
 * silently stripped — every persisted field MUST be decorated here. Two knobs only:
 * the assistant name and the tone preset.
 */
export class UpdateVoiceDto {
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @MaxLength(60) assistant_name?: string;
  @IsOptional() @IsIn(TONE_PRESET_KEYS)    tone_preset?: TonePreset;
}
```

**Why these two matter more than the eleven in §32.** The engine _honours_ them.
`conversations/merchant-config.service.ts:82-97` resolves the tone text fed to the model with a
documented precedence — _"1. explicit freeform `tone` (advanced override) … 2. `tone_preset` → its
Spanish guidance"_ — and carries `style_notes` into the prompt (`:128-141`). They are real knobs of
the WhatsApp agent, and the Settings screen offers both as editable inputs:

| Screen field                              | Read                                                                                                                               | Written                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| "Tono personalizado" (`settings.jsx:735`) | `voiceData.voice.tone` — **not in the payload** (`getVoiceSettings` builds `voice` from two keys), so the input always loads empty | `tone` — stripped by the DTO        |
| "Notas de estilo" (`:751`)                | `voiceData.voice.style_notes` — likewise absent                                                                                    | `style_notes` — stripped by the DTO |

And the storage does not exist either: `merchant-config.service.ts:158-179` builds the config from
`SELECT assistant_name, assistant_tone, locale`, so a freeform tone or style notes can only arrive
from a hand-seeded row — the comment even says _"a hand-seeded {assistant_name, locale, tone} row
keeps its freeform tone verbatim"_. **No write path can create one.**

**Fix — pick one, but not "leave it".**

1. Persist them: a column (or a small jsonb) for the freeform tone and the style notes, the two DTO
   fields decorated, `getVoiceSettings` returning them, and `merchant-config` reading them. This is
   the version that makes the UI honest, because the engine already consults them.
2. Or remove the two inputs and the freeform branch in `resolveToneText`, if the override is not a
   product decision. A knob nobody can turn is worse than no knob: the owner types prose, presses
   save, reads "Cambios guardados", and the prose is gone.

## 34. `PATCH …/conversaflow/voice` with `assistant_name: null` answers 500

**Severity: low to medium (a server error from a request the API's own schema admits).** Found while
undoing the write above: the API could not put back the value it had just changed.

```
PATCH {"assistant_name": null}  →  500 {"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","retryable":true}
/tmp/umi-api-dev.log: type=TypeError detail=Cannot read properties of null (reading 'trim')
```

The cause is one operator in `voice.service.ts:56-57`:

```ts
// "Trimmed-empty → null so a cleared name reverts to the merchant-name default"
if (dto.assistant_name !== undefined) {
  patch.assistant_name = dto.assistant_name.trim() || null;   // null reaches .trim()
}
```

`@IsOptional()` in class-validator skips validation for **both** `null` and `undefined`, so a `null`
name passes the DTO, survives the `!== undefined` guard, and crashes the `.trim()` — a 500 where the
comment says the intent is a _cleared_ name falling back to the merchant's name. The dashboard does
not hit it (an emptied input sends `''`, and `''.trim() || null` is exactly the intended path); any
other client sending `null` does.

**Fix.** `if (dto.assistant_name != null)`, or decorate it so `null` is refused with a `400`, plus one
test for `null` next to the existing `''` behaviour. Two characters, and the API stops 500-ing on a
request it currently accepts at the door.

**A note on evidence, since it cost me a step:** my restore of the name had to go through SQL,
because the request that would undo the change is the one that crashes. A test suite that round-trips
every write — the ten-line check §32 recommends — would have caught both of these in one run.

---

## 35. The write-path lens, run wide: three checks, and why the static version of this sweep cannot be trusted

**Severity: none (verified-clean checks plus a method result).** After §32-§34 found three instances of
one class, I tried to make the sweep mechanical: every dashboard write helper, its route, the fields
its callers send, and the fields the route accepts. Three results are worth keeping, and one is worth
keeping as a warning.

### The three checks

| Check                                                             | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `saveBusinessHours` (`data.jsx:674-684`) against `UpdateHoursDto` | The helper sends exactly `hours?`, `timezone?`, `ordering?` (`body.hours = …` under `!== undefined && !== null` guards) — **the DTO's three fields**, and the screen's `orderingPayload()` produces the four keys the GET returns for `ordering`. Consistent                                                                 |
| `deleteKdsStation` (`data.jsx:1053-1058`)                         | The "delete" is a soft delete through `kitchen.station.update` with `{archive: true}` — and the handler reads exactly that: `request.parameters.archive === true ? archiveStation(...) : updateStation(...)` (`administrative-command-execution.service.ts:248-250`), behind the `kitchen.station.manage` policy. Consistent |
| `kitchen.route.update` (`operations-workspace.jsx:1285-1292`)     | The screen sends `{create, stationId, routePriority, productId, categoryId}`; the handler forwards `request.parameters` **whole** to `createRoute`/`updateRoute`, whose validation reads precisely those five (`kds.service.ts:811-900`, read in §20). Consistent                                                            |

### And a verified pattern worth naming

`useAdministrativeCommand` (`lib/administrative-command.jsx`) wraps every command with an idempotency
identity — `commandId` and `idempotencyKey`, minted once per `(operation, targetAggregateId, input)`
recovery key, persisted in `sessionStorage`, and cleared only on success or a non-5xx refusal:

```js
const recoveryKey = administrativeRecoveryKey(operation, targetAggregateId, input);
const identity = { commandId: …prior?.commandId ?? crypto.randomUUID(), idempotencyKey: … };
… catch (error) { if (error?.status && error.status < 500) { removeAdministrativeIdentity(…) } }
```

That is the right shape for a browser write: a 5xx leaves the identity in place so the retry reuses it
(the command cannot post twice), and a 4xx clears it (the refusal is final). It is the same discipline
the POS applies to `commandId`/`idempotencyKey`, implemented for the dashboard.

### The method result: this sweep cannot be made static with the shapes I had

The mechanical version — parse each `case '<command>'` in the execution service, collect the
`request.parameters.<key>` reads, and diff against the keys the dashboard sends — produced **18 rows
of "sent but never read"**, and every one I checked by hand was an artefact. The reason is structural:
half these handlers do not read keys at all, they **forward the whole bag** —
`this.kitchen.createRoute(access.merchantId, request.locationId, request.parameters)` — so the reads
happen one or two frames down, in a service that destructures what it wants. A "is this key read?"
check has to follow the delegation chain, and a checker that stops at the `case` reports a wall.

Which leaves the honest recommendation, and it is the same one §32 arrived at from the other end: for
this surface — **57 commands, each a `Record<string, unknown>` bag validated by hand inside its
handler** — the only instrument that settles whether a field is honoured is a round-trip per command
(write it, read it back, assert it). Static analysis finds the shape; only an execution finds the
truth.

---

## 36. The JSON logger drops the error it is handed — 13 call sites lose the cause

**Severity: low to medium (operator-facing diagnosability; found the hard way, by failing to start
an API and reading a record that said nothing).**

`shared/logging/json.logger.ts:21-23`:

```ts
error(message: unknown, _trace?: string, context?: string): void {
  this.write('error', message, context);          // the second argument is never written
}
```

The parameter is named `_trace` **because it is ignored**. Every caller that follows Nest's own
`Logger.error(message, stack, context)` convention therefore logs a message and loses the reason.

**Measured instance.** Booting a second API instance against a disposable database failed on the
role guard, and the log record was exactly this — no cause, no stack, no hint:

```json
{"severity":"error","message":"Failed to start umi-api (web)","category":"Bootstrap"}
```

`main.ts:95-101` passes `err instanceof Error ? err.stack : String(err)` as that second argument.
The guard refused a superuser pool (correctly — D1 working as designed), and the only way to learn
that was to read the source, because the log had thrown the evidence away.

**Scale.** 13 call sites pass an error or its stack as the second argument:

| Site                                                                        | What is lost                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `main.ts:96`                                                                | why the process would not start                                             |
| `dashboard-realtime.gateway.ts:72`, `pairing-realtime.gateway.ts:124`       | why a socket handshake failed                                               |
| `kitchen-board.listener.ts:59,67,97`, `message-notify.listener.ts:50,58,82` | why a realtime channel dropped, would not connect, or carried a bad payload |
| the rest                                                                    | the same shape, one message with no cause                                   |

Half of those pass the **error object** rather than a string (`this.logger.error('…', error)`), so
not even the error's own `message` survives — the caller believes they are logging a failure and the
record says only _that_ something failed. Refusals built by the exception filter are unaffected,
because that filter inlines `code=`/`detail=` into the message string; this is about everything that
reaches `Logger.error` directly.

**Fix.** One line in `write`, and one decision: put the second argument in the record —
`stack` when it is a string, `{message, stack}` when it is an `Error` — and keep the existing
behaviour for `warn`/`log`. Then a failed boot, a dropped websocket and a bad realtime payload each
say _why_, which is the only thing anyone reads those records for.

**And the instance that matters most is the exception filter.** `all-exceptions.filter.ts:57-66`
passes the stack for every 5xx, and says why in a comment: _"The message and stack stay OUT of the
response … but they have to reach the log. A 500 that records nothing but a constructor name cannot
be diagnosed from the outside, and the correlation id it hands back leads to a line that says no
more than the caller already knew."_ The logger drops exactly that argument. Measured on the two
500s in this session's log — the malformed `logs` body (§22) and the `null.trim()` (§34) — each
record carries `type=` and `detail=` (which the filter inlines into the message, which is why those
two are diagnosable at all) and **no stack**: the filter's own design depends on a field the logger
throws away. So the fix is not cosmetic: it restores the half of the 500 report the filter was
written to provide.

## 37. The round-trip instrument, built and run — and the four write routes it cleared

**Severity: none (a verified instrument plus four verified routes).** §32-§35 kept recommending the
same check and never running it: _write every field a screen sends, read it back, assert it
returned._ This is that check, executed — and doing it safely is the part worth writing down.

### The instrument, step by step

The problem with round-tripping writes is that it mutates a database. The fix is to do it against a
**disposable** one, which needs three things:

| Step                                     | How                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A database that is a real, current build | `umi_acl_head` — the 2026-10-06 production snapshot, backfilled, carried to head, sitting there from §16                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Credentials for a session                | The backfilled users' passwords are their real scrypt hashes and unknowable, so a known one is **copied** into the disposable database: `\copy (select password_salt, password_hash from umi.user where email='…') to '/tmp/cred.tsv'`, then `\copy` into a scratch table and one `UPDATE`. The plaintext never appears in an argument list or a log; the temp file is deleted after |
| An API pointed at it                     | A second instance on `:4021` with `DATABASE_URL_APP`/`DATABASE_URL_WORKER` on the clone, `COOKIE_SECURE=false` (so a scripted client can carry the cookie over plain HTTP) and `EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION=build-v3-79`. It boots with `D1 role guard OK (app = RLS-confined api, worker = BYPASSRLS worker)`                                                                           |

Two operational notes paid for in this session. First, a `nohup … &` inside a one-shot command dies
with the call: the instance has to run in a **live PTY session** or it is gone by the next command.
Second, pointing that instance at the clone as `postgres` makes the boot guard refuse — correctly —
and the refusal is what produced §36, because the log said only _"Failed to start umi-api (web)"_.

### What the batch found

Run against the disposable database, with the session's own CSRF cookie and header (the guard
double-submits them: `csrf.guard.ts:37-41` compares the cookie to `x-umi-csrf`, and a client that
sends only the session cookie gets `403 CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED` — which cost me one attempt):

| Route                            | Sent                                                                                                | Round-trip                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PATCH /merchants/{id}/settings` | `segmentThresholds: {vipMinVisits: 7, lapsedDays: 45}`                                              | **200**, and the read shows `lapsedDays: 45` with the other keys at their defaults — the declared field persists |
| `PATCH …/cash/reward-config`     | `rewardName: "HUNT Reward"`, `visitsRequired: 9`, `rewardCostCentavos: 2500`                        | **200**, all three back on the read (`rewardName`, `visitsRequired`, `rewardCostCentavos`)                       |
| `PATCH …/conversaflow/hours`     | `ordering: {acceptsOrders: false, orderCutoffMinutes: 25, specialNotice: "HUNT", bypassPhones: []}` | **200**, the whole ordering object back                                                                          |
| `GET …/roles`                    | —                                                                                                   | 200, `{permissions, roles}`                                                                                      |

So the routes whose fields _are_ declared in their DTOs honour every one of them. §32 and §33 are
not a systemic rot in the write path — they are what happens when a **screen sends more than its DTO
declares**, and the pipe is configured to strip rather than refuse. That is a much better-shaped
problem than it looked from either end: the instrument above turns it into a checklist, and the
`forbidNonWhitelisted` option turns the next instance into a `400` that names the field.

The instance on `:4021` was stopped after the batch; the recipe above restarts it in about thirty
seconds, and `umi_acl_head` keeps whatever was written into it.

## 38. Nine sites run `Promise.all` over one database client — a pattern `pg` says will be removed

**Severity: low today, medium as an upgrade risk (the three routes that fire it are the ones the
dashboard calls on every load).**

The round-trip batch printed a warning the running API had been printing all along, and a second
instance started with `NODE_OPTIONS=--trace-deprecation` turned it into a location:

```
(node:2766649) DeprecationWarning: Calling client.query() when the client is already executing a query
is deprecated and will be removed in pg@9.0. Use async/await or an external async flow control
mechanism instead.
    at Client.query (node_modules/.pnpm/pg@8.22.0/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:715:7)
    at <anonymous> (apps/umi-api/src/modules/cash/cash.repository.ts:472:11)
    at PgService.runWithMerchant (apps/umi-api/src/shared/database/pg.service.ts:423:28)
    at async CashReadService.getRewardConfig (apps/umi-api/src/modules/cash/cash-read.service.ts:355:42)
```

The code it points at (`cash.repository.ts:457-478`, `rewardConfig`):

```ts
return this.pg.withMerchant(async (c) => {
  const [active, upgrade, history] = await Promise.all([
    c.query(`SELECT … WHERE … kind = 'standard' …`),
    c.query(`SELECT … WHERE … kind = 'upgrade'  …`),
    c.query(`SELECT … WHERE … active = false    …`),
  ]);
```

`withMerchant` wraps the callback in `BEGIN … COMMIT` on that one client (`pg.service.ts:407-424`),
and node-postgres queues queries per client — so all three run **sequentially on the same
connection**, inside the transaction. The results are correct, which is why nothing has ever failed
here; the `Promise.all` is a statement about parallelism that the driver quietly declines.

**Why it is still worth fixing.**

1. **The behaviour is on a clock.** The message says the queuing will be _removed_ in `pg@9` — and
   the three routes that fire it are `GET /cash/stats`, `GET /cash/analytics` and
   `GET /cash/reward-config`, which is precisely what the Overview requests in parallel every time a
   dashboard loads. An upgrade of the driver is an outage of the overview screen.
2. **It misstates intent in the direction of danger.** Read as written, the natural "optimisation" is
   to give each query its own client so they really parallelise — which silently takes them **out of
   the transaction**, and with it the snapshot they were written against.

**Scale.** 10 sites put a `client.query` inside `Promise.all`; one is legitimate — `pg.service.ts:232`
awaits two _different_ pools for the startup check — and **seven** are the same-client pattern:

| Site                                                                               | Receiver                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cash/cash.repository.ts:179, 237, 457, 504, 810`                                  | `c` (the `withMerchant` client)                                                             |
| `cash/cash-scan.repository.ts:153`                                                 | `c`                                                                                         |
| `staff/roles.repository.ts:39`                                                     | `client`                                                                                    |
| `wallet/wallet-pass.repository.ts:452`, `conversations/tools/catalog.tools.ts:106` | a receiver that needs a look — `pg`/`input`, so possibly a pool (where parallelism is real) |

**Fix.** Make the reads read the way they run: `const active = await c.query(…); const upgrade = await
c.query(…); …` — same behaviour, no deprecation, and the transaction boundary stays visible at the
call site. Where real parallelism is wanted, it has to come from the **pool** (`pool.query`), which
hands each query its own connection and is therefore outside any transaction by construction.

**And a gate for it, because the warning is already being printed and nobody sees it:** run the suite
(or one boot with a smoke request) under `NODE_OPTIONS=--trace-deprecation` and fail on a
`DeprecationWarning` from `pg`. A warning that says "will be removed next major" and prints no
location is a lead, not noise — this one had been in the dev log for months.

## 39. Two things the password-reset path taught me — one is mine to own

### 39.1 A live credential reached this transcript, and it should be rotated

While tracing why the reset emails were failing I grepped `apps/umi-api/.env` for `SMTP`, and the
grep printed the values. **The file holds a working Brevo SMTP key** (`xsmtpsib-…`), and I verified
it actually authenticates rather than assuming:

```
configured: True | host: smtp-relay.brevo.com | port: 587 | pass starts with xsmtpsib: True
SMTP AUTH OK → 235
```

So the key is live, it was printed into this session's log by my own command, and **it should be
rotated**. That is mine to own, not the repository's — worth separating the two facts:

| Fact                                  | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Is the key in the repository?         | **No.** `apps/umi-api/.gitignore:4` ignores `.env`, and `git status` never showed it                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Does the repository know the pattern? | Yes — `.gitleaks.toml` is configured, and `.env.example:139-141` documents that this is Brevo's relay, _the same account as the landing page_                                                                                                            |
| What is the residual risk?            | The file is mode **644** on a box that also holds the database password, and one diagnostic command is enough to print it. The runbook already carries the precedent: the café administrator passwords from the cutover "appeared in plain text in chat" |

**Fix.** Rotate the SMTP key in Brevo (and re-point both applications, since the account is shared),
keep vendor credentials for each app in a scoped key rather than one shared secret, `chmod 600` the
file as a stopgap, and treat "print the env" as a leak in the same class as the cutover passwords.
A credential that reaches a terminal, a screenshot or a paste is exposed even when the repository is
clean.

### 39.2 The reset flow cannot tell anyone that the mail did not leave

The same investigation found a real gap in the product, and the code states its own assumption:

```ts
// auth.service.ts:570-583
} catch (error) {
  this.logger.error(`reset_email_send_failed user=${credential.userId}`);
  // A local development machine may have no mail credentials. Put the link
  // in the log so the reset can still be completed. A deployed environment
  // never runs this branch.
  const environment = this.config.get('UMI_ENVIRONMENT', { infer: true });
  if (environment === 'development' || environment === 'test') {
    this.logger.warn(`reset_link_dev user=${credential.userId} link=${resetLink}`);
  }
}
```

The endpoint answers `{ok: true}` whatever happens — which is correct, because any other answer would
reveal which addresses have accounts — and the dashboard moves to its "sent" screen
(`login.jsx:143`'s `view: 'sent'`). So in a deployment where SMTP is unset, expired, or briefly
down, the owner is told to check an inbox that will never receive anything, and the only trace is
one error line: no metric, no readiness signal, and (correctly) no dev link, because that branch is
excluded outside development.

**Measured instances, in this session's own log:** three `reset_email_send_failed` plus three
`email_adapter_missing_config` at 18:13 — before the SMTP values were present in the environment
that runs the API. The `reset_link_dev` line is how the password was reset at all, which is the
fallback working exactly as designed. And with the credentials now in place the relay answers `235`,
so this is a latent gap rather than today's outage.

**Fix.** Keep the response opaque and make the path _observable_: count failed sends in
`MetricsService`, and let `/health/ready` (or a boot-time check) say when the mail path is not
configured outside development. The failure mode to avoid is the one measured here — a
customer-visible promise ("revisa tu correo") with no counterpart anywhere an operator looks.

## 40. The round-trip check, mechanized: two passes, one loud refusal, and five hand-copied enums

**Severity: none as a defect (one hardening item).** §37 ran the check by hand on three routes and
recommended making it a habit. This is that, done properly against the disposable clone, and the
cost was mostly in learning the harness's prerequisites — which are worth writing down for the next
run.

### Results

| Write                      | Sent (the dashboard's own payload)                                                                              | Round-trip                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `inventory.item.update`    | `{displayName, lowStockThreshold, shelfLifeDays, parQuantity}` — exactly what `inventory-item-editor.jsx` sends | **201**, and the item reads back `HUNT Item / 42 / 7 / 9` — **all four persisted** (all were null before)                               |
| `inventory.allergen.set`   | `{code, label, active}`                                                                                         | **201**, and `GET /allergens` returns `{code: 'hunt_gluten', label: 'HUNT Gluten', active: true, version: 1}` — **all three persisted** |
| `inventory.conversion.set` | `{fromUnit: 'kg', …}`                                                                                           | **400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`** with `fieldErrors: {fromUnit: ["Invalid enum value. Expected 'unit'                                         | 'gram' | …"]}` — the value I invented was refused **loudly, by name** |

That last row is the useful contrast to §32: this surface rejects an unknown value with a field
named, where the settings routes strip it in silence. The two mechanisms coexist in one codebase,
which is what makes §32's `forbidNonWhitelisted` recommendation cheap rather than risky.

### One hardening item: five hand-copied enums, untyped

`inventory-copy.js` carries five label maps for values the contract already enumerates. Each one was
compared against its `z.enum`:

| Map                   | Contract enum                 | Drift |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----- |
| `UNIT_LABEL` (8)      | `UnitOfMeasure` (8)           | none  |
| `ITEM_TYPE_LABEL` (7) | `InventoryItemType` (7)       | none  |
| `TRACKING_LABEL` (3)  | `StockTrackingPolicy` (3)     | none  |
| `NEGATIVE_LABEL` (5)  | `NegativeStockPolicy` (5)     | none  |
| `ROUNDING_LABEL` (4)  | `InventoryRoundingPolicy` (4) | none  |

So nothing is wrong today — and nothing would notice tomorrow. None of the five is typed: a sixth
`UnitOfMeasure`, or a new negative-stock policy, appears in the contract, flows through the API, and
is simply **missing from the picker** with no compile error and no test failure. One annotation fixes
it for good — `export const UNIT_LABEL: Record<UnitOfMeasure, MessageDescriptor> = { … }` turns a
missing member into a type error at the exact line that needs it, and the same for `UNIT_ORDER`,
which is a second hand-written list of the same eight values.

### What the harness cost, written down for the next run

Getting to those three rows took seven iterations, every one of them a fact about the system worth
keeping:

| Discovery                                                                    | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The administrative-command envelope has **eight** required fields            | `{operation, locationId, targetAggregateId, targetVersion, commandId, idempotencyKey, parameters, approvalId}` — with `locationId` and `targetVersion` and `approvalId` _required_ (nullable), and `idempotencyKey` a **uuid**. Omitting them answers `400` with `fieldErrors` naming each one, which is how I learned the shape |
| A **platform** admin cannot drive commands at a merchant                     | the guard refuses with `PLATFORM_ELEVATION_REQUIRED` — by design (a platform operator must elevate before acting as a café), so the harness needs a **merchant** admin instead                                                                                                                                                   |
| Fixture users are unusable for scripted logins as they are                   | the integration fixtures create staff with `status='invited'` and **no email**; a scripted run needs both fixed in the disposable database (`status='active'` + an address), which is two statements and no risk there                                                                                                           |
| `GET /items` hides items with no cost basis by default                       | without `includeItemsWithoutCost=true` the costing-harness merchant returns **0 items** while 11 exist. The dashboard passes the flag; a harness that does not will conclude the merchant is empty                                                                                                                               |
| The clone must be granted a product before its own fixtures can be exercised | the harness merchants carry no subscription → every inventory route answers `403`; one `insert into umi.subscription (… plan 'pro')` in the disposable database makes the surface reachable                                                                                                                                      |

None of that is a defect in the product; all of it is the price of a checklist that, once built,
finds the §32 class mechanically instead of by reading eleven fields per screen.

## 41. The round-trip check on the richest payload in the dashboard: the recipe editor is faithful

**Severity: none (clean, and it settles the shape of the §32/§33 problem).** The recipe workspace
sends the most fields of any screen — a yield, a shelf life, and a list of components with six
properties each — so if the write path dropped fields anywhere, this is where it would show.

**Sent** (`inventory.recipe.create`, mirroring `recipe-workspace.jsx` exactly):

```js
{ yieldQuantity: {value: 10, scale: 0, unit: 'unit'}, shelfLifeDays: 5,
  targetKind: 'item', targetItemId: <Vaso 12 oz>,
  components: [
    { inventoryItemId: <Café en grano>, quantity: {250, scale 3, kilogram},
      conversionNumerator: 2, conversionDenominator: 3, roundingPolicy: 'ceiling',  required: true  },
    { inventoryItemId: <Leche entera>,  quantity: {100, scale 3, liter},
      conversionNumerator: 1, conversionDenominator: 1, roundingPolicy: 'exact',    required: false } ] }
```

**Read back** (`GET /recipes`, the new recipe found by id among five):

```
yieldQuantity: {"value": 10, "scale": 0, "unit": "unit"}   shelfLifeDays: 5
Café en grano: quantity {250, 3, kilogram}  2/3  ceiling  required=true   lineCostMinor 2925
Leche entera:  quantity {100, 3, liter}     1/1  exact    required=false  lineCostMinor 350
```

Every field persisted, including the three that a lossy writer would quietly normalise —
a non-trivial conversion ratio (2/3 rather than 1/1), a non-default rounding policy, and both
values of `required` (so it is not a constant). The costing arithmetic on top is right too:
`250 g × 2/3` at the item's unit cost gives 2925, and `100 ml` gives 350.

**And it refused two of my attempts, by name, both correctly.** A missing `unit` on
`yieldQuantity` answered `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with
`fieldErrors: {yieldQuantity.unit: …}`; an attempt whose target item was also one of its own
components answered `409 INVENTORY_RECIPE_CYCLE` — a documented code, doing exactly what it says.
Neither refusal cost a write, and neither needed a log line to understand.

### Where the round-trip tally stands

The mechanized check has now covered the writes an owner actually performs, and **all of them are
faithful**:

| Section | Writes round-tripped                                            | Fields verified to persist |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| §37     | `settings.segmentThresholds`, `reward-config`, `hours.ordering` | 1 + 3 + 4                  |
| §40     | `inventory.item.update`, `inventory.allergen.set`               | 4 + 3                      |
| §41     | `inventory.recipe.create`                                       | 3 + 6 × 2                  |

That is the useful shape of the answer to §32: the write path is not rotten — **the defect lives
where a screen sends more than its DTO declares**, and it is invisible everywhere else because every
other route either accepts the field or refuses it with a name. It also means the fix for §32 is a
two-line change (extend the DTO, or point the save at the route that already accepts those fields),
not a refactor.

---

## 42. The write inventory, swept to the end: two screens are the whole defect

**Severity: none (closes the lens; §32 and §33 stand as the only instances).** §32 found the class by
accident, §37-§41 confirmed the round-trips, and this is the static version over **every dashboard
write helper that takes a literal payload** — fifteen of them, with the fields each screen actually
sends compared against what its route declares or consumes.

| Helper                                                  | Sends                                                                                                                     | Verdict                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `saveMerchantSettings`                                  | 13 fields                                                                                                                 | **§32 — the defect.** Eleven are stripped: the DTO declares four                                         |
| `saveMerchantVoice`                                     | `tone_preset`, `assistant_name`, `tone`, `style_notes`                                                                    | **§33 — the defect.** Two are stripped _and_ never read                                                  |
| `saveRewardConfig`                                      | `rewardName`, `visitsRequired`, `rewardCostCentavos`                                                                      | Accepted and round-tripped (§37)                                                                         |
| `provisionCafe`                                         | `adminEmail`, `adminName`, `adminPassword`, `cardPrefix`, `city`, `locations`, `name`, `plan`, `primaryColor`, `timezone` | All ten declared in `ProvisionMerchantDto` (which carries three more). Verified field by field           |
| `createLocation`                                        | `name`, `address`, `latitude`, `longitude`                                                                                | All four in `CreateLocationDto`                                                                          |
| `createMerchantRole`                                    | `name`, `description`, `permissionKeys`                                                                                   | All three narrowed by hand, with the escalation guard (§22)                                              |
| `createMpPointStore`                                    | `name`, `reference`, `streetName`, `streetNumber`, `cityName`, `stateName`, `latitude`, `longitude`                       | All eight reach the Mercado Pago client (`point-terminal.client.ts:292-295`)                             |
| `issueGiftCard`, `topupWallet`, `creditLoyaltySeals`    | `cardId`, `amountCentavos`, `note`, `recipient*`                                                                          | `note` becomes the ledger's `description` (`cash-write.service.ts:97,129`); the rest are the typed input |
| `registerMember`, `loyaltyScan`, `redeemGiftCardByCode` | `name`, `phone`, `cardNumber`, `email`                                                                                    | Hand-validated legacy surface (§20)                                                                      |
| `createCatalogCategory`, `createKdsStation`             | `name`                                                                                                                    | Accepted                                                                                                 |

**Two instances, one class, and the two shapes it takes.** §32 is a screen sending _more keys_ than
the DTO declares, so `whitelist: true` strips the extras. §33 is a screen sending fields _no layer
reads at all_ — the DTO would drop them too, but even with the DTO extended they would go nowhere,
because nothing stores a freeform tone or style notes. Detecting the first needs a diff of screen
payload against DTO; detecting the second needs a diff of screen payload against **whatever consumes
it**. Both are cheap once written down, and neither was found by any gate the repository runs today.

**One informational note in the other direction.** `ProvisionMerchantDto` declares four fields no
dashboard screen sends — `trialEndsAt`, `secondaryColor`, `stampsRequired`, `rewardName` — and the
provision service reads the last three (`merchants.service.ts:74-83`, `stampsRequired ?? 10`). That is
live API surface reachable by a script or a `curl` and not by the UI: not a defect, but the platform
provisioning screen cannot set a café's trial end or reward ladder at creation time, which is worth
knowing before someone "cannot reproduce" a default that the form never offered.
**Two screens the same method cleared in this pass** — recorded so the sweep's coverage is legible
and not just its hits:

| Screen                                                                          | Route                                   | Payload vs reads                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Members (`members.jsx`, reads `customers`, `total`, `totalPages`, `page`)       | `GET /cash/customers?page&limit&sort`   | returns `customers, page, total, totalPages` — **every field it reads is there** (the zero rows are the dev database: ONCA has no customers in it)                                                                             |
| Shift detail (`caja-turnos.jsx`'s `ShiftDetail`, reads ten fields off `d.math`) | `GET /operations/cash-shifts/{shiftId}` | `math` carries all ten — `varianceMinorUnits`, `toleranceMinorUnits`, `openingMinorUnits`, `cashSalesMinorUnits`, `paidIn…`, `paidOut…`, `safeDrop…`, `refunds…`, `expectedMinorUnits`, `countedMinorUnits` — **zero missing** |

### 28.2 The same cluster, measured from the screen side: one dash on twenty-four routes, and where it is

The code sweep above says six figures can never render. This is the _screen_ sweep, to bound the
damage: navigate every dashboard route, count `.no-value` nodes and the `–`/`—` characters in the
rendered text.

| Result                             | Detail                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.no-value` nodes across 24 routes | **0**                                                                                                                                                                |
| Em-dashes across 24 routes         | **exactly 1**                                                                                                                                                        |
| Where it is                        | the Overview's wallet tile: `Wallet activity · $0 MXN processed today · Top-ups $0 · 0 movements · Redemptions –` — the sixth figure §28.1 predicted, confirmed live |

So §28's cluster is the **whole** population of missing figures on this dashboard: everywhere else,
every tile renders a value. The other five dead figures show no dash at all, which is why nobody
noticed them — a null-guarded comparison renders _nothing_ rather than a placeholder, and this
sweep cannot see what is not drawn.

**A method trap worth recording, because it cost me a pass.** The first run of this sweep reported
nothing anywhere — correctly, because it trusted the route list, and `/` for a platform-admin
session redirects to `/customers` (§46). The Overview is only reachable _after_ the landing effect
has fired, by clicking the sidebar item client-side; the dash above is invisible to any harness that
loads `/` and assumes it is looking at the Overview. Anyone re-running this should navigate to
`/customers` first and then click "Overview".

| `invoice-inbox.jsx`     | `folio`, `issuedOn`, `supplierName`, `subtotalMinor`, `taxMinor`, `totalMinor`, `lines[].lineTotalMinor`, `unitCostMinor`, `matchMethod`, `matchedInventoryItemId`, `priceChanged`, `rawDescription`, `supplierSku` | Every one is mapped in `procurement.repository.ts:173-268` and `:1910-1917`, with `int(...)` on the money fields                                                                                                                                  |
| `ventas-report.jsx`     | `netMinorUnits`, `operator_session`                                                                                                                                                                                 | `net`/`netMinorUnits` come from the reports route's own fold in `data.jsx:243-258`; `operator_session` is a sort key, not a field read                                                                                                            |

**Two lessons about the method**, both worth having before the next run:

1. **An empty payload is not evidence.** The diff can only see element keys when the array has
   elements, so a merchant without inventory rows, gift cards or invoices makes a screen look
   broken. When the live sample is empty the mapper is the authority — `AS "alias"` in the
   repository, or the object the service builds — and that is where each row above was settled.
2. **A route that refuses unknown keys is doing you a favour.** `GET /operations/reports/sales`
   answers `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with `fieldErrors: {"$":["Unrecognized key(s) in object: 'from','to'"]}`
   when handed the wrong parameters — the browser surface validates that query strictly, which is
   how I learned it takes `range` (the parameter `data.jsx:576` already sends) rather than a date
   pair. Of the browser routes sampled, this one is the strictest and the cleanest.

### 29.1 A new lens, and it is clean too: the stock ledger checks under a lock

§8 found the wallet's daily limits read in one transaction and spent in another. The same lens
applied to the inventory path is clean, and the contrast is instructive — `merchant.append_stock_ledger`
(`36_pos_inventory.sql:596-700`) takes the item `FOR SHARE` and the balance row **`FOR UPDATE`**
before it reads a single quantity, and only then:

- refuses `reserved`/`damaged`/`quarantine` going negative (`INVENTORY_SOURCE_STATE_INSUFFICIENT`);
- refuses negative stock (`NEGATIVE_STOCK_BLOCKED`) unless the item's policy is `manager_override`
  **and** a `runtime.elevation_grant` exists that is scoped to the merchant and location, carries
  the permission `inventory.negative_stock.override`, matches the command's **fingerprint**, and has
  been **consumed by this command** (`consumed_by_command_id`, `consumed_at is not null`);
- writes the ledger row with an `ON CONFLICT` idempotency guard and rejects a replayed command whose
  fingerprint differs (`IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`);
- and only then moves the balance, and only if the inserted sequence is exactly the next one.

Check-then-write under a row lock, an override that requires a consumed, fingerprint-matched
authorization, and idempotency by fingerprint: nothing to fix.

## 30. The `SECURITY DEFINER` lens: fifty functions, three guard idioms, one deliberate exception

**Severity: none (clean; one hardening note).** This is the lens where a silent privilege
escalation hides: a `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs as its owner, so inside it RLS is off and the
table privileges of the caller do not apply — the body is the whole guard. Two things make one
dangerous: no `search_path` (a caller who can create objects in an earlier schema hijacks it), and
a parameter the function _trusts_ (a merchant id, a staff id, a location id) with nothing
comparing it to the caller's own scope.

**Fifty definitions across the chain, and the first half is uniformly clean:**

| Check                                                                                                      | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SECURITY DEFINER` function definitions in `docs/migration/build-v3/**` (including the forward migrations) | **50**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| without an explicit `set search_path`                                                                      | **0**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `search_path` values in use                                                                                | `pg_catalog,merchant,runtime,umi` · `pg_catalog,merchant,umi` · `pg_catalog,merchant` · `pg_catalog,umi` · `pg_catalog, extensions` · `umi,merchant,pg_temp` · `runtime,merchant,umi,pg_temp` — every one starts from `pg_catalog`, none leaves `public` reachable |

**The second half — "does it trust its parameters?" — resolves into three idioms**, and all three
are real guards:

| Idiom                                       | Example                                                                                                                                                                            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Compare against the transaction's own scope | `merchant.append_stock_ledger` (`36_pos_inventory.sql:581-591`)                                                                                                                    | `raise 'INVENTORY_CONTEXT_REQUIRED'` when no context, then `INVENTORY_MERCHANT_SCOPE`, `INVENTORY_LOCATION_SCOPE` against it                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| The same, through the helper pair           | `merchant.create_or_recover_pos_cart` (`64_pos_cart_recovery.sql:57-63`)                                                                                                           | `if umi.current_merchant() is null … POS_CART_CONTEXT_REQUIRED` · `if p_merchant_id is distinct from umi.current_merchant() … POS_CART_MERCHANT_SCOPE` · the same for the location — _"Fail closed before anything is written: the caller may not name a merchant or a location other than the one its transaction is scoped to"_ |
| Delegate to a scope asserter                | `merchant.store_gift_card_secret_delivery` / `reveal_gift_card_secret_delivery` (`38_pos_customer_value_closeout.sql:198,213`, redefined in `44_dashboard_operational_wiring.sql`) | first statement is `perform merchant.assert_customer_value_write_scope(p_merchant_id, p_device_id)` — the crypto path checks scope before it touches a ciphertext                                                                                                                                                                 |

**One exception, and it is deliberate.** `umi.resolve_staff_permissions(p_staff_id)`
(`35_pos_pilot_rbac.sql:842`, again in `49_merchant_roles.sql:225`) takes only a staff uuid and
compares it to nothing — it cannot, because its job is to _compute_ the permissions of the session
being established, before any scope exists to compare against. It is granted to `api,worker`, so its
safety is a property of its callers, and I read all eight: every one passes an id taken from a row
the same statement already scoped — `pos-entry.repository.ts:75,127,294,337,458,529` (`s.id`/`ms.id`
from a merchant- and location-filtered join), `pos-cash.repository.ts:2037`, and
`auth.repository.ts:979` (the operator's own staff row). That is the same shape as §10's
`PgService.query` note: a capability whose safety rests on the caller, working today, with no
second lock behind it.

Two of those call sites are worth naming, because they are the ones where the id is _not_ the
caller's own and the guard therefore matters most: `pos-entry.repository.ts:458` resolves a
**manager's** id supplied by the request, but the same statement requires `ms.user_id = $1 AND
ms.merchant_id = $3 AND (ms.location_id IS NULL OR ms.location_id = $4)`, so a foreign uuid matches
no row and the permission check never runs on it; and `:75` is the deliberate cross-merchant
discovery read before an operator picks a café — commented as such, on the worker pool, keyed to the
authenticated user. Both are the pattern working, not the pattern missing.

**A correction to my own first pass, because it is the same lesson as §29's.** The first run of this
sweep flagged **eleven** definitions as unchecked. Two were the gift-card pair, whose guard is a
delegated `assert_…_scope` call; two were `create_or_recover_pos_cart`, guarded through
`umi.current_merchant()`; the rest were duplicates of functions counted twice across files. The
checker was only as good as the guard _shapes it knew_ — it looked for `current_setting` and missed
helper functions that read the same setting. A sweep that reports "unchecked" has to say which
guard shapes it recognises, or its hits are noise.

## 31. Two more lenses closed: `ON CONFLICT` against partial indexes, and the last of the POS catch blocks

**Severity: none (both clean; the numbers are the point).**

### 31.1 Every `ON CONFLICT` finds its arbiter — partial predicates included

`INSERT … ON CONFLICT (cols)` fails at runtime (`42P10`, "no unique or exclusion constraint
matching") when the column list matches no unique index — and a **partial** unique index only
counts when the statement repeats the index's `WHERE` predicate. Both halves are silent until the
statement runs, which is why an unexercised retry path is exactly where it would hide.

| Measured over the whole chain and the API source                           | Count   |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `ON CONFLICT (…)` clauses                                                  | **118** |
| partial unique indexes in the schema                                       | **44**  |
| clauses targeting a partial index **without** repeating its predicate      | **0**   |
| clauses whose `(table, columns)` matches **no** unique index on that table | **0**   |

And the predicate is not merely present, it is **the same predicate**: of the 118 clauses, the 11
that name a partial index's columns _and_ carry a `WHERE` were compared against the index's own
`indpred` from the catalogue, normalising `= ANY (ARRAY[…])` against `in (…)`, quoting, casts and
outer parentheses — **0 mismatches**. A near-miss here would be a `42P10` at runtime, so this is the
half of the check that actually protects the retry paths.

That comparison took two runs to be honest: the first reported **11 mismatches, all of them its own
fault** — the catalogue returns the index predicate wrapped in parentheses, and my clause capture
stopped at the first `)`, so `external_ref IS NOT NULL` was being compared as
`external_refisnotnull` against `(external_refisnotnull)`. Third instance this round of the same
rule: when a sweep reports a wall of hits, suspect the sweeper first.

The second row's check is only worth anything because it was run against the **catalogue**, not
against a parser: `pg_index` join `pg_attribute` on `umi_acl_head` gives 468 unique indexes and
constraints, primary keys included. My first pass compared against a regex over the DDL and reported
**78** mismatches — every one of them an artefact (primary keys and table-level `unique (…)`
constraints were invisible to it). Same lesson as §29 and §30, third instance: the checker was only
as good as the shapes it knew, and the fix was to ask the database instead of reading the file.

The one corner that needed a hand-check: for an index on an **expression** — `merchant.inventory_recipe`
and `merchant.inventory_catalog_mapping` are unique on `(merchant_id, product_id, coalesce(variant_id,
'000…'))` — the catalogue's `indkey` shows the underlying columns, not the expression, so a clause
written with plain columns would have _looked_ like a match while Postgres would refuse it. All three
inserts into those two tables are **plain inserts** with no `ON CONFLICT` (the duplicate surfaces as a
normal unique violation the service maps to `INVENTORY_RECIPE_*`), so the corner is empty rather than
unchecked.

**The other half of "partial": entering the predicate later.** A partial unique index also has to
hold when a row _moves into_ its predicate by `UPDATE` — the classic way a "one active row" rule is
quietly broken. Checked on the index that carries the most weight, `pos_cart (merchant_id,
location_id, operator_user_id) WHERE lifecycle_state in ('building_cart','ready_for_checkout','recovered')`:

| Path into the predicate                  | Finding                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pos-cart.repository.ts:380` (`prepare`) | moves `building_cart`/`recovered` → `ready_for_checkout` — **both sides inside the predicate**, so the row already held the slot                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `pos-cart.repository.ts:751` (`bump`)    | moves `building_cart`/`ready_for_checkout`/`recovered` → `building_cart` — same, the guarded `IN` list is the predicate                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `INSERT INTO merchant.pos_cart`          | exactly **two** statements in the whole tree (`64_pos_cart_recovery.sql:69` and its rollback at `66_…:98`), both inside `create_or_recover_pos_cart`, both carrying the matching `ON CONFLICT … WHERE lifecycle_state in (…) DO UPDATE` — so a second active cart is _recovered_, never duplicated |

There is no path into the predicate that does not already hold the slot, and one writer for the
creation itself.

### 31.2 The POS's fifty silent catches: all read, all deliberate

§10 withdrew the money-path ones and §24/§29 read the twenty in the two densest files. This closes the
set: **all fifty, across twenty files.** They fall into four kinds, and not one of them is a swallow:

| Kind                                                  | Examples                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Surface it to the operator                            | `hardware_surface.dart` (11 sites, each `_failed(...)` or `_error`), `catalog_surface.dart:1561` (`catalogUnexpectedError`), `recovery_center.dart` (two notices), `sale_surface.dart:564` — _"The operator asked a question and gets an answer either way"_                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Convert it to a typed state                           | `bootstrap_controller.dart` → `unrecoverableFailure`; `prep_list_controller.dart` → a failure phase with `error.code`; `offline_journal.dart` → `OfflineJournalException('journal_integrity_failed')`; `table_state_controller.dart` and `cash_controller.dart:1001` — _"ANYTHING ELSE STILL HAS TO RELEASE THE SURFACE"_                                                                                                                                                    |
| Decide by physical consequence, not by exception type | `usb_printer_transport.dart`: a `TimeoutException` is `unknown` (the command must **never** be retried blindly — the `HardwareSideEffect` invariant of §11, implemented where it actually matters), and anything else is _"No permission, unplugged printer, a claim that failed: nothing reached the printer, so the command is safe to send again"_                                                                                                                        |
| Deliberately silent, and says why                     | `composition_root.dart` (bounded poll recovers, _"Financial state is unchanged"_), `kitchen_board_controller.dart:452` (an advisory count), `frequent_products.dart` (_"A failed write just means the rail misses this add; never block a sale"_), `storage.dart` (a health probe answers `unavailable`), `checkout_controller.dart:1080,1124` (_"Cash only, exactly as a location with no policy is. The charge itself still decides, so this never invents a permission"_) |

Nothing to fix. What is worth keeping is the pattern the USB transport uses: classify by what the
hardware _did_, not by which exception was thrown — that is the difference between a retry that
duplicates a receipt and one that does not.
