## 43. The accessibility gate's "0 violations on 24 routes" is the login page, swept twenty-four times

**Severity: med-high (instrument — it is the only accessibility check in the tree, the
`ux-sweep` README calls `pnpm ux:verify` the standing loop, and its own header calls
the verdict a HARD GATE). Measured 2026-10-08 20:00–20:20 local.**

**Symptom.** `pnpm ux:a11y:report` finished green: 24 routes, 0 serious, 0 critical, exit 0.
Every one of those 24 loads landed on `/login`.

| Fact                                                                                                                                                        | Where                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/tmp/ux/a11y.json`: **24 routes, all 24 with `"url": "http://127.0.0.1:4000/login"`**, identical `passCount: 30`, `failingRoutes: []`, `totals.serious: 0` | run at 20:03 (`a11y-run2.log`)                                 |
| The gate records `page.url()` and never compares it with the route it asked for; the verdict counts only `violations`                                       | `accessibility-gate.mjs:118`, `:148`, `:170`, `:220`           |
| The README states the requirement — the Chromium must be "already signed in, because the Dashboard needs a session and the sweep must not log in as anyone" | `tools/ux-sweep/README.md:5-8`                                 |
| No workflow mentions `ux:` at all, so `ux:verify` (and this gate inside it) never runs in CI                                                                | `rg -c 'ux:' .github/workflows/*.yml` → no match, 10 workflows |
| The docstring's dated claim — "The serious count reached zero on 2026-09-16" — predates the file itself, which landed 2026-09-18 (`5d9fd28`)                | `accessibility-gate.mjs:9-12`                                  |

**The same gate, run against a signed-in browser, is not clean.** Signed into the CDP
profile (`/tmp/ux/chrome-profile`) as `hola@umiconsulting.co`, the identical command:

| Measure                                                                       | Result                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Routes with a serious finding                                                 | **22 of 24** (`/cafes` and the login page are the two clean ones)                                          |
| Rule tally                                                                    | `color-contrast` 22 findings / **209 nodes**; `heading-order` 2 (moderate); `empty-table-header` 1 (minor) |
| Nodes axe could not judge at all (`incomplete`, usually text over a gradient) | 20–40 per route — the 209 is a floor, not a ceiling                                                        |
| Re-run with `--settle 9000` on four routes                                    | identical node counts (3 / 36 / 14 / 22) — not an animation artefact                                       |

A gate that cannot tell "the screen rendered" from "the session was gone" reports the
second as health. The 24 identical `passCount: 30` values are the fingerprint: one page,
measured 24 times.

**A second nondeterminism in the same file: the gate pins neither the theme nor the
language.** The visual spec pins both (`visual-regression.spec.mjs` `pinTheme`/`pinLocale`)
and its comment records the cost of not doing it — an unpinned locale failed four of ten
baselines. The numbers above are the **dark** palette, because that is what this browser's
OS preference resolved to (`data-theme` absent, `prefers-color-scheme: dark`); the same
command on a light-profile machine reports 0 serious on the four routes re-measured in
§44, which is a different, and equally unpinned, truth.

**Fix.**

1. Assert where the browser landed. If `page.url()` is not `BASE + route`, that is a
   finding, not a pass — at minimum fail on `/login` when `/login` was not the request.
2. Sign in as part of the harness (`storageState` from the same credential the other
   sweeps use, `UMI_SWEEP_EMAIL`/`UMI_SWEEP_PASSWORD`) instead of depending on a human
   having opened a window first. `dashboard-shots.mjs` already signs in in-page; the
   accessibility gate is the one that did not.
3. Put the gate in a workflow. Today the only accessibility instrument in the repository
   is also the only one that cannot run unattended.

## 44. In the dark theme, two colour tokens fail: `--ink-3` at 4.21:1 and `--umi-navy` used as ink at 1.59:1

**Severity: med (every dashboard screen in the dark theme; the read-only chips on Ajustes
are effectively invisible there). The default light theme — `umi`, the palette `:root`
serves — is clean on all four routes re-measured. Both failures are arithmetic, not
opinion: WCAG 2.1 AA wants 4.5:1 for text under 18.66px.**

**The same four routes, measured in both palettes** (axe, 1280×720, signed in):

| Route       | `umi` (default light) | `dark`                                                         |
| ----------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/`         | 0 nodes               | 3 nodes — `#727b8f on #0f1728`                                 |
| `/settings` | 0 nodes               | 9 nodes — 5× `#727b8f on #0f1728`, **4× `#223979 on #111a2e`** |
| `/products` | 0 nodes               | 22 nodes                                                       |
| `/reportes` | 0 nodes               | 11 nodes                                                       |

So the palette is the variable, not the markup. The dark theme's neutral ink does not clear
the dark theme's own surface. `--ink-3` is
`#727B8F` in dark (`packages/tokens/dist/dashboard.css:84`, source
`packages/tokens/tokens/dashboard.json:70-73`) against `--surface: #0F1728`; **axe's number
and mine agree at 4.21:1**.

| Token   | Theme | Colour    | On `--surface` | On `--canvas-2` | Verdict                             |
| ------- | ----- | --------- | -------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `ink-3` | dark  | `#727B8F` | 4.21:1         | 4.37:1          | fails AA                            |
| `ink-4` | dark  | `#565E70` | 2.75:1         | 2.88:1          | fails AA and the 3:1 non-text floor |
| `ink-4` | light | `#7D8AAE` | 3.43:1         | 3.04:1          | fails AA                            |
| `ink-3` | light | `#5C678F` | 5.54:1         | 4.90:1          | passes                              |

The tree already knows the `ink-4` half of this — `styles.css:4143-4148` records that the
`.no-value` em-dash "was drawn in `--ink-4` inline, which failed the text-contrast bar" and
was moved to `--ink-3`. The `ink-3` half was never measured, and it is the one carrying
the volume: in a sample of eight routes, **79 of the flagged nodes** were `#727B8F` on
`#0F1728` at 11–13.5px, i.e. every small caption, label and meta line on the surface.

The second defect is a token used as ink that is not an ink. `.chip.read`
(`styles.css:1665-1670`) paints `color: var(--umi-navy)` over `rgba(34, 57, 121, 0.08)`,
and `--umi-navy` is a fixed `:root` value (`#223979`, `dashboard.css:5`) with **no dark
override** — the dark blocks list every other token but not this one. Measured in the
live dark theme:

| Screen       | Node                                                                             | Ratio      |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| Ajustes      | `.chip.read` × 4 — `umi.app/onca`, `ONC · ••••`, `#B5605A`, `#E8C9A3`, 13–13.5px | **1.59:1** |
| Dispositivos | a `.chip` at 10px                                                                | **1.70:1** |

Other `--umi-navy` sites do carry dark overrides (`styles.css:77`, `:94` switch to
`--umi-blue`), which is why this reads as an omission rather than a design choice — and
`--umi-blue: #7692CB` already exists in the dark theme at 5.75:1 on the same surface.

**Fix.**

1. Give the dark theme a legible `--ink-3`. `#7E8799` measures 4.95:1 on `#0F1728`,
   5.14:1 on `--canvas-2` and 5.41:1 on `--canvas` — it clears AA on all three surfaces
   without collapsing into `--ink-2`.
2. Decide what `--ink-4` is for. If it is not for text, say so the way the `.no-value`
   comment does and keep it out of `color:` (eight rules still set it); if it is, it needs
   a value that passes in both themes.
3. Add the dark override for `--umi-navy` (`--umi-blue` is already the dark ink) or switch
   `.chip.read` to an ink token.
4. Make the tokens' own CI measure what it ships: `.github/workflows/tokens-ci.yml` is a
   required check, it regenerates `dist/` and runs 8 parity tests — **none of them looks
   at contrast** (`packages/tokens/test/tokens.test.mjs`). A per-theme `ink × surface`
   ratio table with a 4.5 floor turns §44 into a red check instead of a screenshot review.

## 45. `UX_WORKSPACE` is pinned to the author's home directory, so the whole `ux:*` family is dead anywhere else

**Severity: low-med (portability of the instrument family — 16 `package.json` scripts
declare `ux:*`, and ten of the harnesses behind them share this line).**

Ten harnesses resolve their own dependencies through a hard-coded path:

`const WORKSPACE = process.env.UX_WORKSPACE || '/home/jc/umi';`

| File                                    | Line |
| --------------------------------------- | ---- |
| `tools/ux-sweep/accessibility-gate.mjs` | 48   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/click-audit.mjs`        | 66   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/click-inventory.mjs`    | 46   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/flow-budget.mjs`        | 45   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/perf-throttle.mjs`      | 79   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/memory-shift.mjs`       | 53   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/trace-flow.mjs`         | 40   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/trace-screencast.mjs`   | 40   |
| `tools/ux-sweep/pos-surfaces.mjs`       | 145  |
| `tools/ux-sweep/devtools-probe.mjs`     | 26   |

(`floor-plan-map.spec.mjs:23` carries the same path, as the copy-pasteable "Run: cd
…" line in its header comment.)

On any machine that is not that one — this workstation included — the `createRequire`
resolves from a directory that does not exist, and the script dies before it measures
anything:

```
$ env -u UX_WORKSPACE node tools/ux-sweep/accessibility-gate.mjs --no-fail --routes /login
Error: Cannot find module '@playwright/test'
Require stack:
- /home/jc/umi/noop.js
```

With `UX_WORKSPACE=/home/juan/Projects/umiconsulting/umi` the same command runs. Every one
of the §43/§44 measurements was taken with that variable exported by hand.

**Fix.** Resolve from the repository, not from a path: `createRequire(import.meta.url)`
with a relative `require` (`import { createRequire } from 'node:module'` and
`createRequire(new URL('../../package.json', import.meta.url))`), or read the workspace
root from `process.cwd()`. Then delete `UX_WORKSPACE` from the documented recipe.

`@kalalacafe.mx` user the sweep documents (`pos-surfaces.mjs:70-71`,
`LOCAL_VERIFICATION_PLAYBOOK.md:22-26`) exists in that database. `super_admin` is
deliberately not in `ROLE_LANDING`; it takes `FALLBACK_ORDER`, whose first entry is
`customers` (`role-landing.js:79-85`, `:136-146`) — so **`/` renders the Customers screen**
on this box:

```
after goto(/):            http://127.0.0.1:4000/customers
after goto(/operations):  http://127.0.0.1:4000/operations
after goto(/) again:      http://127.0.0.1:4000/customers
```

The `overview` baseline is an Overview of **Kalala Café · CONGRESO · WED, SEP 16** signed
in as `AD Admin` — a different tenant, a different date and a different role from the one
the gate now runs against. The harness never asserts identity or the landed route, so it
reports a pixel diff and leaves the cause unnamed.

**3. The borrowed profile carries the person's own browser state into the diff.** The
`login` pair fails by 0.04–0.05 of all pixels, and the diff image says why: both fields are
**autofilled** with the credentials saved when the other sweeps signed in, against a
baseline whose email box shows the grey placeholder `admin@tunegocio.mx` and whose password
box is empty. The spec pins the theme and the language and documents why
(`pinTheme`/`pinLocale`), but nothing pins "no saved password in this profile".

Remaining diffs: `overview` 0.03–0.04, `reportes` 0.03–0.05, `operations` (terminal) 0.03
(`/tmp/ux/playwright-results/*/error-context.md`). `operations` (tablet) and both
`floor-plan` tests passed.

**4. `ux:visual` is not only the visual gate.** The config sets `testDir: '.'` with
`testMatch: '**/*.spec.mjs'` (`playwright.config.mjs:14-15`), so the 700-line
`floor-plan-map.spec.mjs` — 200 tables, a slow drag and a rotate — is collected too, and
those two tests are two of the thirteen failures. The package script sells the command as
the visual baselines.

**Fix.**

1. Re-record against the routes the app renders, after deleting the two `catalog-inventory`
   baselines; add a check that every `.png` in the directory is named by a route in the
   spec, and that every route has one.
2. Assert before screenshotting: the landed URL equals `route.path` (with `/` resolved
   through `landingRouteFor`) and the signed-in identity is the one the baselines were
   recorded as. Both are one line each and both failures above become named errors.
3. Run the visual gate in its own browser (`UX_VISUAL_LAUNCH=1` + `UX_STORAGE_STATE`, which
   the spec already supports) instead of borrowing a profile that has a saved password,
   a language choice and an OS theme of its own.
4. Narrow `testMatch` to `visual-regression.spec.mjs`, or move the floor-plan performance
   spec to its own config, so the two instruments stop sharing one verdict.
5. Put it in a workflow. Nine of these thirteen failures are older than the CI that would
   have caught them on the first run after the rename.

## 47. Three more lenses closed: post-sale money (clean, one hardening), the ingress ceiling (withdrawn), and the two instruments that had never been run

### 47.1 Post-sale refunds and voids: clean at three levels, with one hardening item in the database

The dashboard's `/reportes/reembolsos` path (`pos-exception`) is the half of the money path the
rest of this hunt had not touched. Read end to end and checked against the live database:

| Guarantee                                                             | Where it is enforced                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Two concurrent refunds of one sale cannot both pass their checks      | `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('sale_exception:'‖saleId))` before the sale version and exception count are read (`pos-exception.repository.ts:678-706`); the loser gets `OPTIMISTIC_VERSION_CONFLICT` or `STALE_PREVIEW` |
| The approval the preview advertises is required, not suggested        | `if (preview.approvalRequired) { if (!dto.approvalId) throw APPROVAL_REQUIRED … }` (`:797-824`), with the cash threshold from policy (`:530`, `cashRefundThreshold`)                                                              |
| A provider-captured card tender cannot be refunded on a person's word | the handed-in attempt must be a `succeeded` refund **of the capture that paid that tender**, with a provider refund id, covering the amount (`:719-760`)                                                                          |
| The books cannot be over-refunded                                     | trigger `pos_tender_compensation_limit`: `prior + new > source_amount` raises (`docs/migration/build-v3/34_pos_exception.sql:492-506`)                                                                                            |
| A compensation cannot be edited or deleted                            | `*_append_only` triggers on the five post-sale tables (`:508-528`)                                                                                                                                                                |

**Those triggers exist in the live database, not only in the migration.** Asked of `umi_local`:

```
pos_cash_compensation_append_only   pos_cash_compensation_binding   pos_exception_approval_binding
pos_sale_exception_append_only      pos_tender_compensation_append_only  pos_tender_compensation_limit
```

**The hardening item.** The limit trigger locks its source row with `FOR SHARE`
(`34_pos_exception.sql:499`). Shared locks are compatible with each other, so two concurrent
inserts for the same tender each read `prior_amount = 0` — the other's row is uncommitted and
invisible in READ COMMITTED — and both pass. The trigger is therefore a correct backstop for
_sequential_ over-refund and **not** a concurrency guard; the anti-double-refund property rests
entirely on the service's advisory lock, one level up. That is the right order of authority, but
it means the table's own invariant is only as strong as every future writer's memory. One word
fixes it: `FOR SHARE` → `FOR UPDATE` on that row, which serialises the two inserts and makes the
trigger true on its own.

### 47.2 The ingress rate limit: withdrawn as a finding

The lead came from a real measurement — `pnpm ux:first-paint` logged **23 × 429** across the
sweep — and the guard's own comment says a café's dashboard and its tills share one address
bucket (`ip-rate-limit.guard.ts:12-34`). Chased to the end, it does not hold:

| Question                                           | Answer, measured                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What ceiling applies to a till?                    | The till sends `authorization: Bearer <access token>` (`apps/umi-pos/lib/core/network/api_client.dart`), which `verifiedUserId` accepts → **`RATE_LIMIT_IP_AUTHENTICATED_PER_MINUTE`, default 3000**, not the anonymous 300 (`config.schema.ts:133-146`) |
| How much can the dashboard consume?                | Three dashboard screens left open and idle for 60 s: **50 API requests** (`/` 24, `/cash-shifts` 15, `/kitchen` 11)                                                                                                                                      |
| What does the till show if it ever does get a 429? | A named message, not a generic failure: `RATE_LIMITED` → `operatorPinRateLimited` (`entry_surface.dart:327`, `catalog_surface.dart:3182`), and `operator_error_message.dart:40` for the rest                                                             |

Starving a signed-in till would take >3000 requests/minute from one address. The 429s this
workstation produced were the guard doing its documented job against a sweep that hammers 24
routes, and the instrument counted and printed every one of them. Recorded so the next hunter
does not spend a pass on it.

### 47.3 The flow budget and the first-paint budget: run for the first time, both healthy

`pnpm ux:flows` (nine dashboard flows with a tap budget and a millisecond budget each) and
`pnpm ux:first-paint` (`ux:verify`'s own step) had never been run on this machine.

| Flow                         | Measured           | Budget   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------ | -------- |
| shell-open-orders            | 1 tap, 251 ms      | 1 / 3000 |
| reportes-open-refunds        | 2 taps, 487 ms     | 2 / 4000 |
| cash-open-registers          | 2 taps, 488 ms     | 2 / 4000 |
| products-to-inventory        | 1 tap, 229 ms      | 1 / 2500 |
| catalog-open-create-product  | 1 tap, 235 ms      | 1 / 2500 |
| orders-filter-in-preparation | 1 tap, 234 ms      | 1 / 2500 |
| orders-switch-channel        | 1 tap, 239 ms      | 1 / 2500 |
| customers-search             | 1 tap, 816 ms      | 1 / 3000 |
| customers-open-profile       | **not measurable** | 1 / 3000 |

Eight of nine inside budget, with the step effects holding (`expectUrl`, `aria-pressed`, `class`
containing `on`, the typed value). The ninth fails on a precondition rather than a UI defect: the
flow clicks `button.customer-row`, and this database has **no customers** — the screen says "0
customers / No customers found", which is the same empty dataset §46 traced. Worth one line in
the budget file so the instrument reports "not measurable here", never "failed".

First paint, all 24 dashboard routes, no throttling: **median FCP 172 ms, median load 131 ms,
0 degraded shells, 0 failures**, slowest route `/login` at 336 ms. The plan's "loads in less than
1 second" holds with room to spare on this box — which says nothing about the reference tablet
until `pnpm ux:perf` (slow-4g + 4× CPU) is run on it.

## 48. The whole POS database-check family is dead: a frozen migration list, and then a fixture the current constraints refuse

**Severity: med (eleven documented verification commands, and the properties they were written to
prove — device scoping fails closed, a revoked device cannot replay, history is append-only —
have therefore never been executed against the schema that is actually in the tree). Measured
2026-10-08 20:30–20:35 against a disposable database.**

Eleven commands route into `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh`: the eight
`scripts/umi-pos-*-db-check.sh` wrappers (sale, checkout, cash, exception, inventory,
device-pairing, offline, customer-value), `scripts/umi-pos-customer-value-concurrency-check.sh:24`,
and the `umi-pos:*-db-check` scripts in `package.json`. Run for the first time:

```
$ PGHOST=127.0.0.1 PGPORT=4003 PGUSER=postgres bash scripts/umi-pos-sale-db-check.sh
== building a disposable build-v3 in umi_pos_check_2837568 ==
  DDL FAILED at 99_verify:
99_verify.sql:1113: ERROR:  missing merchant.table_reservation
```

Two seconds, one database created and dropped, and nothing measured.

**Cause 1 — the file list is frozen at 2026-06 and the verify file is current.** The script applies
an explicit list (`scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:103`) that stops at `62_floor_plan`, then runs
`99_verify.sql`. The chain's own runner carries the full list
(`docs/migration/build-v3/00_run.sh:8`, 50 entries through `79_cycle_anchor`); the verifier's copy
is missing 27 of them — including `65_table_reservation`, which is the exact table
`99_verify.sql:1113` then asks for. The error message names the verify file, which is the one place
the fault is _not_.

**Cause 2 — with the list fixed, the fixtures are stale against a constraint added later.** Copied
the script to `/tmp`, replaced its list with `00_run.sh`'s and ran it against a fresh disposable
database (`umi_pos_hunt_check`):

| Result                            | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 21 assertions **PASS**            | merchant isolation (3), location narrowing (3), device scoping fails closed (4), append-only (2), audit hash chain (2), offline replay authority (5), revoke ends sessions (2)                                                                                                         |
| Then it stops                     | `ERROR: new row for relation "pos_payment_attempt" violates check constraint "payment_attempt_success_provenance_ck"` under "## 8. Gate 3D exception isolation and immutability"                                                                                                       |
| Why                               | `70_tender.sql:231-232` requires `status <> 'succeeded' or proof_source is not null` — "a success must name which KIND of proof produced it". The fixture inserts `('cash',1000,'MXN','succeeded',false,'gate-3d-pay')` with no `proof_source` (`scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:256-259`) |
| Same fixture family also stale at | `:453` (cash 2000), `:1233` (stored_value), `:1313` (gift_card) — all `succeeded` with no provenance, so sections 8 and beyond cannot get past their own setup                                                                                                                         |

**The constraint is right and the fixture is wrong**, which is the good version of this finding: the
migration states the rule for exactly these rows in its own backfill ("`method = 'cash'` →
`'cash'` — the drawer", `70_tender.sql:190-193`), so the fix is the rule applied to four inserts.

**Fix.**

1. Stop hand-copying the chain. Either read the directory and sort by numeric prefix, or source the
   list from `00_run.sh`; then assert that the applied set equals the directory's contents so the
   next migration cannot silently fall off the end. Same for the 8 wrappers.
2. Give the four `succeeded` fixtures a `proof_source` (`'cash'` for the cash pair,
   `'internal_ledger'` for stored_value and gift_card), following `70_tender.sql`'s own backfill
   table — not a guessed value.
3. Fail loudly on the _list_ rather than on the verify: a missing file in the list should be its own
   error (`DDL list is stale: 65_table_reservation exists in the directory and is not applied`).

**What this says about the tree as a whole.** §24 counted 78 POS scripts no workflow invokes; §46
found one family that fails 13 of 16; this is a third family that fails in two seconds and reports
it as a verify error. They are the same defect wearing three names: verification that is never
executed is not verification, and the instruments that were never run are the ones that quietly
stopped working.

## 49. The same family, made to run: 84 assertions hold, three real disagreements appear, and one fixture contradicts the schema it is checking

**Severity: med (the three disagreements are unverified statements about money authority; the
silent death is an instrument defect). Measured 2026-10-08 20:45–20:55.**

To find out what the family would report if it could run, I copied `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh` to
`/tmp`, replaced its frozen file list with `00_run.sh`'s, and repaired the five fixtures that the
newer schema refuses — four `pos_payment_attempt` rows needing `proof_source` (`'cash'` for the cash
pair, `'internal_ledger'` for stored_value and gift_card, per `70_tender.sql:190-193`) and one
`cash_shift` needing `holding_device_id`/`holding_device_credential_version`. The repository was not
modified. Against a disposable database:

| Section                                                                                                                                                          | Result                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1 merchant isolation, 2 location narrowing, 3 device scoping fails closed, 4 append-only, 5 audit hash chain, 6 offline replay authority, 7 revoke ends sessions | **21 PASS, 0 FAIL** — the load-bearing properties hold on today's schema |
| 8 Gate 3D exception isolation and immutability                                                                                                                   | **24 PASS, 0 FAIL**                                                      |
| 9 Gate 3D.1 pilot RBAC                                                                                                                                           | 2 FAIL (below)                                                           |
| 10 Gate 3E inventory authority                                                                                                                                   | 13 PASS, 1 FAIL (below)                                                  |
| 11 Gate 3F customer value                                                                                                                                        | **cannot start** (below)                                                 |
| Total                                                                                                                                                            | **84 PASS, 3 FAIL, then a silent exit 1**                                |

### 49.1 The reviewed RBAC counts and the schema disagree, and nothing had compared them

```
FAIL  Supervisor receives the exact reviewed grant count (expected '85', got '86')
FAIL  Manager receives the exact reviewed grant count (expected '122', got '128')
PASS  Cashier receives the exact reviewed grant count (48)
```

The check calls these "the exact reviewed grant count" (`scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:664-672`), so
the tree ships a role set that contradicts a reviewed security number. Two different databases
agree on the direction:

| Where                                                | manager | supervisor |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ---------- |
| The reviewed baseline in the check                   | 122     | 85         |
| A fresh build of the chain (my disposable database)  | **128** | **86**     |
| `umi_local` (the database the product is running on) | **129** | **87**     |

Six to seven extra permissions for Manager and one to two for Supervisor. Nothing in the tree says
which side is right, and no gate has compared them since the check was written. One of the two is a
defect: either the grants were widened without the review noticing, or the reviewed number is stale
— and only a person can say which, which is exactly why the number is asserted rather than
described.

**And there is a third number, from the artifact the pilot actually cites.**
`docs/product/UMIPOS_PILOT_RBAC.md:36-44` publishes a "Perfiles canónicos" table with a column
headed **"Grants POS"**: Owner 131, Admin 130, **Manager 120**, **Supervisor 85**, Cashier 48,
Staff 48, Viewer 9, super_admin 0. Three artifacts, three answers for Manager:

| Artifact                                                                 | Manager       | Supervisor | Measure                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `docs/product/UMIPOS_PILOT_RBAC.md:39-40` (the review the pilot cites)   | **120**       | 85         | "Grants POS" — undefined in the file            |
| `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:664-672` ("the exact reviewed grant count") | **122**       | 85         | every row in `umi.role_permission` for the role |
| the schema — fresh chain build / `umi_local`                             | **128 / 129** | 86 / 87    | same as the check                               |

The document's number and the check's number are two different measures wearing one word
("grants"), which is itself the defect that makes the other two unexplainable: with the POS-domain
definition written down nowhere, nobody can say whether Owner's 131 in the document becoming 145 in
the database is growth or a category error. The same-measure comparison is the check's, and it
says Manager grew by six and Supervisor by one — Cashier, the one role the check also asserts, is
exactly 48 in all three places.

### 49.2 One assertion holds a function signature in a string literal

```
FAIL  readonly cannot execute the ledger or projection authority
      (expected 'f|f', got 'ERROR: function "merchant.append_stock_ledger(uuid,…,jsonb)" does not exist)
```

The call is `has_function_privilege('readonly','merchant.append_stock_ledger(uuid,uuid,…,jsonb)','execute')`
(`scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:881-884`) — a 21-argument literal. The function now has **22**
identity arguments: `76_recipes_inventory.sql` added `p_lot_id uuid`, and because it carries a
default the ordinary 21-argument _calls_ in the same section still resolve (that is why 13 other
assertions pass), while the textual signature lookup must name all 22 and therefore errors. The
assertion about a privilege silently became an assertion about a type signature.

### 49.3 Section 11's fixture writes a column the schema refuses to have, and fails silently

```
== 11. Gate 3F customer, loyalty and stored value ==
$ q -c "insert into merchant.loyalty_gift_card(id,merchant_id,code,status,public_reference,
        code_hash,masked_code,currency,amount_cents,customer_id) values(…)" >/dev/null
(nothing printed; exit 1)
```

`merchant.loyalty_gift_card` has **no `code` column**, and that is a design decision stated in the
file that creates it: _"The code is bearer value. Store its SHA-256 digest and a display-safe
suffix. The clear code exists only in the issue response and in the customer's URL"_
(`20_merchant.sql:834-835`). The fixture also writes `masked_code = 'temporary'`, which the table's
own check refuses (`^.{4}-[A-Z0-9]{4}$`, `:837`). The assertion immediately below this fixture is
**"gift-card secret is stored only as a hash"** — the fixture is written against the design the
check exists to prevent. It cannot run against any schema in the tree.

**And it says nothing when it fails.** `q()` merges stderr into stdout
(`scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:66`), and the fixture call then discards both with `>/dev/null`, so
`set -e` turns a failed insert into a bare exit 1. Under `bash -x` the last line before the `cleanup`
trap is the psql invocation itself, with no message after it — the reason is thrown away before
anyone can read it. That is §36's defect (a logger that drops the error it is handed) reproduced in
a verification script.

### 49.4 The family can only be run once per machine

The script creates two cluster-scoped roles unconditionally and discards any error:

```
q -c "create role inventory_api_login inherit; grant api to inventory_api_login;" >/dev/null
q -c "create role customer_value_worker_login inherit; grant worker to customer_value_worker_login;" >/dev/null
```

Its EXIT trap drops the database, never the roles. Measured: the first run created them; the second
run of the same command on the same cluster **died right after `seeded 2 cafés…` with exit 1 and no
output at all** — the only symptom of "role already exists". I dropped the two roles afterwards, so
the cluster is as I found it. The family is single-shot per machine, which is another reason nobody
noticed it was broken.

### 49.5 Fix, in order

1. Take the applied file list from the directory (or from `00_run.sh`) and assert it equals what the
   migration directory holds — §48 cause 1.
2. Five fixture repairs: `proof_source` on four payment attempts, `holding_device_id` on the shift —
   §48 cause 2 and this section.
3. Rewrite section 11's fixture against the real table (`code_hash` + a mask that satisfies its own
   check), since the assertion below it is the point.
4. Replace the 21-argument literal with `pg_get_function_identity_arguments`, so the next parameter
   cannot turn a privilege assertion into a type error.
5. Make the role creation idempotent (`if not exists (select from pg_roles …)`) and drop them in the
   trap; never discard a fixture's stderr.
6. Decide the RBAC question (§49.1) in a commit that says which side moved, and pin the new number.
7. Run this family in CI. It asserts 84 database-level properties in **four seconds**.

## 50. Two more never-run families: one healthy, one gated behind the dead verifier

### 50.1 The KDS concurrency check works, and proves the chain is fine when enumerated properly

`scripts/umi-pos-kds-concurrency-check.sh` is not built like §48's family: it enumerates nothing
itself, it calls `docs/migration/build-v3/00_run.sh` — the runner with the complete list — and it
runs with `ON_ERROR_STOP=1`. Run for the first time on 2026-10-08 20:36:

```
$ PGHOST=127.0.0.1 PGPORT=4003 PGUSER=postgres bash scripts/umi-pos-kds-concurrency-check.sh
99_verify.sql:1113: NOTICE:  umi base tables:     22
99_verify.sql:1113: NOTICE:  merchant base tables:  145
99_verify.sql:1113: NOTICE:  runtime base tables: 27
99_verify.sql:1113: NOTICE:  build-v3 verify: OK
 ✓ src/modules/kds/kds.repository.integration.spec.ts (29 tests) 626ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)      Tests  29 passed (29)
exit=0
```

**Two things follow.** First, the kitchen-order concurrency work is healthy: 29 integration tests
pass against a database built from the chain, on the same machine where the a11y gate, the visual
gate and the DB-check family were all red. Not every unrun script is rotten — this one is fine and
nobody runs it either. Second, `99_verify` passes on a chain built from `00_run.sh`'s list, which is
the independent confirmation that §48's diagnosis is the list and not the schema: same files, same
server, opposite result.

### 50.2 The largest concurrency check in the tree cannot start, and says nothing

`scripts/umi-pos-customer-value-concurrency-check.sh` is **33 KB** — the longest verification script
in the repository, and the one that would exercise the stored-value races (double spend of a wallet,
two cards redeeming one balance, a refund racing an authorization). Measured:

```
$ bash scripts/umi-pos-customer-value-concurrency-check.sh
exit=1        # ~2 s, zero bytes of output
```

Its fourth statement is `UMI_POS_DB_NAME="$DB" UMI_POS_DB_KEEP=1 bash "$ROOT/scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh" >/dev/null`
(`:24`). It inherits both of §48's failures and adds one of its own: the parent's output, including
the DDL error, goes to `/dev/null`, so the whole script reports a bare `exit 1`. Its 33 KB of
assertions have never executed, and when they fail they do not say why. Its own cleanup trap did
drop the database it created (verified: no `umi_pos_value_race_*` left).

**Fix, in one line each.** Point it at the same enumeration the KDS check uses (or at a
`00_run.sh`-enumerated build), and stop discarding the parent's output — a harness that hides its
own setup error will hide the next one too.

## 51. `ux:memory` reports a leak the app does not have — and its own shape cannot see the leak it was built for

**Severity: med (instrument: a false alarm about memory, in the one harness written to find it). A
by-product of chasing it is the strongest negative result in this report, with the numbers in
§51.3.**

### 51.1 What the instrument said

```
$ pnpm ux:memory
baseline: heap 11.7MB, DOM 318 nodes, 209 listeners
t+0.3m: heap 31.5MB, DOM 2400 nodes, 1294 listeners
…
t+2.9m: heap 68.3MB, DOM 3826 nodes, 1527 listeners
still climbing at the end of this 3.1-minute window (heap 7.46 MB/min …) — investigate:
retained over 3.05m: heap 18.7MB, DOM 2358, listeners 1300
(25 429s seen)
```

Read literally that is a dashboard leaking 6 MB a minute on a till that stays open all day. It is
not, and the three checks below say why.

### 51.2 Three measurements that disagree with it

**Same screen, loaded nine times.** `/customers`, `networkidle`, forced GC before every reading:

| Sample     | heap       | nodes   | listeners |
| ---------- | ---------- | ------- | --------- |
| First load | 9.9 MB     | 316     | 183       |
| Ninth load | **9.9 MB** | **316** | **183**   |

Byte-identical. There is no accumulation across loads on this screen at all.

**The same four routes, 172 loads, with readiness waits.** Sampling on `/customers` after GC, the
numbers do not climb — they **oscillate between two states**:

```
t+1.4m  heap 19.6MB  nodes  806  listeners 1120
t+1.5m  heap 24.2MB  nodes 3075  listeners 1341
t+1.6m  heap 22.9MB  nodes 2092  listeners 1252
t+1.8m  heap 19.7MB  nodes  806  listeners 1120
t+2.3m  heap 19.5MB  nodes  806  listeners 1120
t+2.5m  heap 22.2MB  nodes 2093  listeners 1252
```

Two render states of one URL, and the instrument compares its last sample against its first as if
the difference were retention. The cause is in its own output: **25 × 429**. That loop asks for
~70 page loads a minute at ~8 API calls each (~560/min), against the API's per-principal ceiling of
**240/min** (`operational.interceptor.ts:16`, `LIMITS.user = 240`) — so a share of the loads comes
back partially rendered with a smaller DOM, and the "retained" delta is partly "this load got
throttled and that one did not". For the record, the same 429 storm appeared in §47.3's first-paint
run (23 of them), so the sweep's own pacing is above the ceiling in more than one instrument.

**The shape a shift actually has.** A full `page.goto` destroys the document, so per-navigation
leaks cannot survive it — but an operator moves between screens by clicking. Forty-two client-side
navigations (Orders → Reports → Cash and shifts → Kitchen → Customers → Overview, seven rounds),
GB-forced after each round:

| Round     | 1    | 2    | 3    | 4    | 5    | 6    | 7    |
| --------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| heap MB   | 11.3 | 11.5 | 11.6 | 11.7 | 11.7 | 11.7 | 11.8 |
| nodes     | 424  | 412  | 424  | 412  | 424  | 398  | 410  |
| listeners | 196  | 192  | 196  | 192  | 196  | 192  | 196  |

Flat. Within 0.5 MB over six rounds, DOM and listener counts constant — so this is _not_ a leak
result dressed up as one.

### 51.3 The negative result, stated with its bound

**No memory growth is visible in the dashboard under either shape I could drive**: nine identical
loads of one screen, and forty-two client-side navigations across six screens. The bound is the
instrument's own honesty note, and it applies to me too: a three-minute window on a mostly empty
database (0 customers, 0 orders) cannot rule out a leak that needs data volume or hours. What it
does rule out is the specific claim `ux:memory` printed.

### 51.4 Fix, for the instrument and for its siblings

1. **Reject a rate-limited sample instead of averaging it in.** A 429 is a measurement failure: the
   screen never rendered. Either discard the sample and say so, or keep the sweep under
   `LIMITS.user` (240/min) with a pacing calculation rather than a hand-picked `--delay 3000`.
2. **Anchor both ends on the same rendered state.** The instrument already returns to the first
   route before the final sample; it needs the other half — wait for the screen's data to land
   (its baseline is 318 nodes against 3 000+ when the screen is actually painted), and refuse to
   compare samples whose node counts differ by more than a tolerance.
3. **Drive the navigation the way the product is used.** Its own docstring names the leak it is
   looking for — "a subscription re-created per navigation" — and `page.goto` cannot produce one.
   Click the sidebar.

## 52. The reviewed RBAC matrix and the database disagree by name: four roles hold capabilities the review does not list

**Severity: high (money and stock authority, and it is one-directional). Measured 2026-10-08 21:0x
against a fresh chain build and against `umi_local`; the drift is in both.**

§49.1 had three numbers for Manager and no way to say which side was right. There is an authority in
the tree after all: `config/umipos-pilot-role-grants.json` is the pilot RBAC matrix — the file
`docs/product/UMIPOS_PILOT_RBAC.md` publishes, that generates `35_pos_pilot_rbac.sql`, and that
`pnpm umi-pos:check-pilot-rbac` validates (it answers _"Pilot RBAC matrix and generated SQL are
valid."_, exit 0, run today). Its Manager profile lists exactly **120** permissions, matching the
document. The database has 128.

Built a disposable database from the chain, dumped every `umi.role_permission` row, and diffed it
against the matrix **by key**:

| Role                   | In the database but not in the reviewed matrix | Missing from the database                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| owner                  | **10**                                         | 0                                                                                                                                                                             |
| admin                  | **10**                                         | 0                                                                                                                                                                             |
| manager                | **8**                                          | 0                                                                                                                                                                             |
| supervisor             | **1**                                          | 0                                                                                                                                                                             |
| cashier, staff, viewer | 0                                              | 0                                                                                                                                                                             |
| super_admin            | 141                                            | 0 — **by design**: the matrix's `0` means "no _pilot_ grants" for a platform role, and a blanket grant in the chain gives it everything. Recorded so nobody reads it as drift |

The eight capabilities Manager has and the review does not:

```
catalog.manage              inventory.conversion.manage   inventory.invoice.capture
inventory.item.manage       inventory.production.produce  inventory.recipe.manage
register.manage             table_order.credential.manage
```

(owner and admin hold the same ten plus `inventory.recipe.approve` and `inventory.invoice.approve`;
supervisor holds `inventory.production.produce`.)

**Where they come from**, so the fix has an address: `44_dashboard_operational_wiring.sql:8-11`
grants `catalog.manage` and `register.manage` to owner/admin/manager;
`76_recipes_inventory.sql:1039-1056` grants the inventory set to owner/admin/manager (and
`inventory.production.produce` to supervisor as well); `42_pos_kitchen.sql` carries the
`table_order.*` grants.

**Three things follow, and the third is the one to act on.**

1. **The direction is one-way.** No role is missing a grant the matrix declares, and nobody has
   extra authority taken away. Every drift is _more_ power in the database than in the review.
2. **`umi-pos:check-pilot-rbac` passing is not evidence about the database.** It compares the matrix
   with the SQL it generates from the matrix — both sides are the matrix. The grants above arrive
   from three _other_ migration files, which that check never reads. A gate that validates an
   artifact against itself cannot see the schema grow past it.
3. **The only check that could have caught it asserts a third number and cannot run** — §48's frozen
   file list, and §49.1's `122`/`85` baseline, which matches neither the matrix (120/85) nor the
   schema (128/86).

**Fix.** Make the matrix the single source and _check the database against it_: a gate that reads
`config/umipos-pilot-role-grants.json` and asserts the `umi.role_permission` set per role, run in the
same disposable-database CI step §48 asks for. Then the choice is explicit and reviewable — either
the eight capabilities belong to Manager (update the matrix and the pilot document in the same
commit, which is the review) or they do not (delete the grants from `44`/`42`, or move them behind
the approval boundary the matrix's `approvals` file describes).

## 53. The click inventory, run for the first time: 852 controls, none unnamed, and seventeen below the project's own 44 px touch floor

**Severity: low-med (touch targets on the café tablet; nothing checks the floor, so the seventeen
have been there for as long as the screens have).** `pnpm ux:inventory`, all 24 dashboard routes,
1280×720, 2026-10-08 21:1x:

| Across 24 routes           | Count   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Clickable controls         | **852** |
| Without an accessible name | **0**   |
| Below the 44×44 px floor   | **17**  |
| Disabled                   | 21      |
| Console errors             | 0       |

Zero unnamed controls out of 852 is worth stating plainly: whatever else is wrong, the dashboard's
accessible names are complete, and the instrument that says so had never been run either.

**The seventeen, by screen** (`/tmp/ux/inventory.md`, sizes in px):

| Screen         | Control                                                         | Size                   | Family                                              |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `/reportes`    | `Product` 39×17, `Units` 26×17, `Net sales ▼` 58×17             | 17 px tall             | table sort headers — the tap target _is_ the header |
| `/cash-shifts` | `on` (a switch) **13×13**                                       | smallest in the report | custom toggle                                       |
| `/cash-shifts` | `Search drawer or operator` 178×20                              | 20 px tall             | text input                                          |
| `/inventory`   | `All 0`, `Low stock 0`, `No cost 0`, `No stock 0`, `Archived 0` | 32 px tall             | filter chips                                        |
| `/inventory`   | `Open commands` 42×44                                           | 2 px narrow            | chip                                                |
| `/staff`       | `Actions for Cocina KDS` ×4 (one per row)                       | 40×44                  | row action button                                   |
| `/settings`    | `Birthday gift`, `Self-registration`                            | 44×26                  | toggles                                             |

Three families, three fixes: give the sortable `<th>` a ≥44 px inner target (padding, not a bigger
font), put the chips and toggles on the 32→44 ladder the token already defines, and widen the 40×44
row-action buttons by four pixels. The 13×13 switch is the one to look at first — it is smaller than
the OS's own minimum for a control that changes settings.

**And it is a report, not a gate.** `click-inventory.mjs` exits 0 on its findings
(`:128`; exit 1 is reserved for the harness itself failing), and no workflow runs it (§24), so the
17 are visible only to somebody who asks. `packages/tokens` already has a test asserting the
_token_ is at least 44 px — the floor exists and is checked as a value; nothing checks that the
screens use it.

### 53.1 The sibling classifier, cross-checked against the same 861 controls

`pnpm ux:click-audit` (classification only — it clicks nothing without
`UX_CLICK_CONFIRM=disposable`) over the same 24 routes: **861 controls, 30 classified
destructive/disabled**, concentrated where the work is — `/floor-plan` 13 (the plan-mutation and
publish families), `/settings` 7, then one or two each on `/operations`, `/kitchen`, `/products`,
`/inventory`, `/hours`, `/profile`, `/diagnostics`, `/login`.

## 54. `ux:perf` measures the dev server against a production budget — and the production bundle really does miss it

**Severity: med (a documented plan claim — "loads in less than 1 second" on the reference tablet —
measured false on the honest target, with the cause in one file). Measured 2026-10-08 21:2x.**

### 54.1 What the instrument printed at its default target

`pnpm ux:perf` (`perf-throttle.mjs --network slow-4g --cpu 4`, all 24 routes, `UX_BASE` defaulting to
the dev server on `:4000`):

```
median FCP 9860ms, median load 9261ms; 0 degraded shell(s), 0 429(s), 0 failure(s)
No: 24 route(s) missed 1000 ms to first contentful paint and 24 missed it to the load event
```

Every route misses the budget by ~10×. **And every route misses it by the same amount**: FCP spans
9844–9870 ms (26 ms of spread across 24 different screens), the load event 9254–9269 ms (15 ms).
A per-screen measurement with no per-screen variation is not measuring the screens — it is
measuring the one thing they all share, which on a Vite dev server is the unbundled module graph.
The instrument reports "24 missed" and never says which target it measured (§51.4's problem in
another harness: numbers without their subject).

### 54.2 The same instrument, the same throttle, against the production build

Built the dashboard (`VITE_UMI_ENVIRONMENT=development pnpm --filter @umi/dashboard build`), served
the output with `vite preview` on `:4010`, signed in, and re-ran the identical profile on three
routes:

| Target                         | FCP (median) | Load (median) | Shell mounted |
| ------------------------------ | ------------ | ------------- | ------------- |
| Vite dev server, 24 routes     | 9860 ms      | 9261 ms       | 11150 ms      |
| **Production build, 3 routes** | **1784 ms**  | **1196 ms**   | **2759 ms**   |

The honest number under Lighthouse's mobile slow-4G and 4× CPU is **1.78 s to first paint and
1.20 s to the load event** — five and a half times better than the dev server, and still **1.2–1.8×
over the plan's one-second bound**.

### 54.3 The cause is one chunk, and the bundler says so itself

The production run's spread is as flat as the dev run's: FCP 1784 / 1784 / 1784 ms and load 1195 /
1199 / 1196 ms across `/`, `/reportes` and `/products`. Same conclusion, now on the real artifact:
the cost is the shell every route carries. The build output names it:

```
dist/assets/index-BUPsfDAA.js   942.01 kB │ gzip: 239.40 kB
dist/assets/floor-plan-*.js     385.70 kB │ gzip: 117.38 kB   (lazy — proves the mechanism works)
dist/assets/index-*.css          79.50 kB │ gzip:  15.46 kB
(!) Some chunks are larger than 500 kB after minification. Consider using dynamic import() to
    code-split the application
```

**239 kB gzip of main chunk plus 15 kB gzip of CSS on every screen.** At slow-4G's effective
throughput that is ~1.3 s of transfer before a byte of screen code runs, which is the 1.78 s FCP.
The floor-plan route already ships as a 117 kB gzip lazy chunk, so the code-splitting mechanism is in
the tree and working; the main chunk just has not been split.

### 54.4 Fix, and what is still unmeasured

1. Split the main chunk. The bundle warning is the tool's own advice, the lazy `floor-plan` chunk is
   the proof the pattern works, and the uniformity of the measurements says every screen pays for
   all of it today.
2. Point the instrument at the artifact the budget describes: make `UX_BASE` explicit (or default to
   a preview server) and print the target next to the verdict, so "24 routes missed" can never again
   mean "the dev server is slow".
3. **Still unmeasured:** the reference tablet itself. This is Lighthouse's emulation on a workstation
   with a 4× CPU slowdown — the industry-standard stand-in, and 1.8× over the bound is worth acting
   on, but the plan's sentence is about the tablet, and only the tablet can settle it.

## 55. The eight integration files no family names: seven pass, and the eighth is a trap that fires the moment somebody adds them

**Severity: med (a deterministic suite failure, latent until the recommended fix for §19 is applied).
Measured 2026-10-08 21:0x against a pristine build.**

§19 counted the files; this runs them. Built a disposable database
(`psql -c 'create database umi_hunt_int'` → `docs/migration/build-v3/00_run.sh umi_hunt_int` →
`build-v3 verify: OK`), provisioned the harness roles
(`apps/umi-api/test/integration/harness-roles.sql`), and pointed `DATABASE_URL_APP` /
`DATABASE_URL_WORKER` at it:

```
$ npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts <the eight files>
 ✓ mercado-pago/point-notification.integration.ts   (5 tests)
 ✓ pos-cash/register-reclaim.integration.ts
 ✓ tender/tender.integration.ts
 ✓ inventory-costing/inventory-costing.integration.ts
 ✓ fiscal/fiscal.integration.ts
 ✓ auth/pos-pin-eligibility.integration.ts          (6 tests)
 ✓ auth/pos-device-proof.integration.ts             (6 tests)
 FAIL tender/point-refund.integration.ts
      duplicate key value violates unique constraint "session_token_hash_uidx"
 Test Files  1 failed | 7 passed (8)      Tests  93 passed | 7 skipped (61 in 5.44s)
```

**Seven of eight are green — 93 assertions in five seconds.** The eighth cannot build its fixture:

```
src/modules/tender/point-refund.integration.ts:363
  INSERT INTO runtime.session (id,merchant_id,principal_type,principal_id,token_hash,expires_at)
  VALUES (…, repeat('c',64), …)
src/modules/fiscal/fiscal.integration.ts:399
  INSERT INTO runtime.session (…, token_hash, …)  VALUES (…, repeat('b',64), …)   ← and repeat('c',64)
```

Two files hand themselves the **same token hash**, against a unique index on the column. In one
process the second insert dies, and because the family is deliberately serialised into a single fork
(`vitest.integration.config.ts`: `fileParallelism: false`, `singleFork: true`) "one process" is
always. Point-refund can therefore never pass in any run that also includes fiscal.

**Why it is invisible today, and why it will not stay that way.** Neither file is named by
`test:integration:schema` (the family `.github/workflows/umi-api-ci.yml:252` runs), so they never
meet; the files that _are_ in that family happen to have picked distinct literals (`'b'` in
point-notification, `'d'` in point-card-refund, `'e'` in the realtime family, plus several that
generate the hash in SQL). The trap springs on the first person who does what §19 asks — add the
eight un-named files to a family — or who runs two of them by hand, which is how I hit it.

**The right pattern is already in the tree.** `pos-offline.integration.ts:460-464` builds the hash
instead of choosing one:

```sql
VALUES ($1::uuid,$2::uuid,'user',$3::uuid,
        md5($1::text||clock_timestamp()::text), now()+interval '2 hours')
```

Unique per insert, impossible to collide with any sibling.

**Fix.**

1. Adopt the `md5($1::text||clock_timestamp()::text)` form (or a per-file literal) in
   `point-refund.integration.ts` and `fiscal.integration.ts`.
2. Add the eight files to a family — they pass, they take five seconds, and that is what §19 asked
   for.
3. Make the collision impossible to reintroduce: a five-line check that no two `*.integration.ts`
   files insert the same session-token literal, run beside the families. The literals are
   `repeat('x',64)` in SQL and `'x'.repeat(64)` in JS; both are greppable.

## 56. §54 confirmed by transfer sizes — and the probe whose "unused %" would decide the fix cannot be trusted

### 56.1 Every route downloads the whole application, in bytes

Against the production build, counting what the browser actually fetched per route
(`performance.getEntriesByType('resource')`, `encodedBodySize`):

| Route         | JS (gzip) | JS (raw) | CSS (gzip) | Files                             |
| ------------- | --------- | -------- | ---------- | --------------------------------- |
| `/`           | 263 KB    | 989 KB   | 15 KB      | `index`, `messages`               |
| `/kitchen`    | 263 KB    | 989 KB   | 15 KB      | `index`, `messages`               |
| `/products`   | 263 KB    | 989 KB   | 15 KB      | `index`, `messages`               |
| `/reportes`   | 263 KB    | 989 KB   | 15 KB      | `index`, `messages`               |
| `/floor-plan` | 377 KB    | 1 366 KB | 17 KB      | `index`, `messages`, `floor-plan` |

Four screens out of five fetch byte-identical JavaScript: the same 989 KB raw / 263 KB gzip,
regardless of what the screen needs. Only `/floor-plan` differs, and it differs by adding its lazy
chunk. This is §54's cause measured a second way — transfer, not score — and it is the number to
watch after any code-splitting change: today the answer is "one bundle for everything, with one
exception that proves the mechanism works".

### 56.2 The probe that reports "4% unused" is measuring something else

`tools/ux-sweep/devtools-probe.mjs` prints, per route, `JS 304/318KB used, 4% unused` — a number
that reads as "the bundle is already optimal, splitting would gain 4%". Against the same route the
transfer measurement above says 989 KB raw. Both cannot be about the same thing, and the probe's is
the one that is wrong:

```js
for (const script of coverage.result || []) {
  for (const fn of script.functions) {
    const size = fn.ranges.reduce((sum, r) => sum + (r.endOffset - r.startOffset), 0);
    totalBytes += size;
    if (fn.ranges.some((r) => r.count > 0)) usedBytes += size;
  }
}
```

Two independent defects in nine lines. **(1)** It sums _function ranges only_: every byte that is not
inside a function — string tables, module-level code, the literals a bundle is mostly made of — is
excluded from both numerator and denominator, which is why its "total" is 318 KB for a route that
downloads 989 KB of JavaScript. **(2)** `fn.ranges` includes nested functions, so an inner function's
bytes are counted once for every enclosing function that contains it. The percentage survives both
errors looking plausible, which is the worst property a metric can have.

**My own two attempts to compute the honest version, recorded because they failed the same way.**
Summing function ranges gave 132% (nested double-count, again). Using `Debugger.getScriptSource` for
the real denominator and merging the _executed_ intervals gave 100.0% on both `/` and `/kitchen` —
because `takePreciseCoverage` returns the script's root function, whose range covers the entire file
and whose count is always > 0, so a naive union paints everything as used. Getting this right means
excluding the root function and merging ranges per function, which is what Chrome's own Coverage
panel does and what this probe does not.

**Fix.** For the code-splitting decision, use the transfer table in §56.1 — it is exact and it is
what changes when a chunk is split. If the tool wants a coverage percentage, implement it the way
DevTools does (source length as the denominator, root function excluded, intervals merged), or print
the raw numbers (`coveredChars / sourceChars`) and stop calling the ratio a share of the bundle.

---

## 57. `ux:lighthouse` needs the shared window in the foreground — which on this workstation is somebody else's test

**Severity: low (instrument; recorded so the next person does not read a null score as a finding).
Measured 2026-10-08 21:5x.**

`pnpm ux:lighthouse` (or `perf-lighthouse.mjs --preset mobile`) answered:

```
Lighthouse reported a runtime error: NO_FCP — The page did not paint any content.
Please ensure you keep the browser window in the foreground during the load and try again. (NO_FCP)
scores: performance null, accessibility null, best-practices null, seo null
browser still up: true (2 -> 2 pages)
```

The wrapper's own docstring covers the two hazards it thought it had — that Lighthouse would kill the
borrowed browser, and that it would clear the session — and both held (2 pages before, 2 after). The
one it does not cover is the one that stopped it: Lighthouse measures a page it opens, and a page in
a background window on this compositor never paints, so every category comes back `null`.

**Why I did not fix it by foregrounding the window.** `hyprctl clients` shows this desktop carrying
four windows: two Chromium dashboards, a kitty terminal, and **`Co.umiconsulting.umi_pos.estacion` —
the native POS that another session is driving with real pointer events**. Bringing the browser's
workspace forward moves windows under a driver that clicks by screen coordinate. The value of a
second performance opinion does not pay for corrupting somebody else's money-path test, so the
audit is recorded as not run and §54's confirmation came from transfer sizes (§56.1) instead.

**Fix, for whoever owns the harness.** Say it before the run, not in the metrics table: check
`document.visibilityState`/the window's focus state up front and refuse with "this audit needs the
browser's window in the foreground; it is on workspace N behind something else" — an instrument that
answers `null` in every category is indistinguishable from one that measured nothing. Where an
unattended run matters, Lighthouse's own launcher (`chrome-launcher`, headless, with the session's
cookies passed as `extraHeaders`) avoids the shared window entirely.

## 59. The click audit in its real mode, run for the first time — 120 clicks, nothing broken, and the sweep's own rate limiting in the way

**Severity: none for the product (clean); low-med for the instrument family (a shared pacing defect
that has now distorted four measurements). Measured 2026-10-08 22:1x–22:3x.**

### 59.1 How it was run, safely

`click-audit.mjs` clicks "safe" controls only when the operator names something disposable
(`UX_CLICK_CONFIRM=disposable`), which is why it had never been run: the local dashboard points at
`umi_local`, which is somebody's working database. The safe way — and the recipe, since none was
written down:

1. A disposable database: `umi_acl_head` (the hunt's clone).
2. An API against it: `DATABASE_URL_APP/WORKER=…/umi_acl_head PORT=4021 EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION=build-v3-79 pnpm exec nest start`.
3. A **second** dashboard whose proxy points there and which therefore cannot touch the operator's
   data: `VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET=http://127.0.0.1:4021 pnpm dev --port 4002`
   (`vite.config.js:13` is the knob; `pnpm dev` starts on 4000 by default, which is why the port had
   to be explicit).
4. Signed in on `:4002`, then `UX_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:4002 UX_CLICK_CONFIRM=disposable node tools/ux-sweep/click-audit.mjs --limit 5`.

### 59.2 The result: the product is clean under a click sweep

Across all 24 routes, five controls clicked on each:

| Measure                   | Result                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Clicks                    | **120** (33 navigated — 13 to `/`, 11 to `/orders`, 9 to `/cafes`; 87 stayed on the screen) |
| Page errors (uncaught JS) | **0**                                                                                       |
| Failed requests           | **0**                                                                                       |
| Dialogs opened            | 0                                                                                           |
| Off-origin clicks         | 0 (the guard never had to act)                                                              |
| Console errors            | **30, every one of them a 429** — and none from the product                                 |

There is no dead button in this set: no click produced an exception, a broken request or a
navigation the screen could not survive. For a surface that has never been clicked through before,
that is the answer worth having.

### 59.3 The 429s are the sweep's, and they are now four instruments old

Every console error in the run is `429 Too Many Requests`, produced by the sweep itself: walking 24
routes and clicking five controls each asks the API for far more than the per-principal ceiling of
**240 requests/minute** (`operational.interceptor.ts:16`, `LIMITS.user = 240`). The same artefact now
appears in four measurements, each handling it differently:

| Instrument                            | What it did with the 429s                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ux:first-paint` (§47.3)              | printed `23 429(s)` in its summary — honest, and the numbers stood                                                                                        |
| `ux:memory` (§51)                     | counted `25 429s` and still compared two _differently rendered_ states as if the difference were retention — the one case where it changed the conclusion |
| `ux:first-paint` transport note (§54) | 0 429s, because the dev server's module graph dominates; the pattern is not universal                                                                     |
| `ux:click-audit` (this run)           | records them as **console errors**, the one column an operator reads as "the app threw"                                                                   |

One shared pacing helper — a token bucket sized to the API's own ceiling, or a `--pace` flag every
harness honours — would fix all four at once, and would make §51's memory numbers mean what they
claimed. Until then, any sweep figure taken while `429` appears in its output is a figure measured
against a partially-served application, and the instrument should say so in the verdict rather than
in a bracket.

### 59.4 One more thing the two runs show

The same 24 routes carried **852 controls** in §53's inventory and roughly half that here
(`/customers` 29 → 6, `/inventory` 47 → 6, `/operations` 49 → 6), because this run's database is
sparse. The instrument's counts describe the _data as much as the interface_ — worth stating where
somebody might otherwise compare two runs and read a regression.

## 60. The costing probe is pinned to a navigation shape the app documented moving away from — and the screen it never reached is healthy

**Severity: low (instrument). Measured 2026-10-08 22:3x.**

`node tools/ux-sweep/costing-screen-probe.mjs` — "does the Costos y márgenes screen read the four
costing routes, and does it tell the truth about a number" — dies on twenty seconds of waiting:

```
locator.waitFor: Timeout 20000ms exceeded.
  waiting for getByRole('button', { name: /^(Costos y márgenes|Costs and margins)$/ }) to be visible
  at tools/ux-sweep/costing-screen-probe.mjs:142
```

It lands on `/` and looks for a **sidebar button** named "Costos y márgenes"
(`costing-screen-probe.mjs:30`, `:139-142`). The label is still correct; the _shape_ is not, and the
application says so itself:

| Fact                                                                                                                                                                                 | Where                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| The module registry records the move in a comment — "`catalog-inventory` + `inventory-costing` become `products` + `inventory`, and costing moves in as a tab of the thing it reads" | `apps/umi-dashboard/src/lib/module-registry.js:194-195` |
| It is declared as a child entry, `{ id: 'inventory/costos', label: msg\`Costos y márgenes\` }`                                                                                       | `:232`                                                  |
| The old path survives as a redirect, `/inventory-costing` → `/inventory/costos`                                                                                                      | `app.jsx:440`                                           |
| And `/` does not even show that region first for this session: it lands on `/customers` (§46)                                                                                        | measured                                                |

**So the probe cannot reach the screen it was written to inspect**, and it reports a locator timeout
instead of the one sentence that would fix it ("the nav shape moved: `Costos y márgenes` is now
`/inventory/costos` inside the Inventory hub").

### 60.1 The verification it never got to do, done by hand

Same idea, current navigation: go to `/inventory/costos` and watch what it reads.

| Route called                                                                | Status |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| `inventory-costing/low-stock?windowDays=28`                                 | 200    |
| `inventory-costing/days?from=2026-09-11&to=2026-10-08`                      | 200    |
| `inventory-costing/cost-basis?includeWithoutReceipts=true`                  | 200    |
| `inventory-costing/plates?includeUnmapped=true&consumptionFrom=…&limit=200` | 200    |

Four routes, four 200s, and a screen that renders figures with **zero** `–` placeholders — so the
answer to the probe's question is "yes, and it tells the truth about the numbers I can see". The
screen is healthy; the instrument is the thing that rotted, which is the same verdict as §46 and
§55 (three different tools, one cause: the app moved and the tool held the old map).

**One thing that looks like a defect and is not:** each of the four routes is called **twice** per
load. That is React's development double-invocation (`<React.StrictMode>` at
`apps/umi-dashboard/src/main.jsx:17`) against the dev server, not duplicate fetching in the product;
recorded here so the next reader does not file it.

**Fix.** Navigate by route (`/inventory/costos`) or expand the Inventory group before looking for
the child, and fail by name when the shape has changed rather than after a 20-second wait.

## 61. The advisory-lock lens: thirteen sites, read for the two ways this goes wrong — clean

**Severity: none. Recorded so the lens is spent rather than re-run.** Advisory locks are how this
codebase serialises races at the database (§8's TOCTOU fix, §49.1's refund lock), so the two classic
failures are worth checking once, globally: a **session-scoped lock whose release can be skipped** (it
stays held on a pooled connection, and every later taker blocks), and **the same logical resource
locked under two different hash functions** (the two locks never meet, and the mutual exclusion
silently is not there).

All thirteen sites, with the key each one actually holds:

| Site                                       | Key                                                                 | Hash                    |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `cash.repository.ts:568`                   | `reward_config:<merchantId>`                                        | `hashtext`              |
| `cash-register.repository.ts:131`          | `register:<merchantId>:<personId>`                                  | `hashtext`              |
| `cash-scan.repository.ts:414`, `:525`      | `card:<cardId>`                                                     | `hashtext`              |
| `identity.resolver.ts:128`                 | `<merchantId>:<phone or channel:new>`                               | `hashtext(…)::bigint`   |
| `auth.repository.ts:747`, `:852`           | refresh-family id                                                   | `hashtextextended(…,0)` |
| `conversations.repository.ts:67`           | conversation key                                                    | `hashtextextended(…,0)` |
| `pos-offline.repository.ts:34`             | `<deviceId>:<credentialVersion>`                                    | `hashtextextended(…,0)` |
| `pos-exception.repository.ts:682`, `:1643` | `sale_exception:<saleId>`                                           | `hashtextextended(…,0)` |
| `pos-inventory.repository.ts:2027`         | `<merchantId>:<locationId>:<inventoryLocationId>:<inventoryItemId>` | `hashtextextended(…,0)` |

**The session-scoped one is correct.** `pos-offline` is the only `pg_advisory_lock` (not `…_xact_lock`)
in the tree, and it does the two things that make that form safe: it takes a **dedicated connection**
from the pool (`this.pg.app.connect()`) so no unrelated query can inherit the lock, and its caller
holds the returned release in a `try/finally` (`pos-offline.service.ts:121-132`, `finally { await
release() }`), so an exception in the middle cannot return a locked connection to the pool.

**No key is locked under two hashes.** The `hashtext` family and the `hashtextextended` family hold
different-looking keys for different resources (`card:*`, `register:*`, `reward_config:*`, an
identity, versus a device, a sale, an inventory item, a refresh family), and no two sites name the
same resource. Worth noting for whoever adds the next one: `hashtext` and `hashtextextended` produce
different values for the same string, so _choosing the wrong one of the two_ is exactly how a lock
stops being a lock — the two forms are one keystroke apart in a diff.

**A note on deadlock, from the same read.** Every `…_xact_lock` here is taken at most once per
transaction along the paths I could follow (the refund path takes `sale_exception`, then inventory's
lock — one order, no reverse), and the offline path's session lock is taken before its own work
begins. I found no unit of work that takes two of these keys in an order another reverses.
