## 62. The business date: the post-sale paths take it from the database server's clock, and the divergence is open right now

**Severity: med-high (money booked to the wrong trading day, for six hours every evening in this
café's timezone). Measured live 2026-10-09 04:23 UTC / 21:23 local.**

### 62.1 The divergence, measured

```
umibv3-pg=# show timezone;  → Etc/UTC
select now()                        → 2026-10-09 04:23:37+00
       current_date                 → 2026-10-09          ← the server's day
       (now() at time zone 'America/Mexico_City')::date
                                    → 2026-10-08          ← the café's trading day
       they agree?                  → f
merchant.merchant: timezone = America/Mexico_City, business_day_start = 00:00:00
apps/umi-api/src/shared/database/pg.service.ts: no session time zone is set
```

The database container runs UTC, the café runs UTC-6, and the API never sets a session time zone —
so `current_date` inside an API transaction is _the server's calendar date_. Every evening between
UTC midnight and local midnight those two disagree: six hours for Mexico City, seven for the
Mazatlán clock the counter terminal itself runs on. Right now is inside that window.

### 62.2 What the platform does everywhere else, and even tests

The convention exists, is documented in the trigger that implements it, and is pinned by a test:

| Fact                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Where                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `merchant.tg_business_date()` derives the column from `merchant.timezone` and `business_day_start`, subtracting the day start before casting — "what makes an 01:00 sale belong to the previous trading day" | `docs/migration/build-v3/60_triggers.sql:247-263` |
| It is attached to `customer_order` (from `placed_at`) and `pos_cart` (from `created_at`), firing on insert **or update** so the column cannot be forged                                                      | `:266-278`                                        |
| The procurement tables carry the same trigger (`purchase_order`, `purchase_order_receipt`)                                                                                                                   | `69_procurement.sql:598`, `:606`                  |
| The repository-side mirror is asserted by a test — and it explicitly forbids the `coalesce(location.timezone, merchant.timezone)` variant                                                                    | `gate-3c-cash-migration.spec.ts:153-158`          |

### 62.3 The three places that skip it

Twelve `current_date` sites survive in non-test API code, in exactly two modules — the post-sale
paths — and none of them is corrected by a trigger:

| Site                                                | What it writes                                                                                                                               | Trigger that could fix it                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `pos-exception.repository.ts:856`                   | `merchant.pos_sale_exception.business_date = current_date`                                                                                   | none — the table's triggers are append-only and approval-binding (verified against the live catalogue) |
| `pos-exception.repository.ts:1051`                  | `merchant.pos_exception_receipt.business_date = current_date`                                                                                | none (append-only only)                                                                                |
| `pos-customer-value.repository.ts` ×9, e.g. `:1218` | `'businessDate', current_date` into the jsonb that `merchant.append_stored_value_fact` writes to `loyalty_stored_value_ledger.business_date` | none that derives it — and the _only_ thing that touches the column is:                                |

```sql
-- 37_pos_customer_value.sql:400, inside prepare_stored_value_fact()
new.business_date := coalesce(new.business_date, new.occurred_at::date, current_date);
```

All three branches of that `coalesce` produce the server's date: the caller passes `current_date`,
`occurred_at::date` casts a `timestamptz` in the _session's_ (UTC) zone, and the last is
`current_date` again. Nowhere is `merchant.timezone` consulted.

### 62.4 The same refund, two different days

Within one transaction, `pos-exception` already has the right value and uses it for the cash side:
the cash compensation posts to **the shift's derived business date** (`pos-exception.repository.ts:2231`,
`shift.businessDate`). The exception row (`:856`) and its compensating receipt (`:1051`) post to
`current_date`. So a refund taken at 21:00 local in this café writes a receipt dated the 9th and a
drawer ledger line dated the 8th, and a day-close reconciliation that groups by business date finds
a refund on one side and its drawer movement on the other. The sale it reverses is on the 8th
(`customer_order` is trigger-derived), so the exception is the row that disagrees with both.

### 62.5 Fix, and the test that would have caught it

1. **Pass the derived day, do not compute one.** `pos-exception` already reads the source receipt's
   `business_date` (`:837`, `:1031`) and the shift's; use those for the exception and its receipt
   instead of `current_date`. For the stored-value jsonb, fill `businessDate` from the same value the
   surrounding transaction is booked to — not from the server clock.
2. **Or make the column underivable-from-a-clock** the way the other tables are: a business-date
   trigger on both tables. Note `pos_sale_exception` has no `created_at` column to derive from, so
   option 1 is the fit there — which is also the design the cash side already follows.
3. **Pin it with a test.** Every integration suite here runs with the database in UTC and a merchant
   in UTC-6, which is exactly the condition that breaks it — but nothing asserts the _dates_ the
   refund writes. One assertion per write path ("the exception, its receipt and the cash ledger line
   carry the same `business_date`, and it equals the shift's") fails today and would have failed on
   the day this was written.

## 63. The business-day rule, counted: three hand-copied implementations and twenty-two sites that skip it

**Severity: med (this is §4 and §62 seen as one defect — the daily cash limit, every cash report
window, and three money tables' dates). Re-verified 2026-10-08 22:4x.**

§4 found six sites that build "today" from the server _process's_ midnight; §62 found twelve that
take the _database session's_ `current_date`. They are the same defect with two clocks behind it,
and the count is larger than either section says.

**What the platform knows the rule is** — the same expression, written out three times by hand:

| Implementation                                                       | Expression                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The trigger that derives the column on orders, carts and procurement | `((v_at at time zone v_tz) - v_day_start::interval)::date` (`60_triggers.sql:262`)                                                                                      |
| The fiscal period rollover                                           | `(((now() at time zone m.timezone) - m.business_day_start::interval)::date)` (`fiscal.repository.ts:243`)                                                               |
| The costing day-of-sale                                              | `((now() AT TIME ZONE m.timezone) - m.business_day_start::interval)::date`, with the rule spelled out in a comment above it (`inventory-costing.repository.ts:201-209`) |

Three copies, all identical in form — so nobody has drifted yet, and anyone changing the rule has
three places to change and twenty-two to remember.

**The twenty-two that do not use it**, counted by kind:

| Clock                                                                 | Sites                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | What they bound                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The Node process's local midnight (`new Date(); x.setHours(0,0,0,0)`) | **10** — six in `apps/umi-api` (`cash-write.service.ts:71`, `cash-read.service.ts:140,169,176,179,215`) and **four this hunt had not counted**, in the legacy service: `apps/umi-cash/src/app/api/[slug]/admin/analytics/route.ts:30,39,44,181` | §4's list, plus the analytics windows in `umi-cash` (today, 30 days, 8 weeks, this month) |
| The database session's `current_date` (UTC here)                      | **12** — three in `pos-exception`, nine in `pos-customer-value`                                                                                                                                                                                 | the exception row, its compensating receipt, and the stored-value ledger facts (§62)      |

**The one that costs money daily** is still the first row's first site: `cash-write.service.ts:71`
bounds `STAFF_DAILY_TOPUP_LIMIT`. On a VPS running UTC, a Mazatlán café's "day" turns over at 18:00
local, so the same cashier can take two daily allowances inside one operational day — mid-dinner
service. §4 reported it; the code has not changed.

**Fix, and it is one fix rather than twenty-two.**

1. **One implementation per clock.** A PostgreSQL function (the trigger's body is already written —
   expose it as `merchant.business_date_for(merchant_id, at timestamptz)` and delete the two inline
   copies) and one Node helper for read windows, called by the ten `setHours` sites. The rule then
   has one home again, and the number of places to change when it changes is one.
2. **Make it checkable.** A test that runs the cash-report window, the top-up limit and a refund with
   the merchant in a timezone away from the server's (UTC-6 against a UTC container is the condition
   every suite already runs in) and asserts the _dates_, not the money: the top-up limit's window, the
   report's day buckets, the exception, its receipt and the ledger facts should all agree with the
   café's trading day.
3. **Pin the containers only as a second line of defence.** §4 suggested it and it is still not done
   — but a `TZ` that makes the two clocks agree would _hide_ the defect rather than fix it, which is
   why it belongs after (1) and (2), not before them.

## 70. The shared status component prints contract enum values in English on a Spanish screen

**Severity: low (labels, not money). Measured live on 2026-10-08 23:4x, in both locales.**

`operations-workspace.jsx` renders one `Status` component for every domain the Operations and Kitchen
screens show (`:118-150`). It knows fourteen states:

```
active inactive archived pending needs_review blocked failed available in_use
printed not_printed queued printing reconciliation_required
```

and for anything else it falls back to the raw contract value:

```js
const raw = value ? (STATE_LABEL[key] ? i18n._(STATE_LABEL[key]) : String(value).replaceAll('_', ' ')) : t`desconocido`;
```

The fallback **does not go through `i18n._` at all**, so an unlisted state is printed verbatim, in
every locale. Which states those are is measurable — the screens fetch their items from
`GET /operations?domain=…`, so I read the live payload per domain and compared the statuses actually
present against the map:

| Domain               | Statuses in the live payload   | Printed raw                |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| kitchen              | `completed`, `queued`, `ready` | **`completed`, `ready`**   |
| cash_shifts          | `counting`                     | **`counting`**             |
| devices              | `active`, `revoked`            | **`revoked`**              |
| receipts             | `printed`, `not_printed`       | none — both are in the map |
| inventory, customers | no rows in this database       | —                          |

**Seen from the screen, in Spanish.** With the dashboard set to `es`, the Kitchen list reads:

```
Orden pos-cart:d4cce500-… | normal | · | 8 oct 2026, 12:05 a.m. | ready      | ⧉
Orden pos-cart:9347b86a-… | normal | · | 8 oct 2026, 12:05 a.m. | completed  | ⧉
```

So a Mexican café's operator reads "ready" and "completed" in English on a Spanish screen, next to
states that _are_ translated ("En cola" for `queued`). The priority column has the same shape —
`normal` is printed straight from the payload — though "normal" is spelled the same in both
languages, which is why it is invisible until the day a payload carries `high`.

**Fix.**

1. **Type the map against the contract's status union** (`Record<OperationStatus, MessageDescriptor>`),
   the same hardening §40 asked for on the five inventory label maps: then the next enum member is a
   compile error instead of a line of English on a Spanish screen.
2. **Make the fallback loud.** A state the screen cannot name should say so — the "desconocido"
   branch already exists for an empty value — rather than wearing the enum, which is how `revoked`
   and `counting` have been on screen without anyone reading them as a defect.
3. A cheap regression test: every status the contract's `operations` domains can emit is either in
   the map or asserted as deliberately raw.

### 70.1 The same fallback, a second map, and it is missing the two states the cash machine writes

Looking for the class rather than the instance turned up a sibling on the screen next door, with a
live symptom on the state the till is in as I write this.

`screens/registros.jsx:9-15` labels the register's status with five keys:

```
available  in_use  reconciliation_required  blocked  archived
```

and falls back the same way — `String(status || '').replaceAll('_', ' ')`, straight to the screen
(`:52-54`). What the API actually writes into `merchant.physical_register.status` is a different list
(`pos-cash.repository.ts:1994-2003`, the shift transition that mirrors the shift's own state):

```
in_use  counting  reconciliation_required  suspended
```

So **`counting` and `suspended` have no label**, and `counting` is not hypothetical: measured live on
`/cash-shifts/registros` while the drawer sits in that state (§15's shift), the cell renders

```
counting   [sub-pill]
```

— the contract's enum, in English, on a Spanish screen, in the register list. `suspended` is written
by the same statement and will read the same way the first time a register is suspended.

**How it was found, recorded because the first detector was wrong.** I swept every route for
`.status-plain` nodes, assuming that class meant "no label". It does not: the component
(`operations-workspace.jsx:148`) uses it for "no _tone_", so a labelled state lands there too, and the
sweep returned `Active` (a translated label) next to `ready`/`completed` (raw) with no way to tell
them apart. The corrected sweep matched elements whose text is exactly a lowercase enum token inside
a status-ish container (`pill|state|status|plain`), which is what turned up the register's `counting`
— and the lesson is the same one §43 taught: a class name is not a contract, so a detector built on
one has to be checked against what the class actually means before its numbers are believed.

**Fix.** Add the two states to the map (and type it, as §70 says). The general shape for both maps:
the contract's status unions are the vocabulary, the maps are the labels, and the fallback should say
it does not know rather than print the enum, which is the only reason a raw `counting` has been
sitting in the register list without anyone reading it as a defect.

## 71. The Orders header calls "today" a number that counts whatever was loaded — and the live data makes it false right now

**Severity: low-med (three dashboard figures whose scope is mislabeled, one of them an average of
money). Measured live 2026-10-08 23:5x.**

The Orders screen's header is built from one variable:

```js
// screens/orders.jsx:92
const totalToday = allOrders.length;
…
note={t`${displayed.length} de ${totalToday} mostrados.`}          // :125  — honest
count={{ value: totalToday, label: t`hoy` }}                        // :126  — claims "today"
${totalToday > 0 ? Math.round(totalRevenue / Math.max(totalToday, 1)) : '–'}   // :245  "Ticket promedio"
```

and `allOrders` comes from one request per filter chip:
`GET /merchants/{id}/orders?filter=all&locationId=…`. That endpoint:

| Fact                                                                                                                         | Where                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| filters by **status only** — `'active'` and `'all'` are group shortcuts, "anything unrecognised applies no status predicate" | `orders.repository.ts:17-18`, `:213-221` |
| has **no date parameter at all**                                                                                             | the whole query, `:40-166`               |
| is capped at `limit: 200`, newest first                                                                                      | `orders.service.ts:45`                   |

So the three figures are "over the last 200 orders the merchant ever took", and two of them say
otherwise: the tile is labelled _hoy_, and the money figure is labelled _Ticket promedio_ next to it.

**Measured, on the live data:**

```
merchant.customer_order:  business_date 2026-10-07 → 7 rows   (every order the database has)
the café's trading day:   2026-10-08
the screen:               Orders | 7 de 7 mostrados. | 7 hoy | … | Ticket promedio $X | Cancelaciones 0
```

All seven orders belong to **yesterday's** business date, and the tile says _hoy_. Because nothing in
the query knows about days, it will say _hoy_ tomorrow as well — and on a café with more than 200
orders it will say _200_ forever, with the average and the cancellation count computed over that same
sliding pile. The one label that is honest is the one next to the number: "7 de 7 mostrados".

**Fix.**

1. **Give the endpoint the day it is missing** — a `date=today` (or `from`/`to`) parameter resolved
   with the §64 rule (`merchant.timezone` minus `business_day_start`), which is the same derivation
   the orders' own `business_date` column already carries. Then `totalToday` is true by
   construction, and the average and cancellation figures inherit it.
2. **Or relabel all three honestly** — "órdenes cargadas", "ticket promedio de lo cargado" — which
   costs one string each and stops the dashboard from asserting something the API never computed.
3. **Test it where it breaks:** an order with `business_date` = yesterday must not count in _hoy_.
   With today's data (7 orders, all yesterday) that assertion fails on the first run.

---

## 72. "Hoy" on a customer's profile means "in the last 24 hours" — and the codebase has a second `daysBetween` that gets it right

**Severity: low (a label on a profile and in the customer KPI), and it is the fifth mechanism of the
date defect §62–§65 chased. Measured by construction 2026-10-09 00:0x.**

The customer profile shows a recency line — `Hoy`, `Ayer`, `Hace N días` — read straight off a
number the API computes:

```js
// screens/customers.jsx:377-390
k.recencyDays == null ? t`Sin pedidos` : k.recencyDays <= 0 ? t`Hoy` : k.recencyDays === 1 ? t`Ayer` : …
```

and the API computes it as **elapsed time, not days**:

```ts
// customer-kpis.ts:97-106
export function daysBetween(fromIso, toIso): number | null {
  const from = new Date(fromIso).getTime();
  const to = new Date(toIso).getTime();
  return Math.max(0, Math.floor((to - from) / 86_400_000));
}
// customers.service.ts:294-295
const recencyDays = daysBetween(lastOrderAt, nowIso);
const tenureDays  = daysBetween(firstOrderAt, nowIso);
```

Both arguments are **instants**, and the arithmetic floors whole 24-hour periods — so the result is
"how many complete days of elapsed time", which is not the question the label asks. Run it:

```
last visit 2026-10-07 22:00 (-07:00), viewed 2026-10-08 10:00 (-07:00)
  → recencyDays = 0  →  the profile says "Hoy"
  → calendar days apart: 1
```

So a guest who came **last night** reads "Hoy" for the whole of the next day until the same hour
passes — which for a café is exactly the window its evening guests are looked at: the following
service. The same helper feeds `tenureDays`, where being up to a day out on "hace N meses" is
harmless; the recency line is where it is read as a fact.

**And the repository already contains the right implementation, under the same name.**
`inventory-costing-domain.ts:273-280`:

```ts
/** Whole days between two business dates. UTC arithmetic: no DST, no drift. */
function daysBetween(from: string, to: string): number {
  const start = Date.parse(`${from}T00:00:00Z`);
  const end   = Date.parse(`${to}T00:00:00Z`);
  if (Number.isNaN(start) || Number.isNaN(end)) throw new Error(`daysBetween: not a business date: …`);
  return Math.round((end - start) / 86_400_000);
}
```

Business dates, anchored at midnight, `Math.round`, and it _refuses_ anything that is not a date. Two
functions, one name, opposite semantics — and the customers' one is the one whose output is printed
as a day.

**Fix.**

1. Convert both instants to the **café's business date** and subtract dates — the shape
   `inventory-costing-domain.ts` already uses, with the derivation §64 asks for
   (`merchant.timezone` minus `business_day_start`) instead of a fixed UTC offset.
2. Rename one of the two functions while doing it (`elapsedDays` vs `businessDaysBetween`), so the
   next reader cannot pick the wrong one by name.
3. Test the case that reads wrong today: a visit at 22:00 yesterday, viewed at 10:00, must say
   _Ayer_.

**And this is the fifth door to the same room.** The business date is wrong-in-place five ways now:
the database session's `current_date` (§62), the Node process's midnight (§63), the browser's
`toISOString` (§65), the report window that skips the rollover hour (§64), and a duration standing in
for a date (§72). One owner for the date would close all five at once; that is why §66 puts it first.

## 73. The recovery list's "version" is always empty — and the failures it exists to explain are the version ones

**Severity: low (diagnostics quality, not money). Measured 2026-10-09 00:1x, on the live Diagnostics
screen and its own table.**

The Diagnostics screen's Recovery tab lists refused commands. In this database there are eight, and
the screen shows them faithfully — `pos.checkout | OPTIMISTIC_VERSION_CONFLICT | Oct 7, 6:38 PM |
Failed | Recover`, three times, plus five `cart.line.add | CART_VALIDATION_FAILED`.

Each row is built from `merchant.business_command`, whose query selects the version of the aggregate
the command expected:

```sql
-- dashboard-operations.repository.ts:202, the `recovery` domain
NULL::bigint AS "amountMinorUnits", NULL::text AS currency,
c.expected_version AS version, c.correlation_id AS "correlationId"
```

**That column is empty in every row the table has ever held.**

| Measure                                                       | Result                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `business_command` rows in the live database                  | **175**                                                                  |
| Rows with `expected_version` set                              | **0**                                                                    |
| Call sites of `claimCommand(...)` that pass `expectedVersion` | **0** (the field is `expectedVersion?: number`, `integrity.types.ts:13`) |
| What the failure rows carry instead                           | `response_data = {"failureClass": "conflict"}` — no numbers at all       |

So the one road the recovery list is for — a command refused because the thing it targeted had moved —
records neither the version the client expected nor the one the database had. Three conflicts on the
same till in eight minutes (§15.1's neighbourhood: Stale client state) cannot be told apart from three
real races by anyone reading the row, and an engineer debugging a merchant report has the failure
_name_ and nothing else.

**What is _not_ broken**, checked before writing this up: the screen's Recover button does not send
that null. `RecoveryDialog` (`operations-workspace.jsx:1364-1430`) calls `command.recover(row.id)` and
then a domain recovery by command id, so no command is issued with `targetVersion: null`; the
`targetVersion: row.version` sites in the same file belong to other domains' rows, whose queries do
select a real version.

**Fix.**

1. **Pass the version where a command already knows it.** Every optimistic command receives one — the
   checkout carries the cart's expected version, the cash commands carry `expectedShiftVersion` — so
   `claimCommand(..., { expectedVersion })` is a one-key addition at those call sites, and the column
   stops being decorative.
2. **Record the conflict's two numbers.** `response_data` is already a jsonb; `{failureClass,
expected, actual}` turns "OPTIMISTIC_VERSION_CONFLICT" from a label into a diagnosis, and it is the
   difference between a support ticket that can be answered and one that cannot.
3. **Or delete the column** and the field from the feed, so no screen promises a version it can never
   show — the same choice §28's six dead figures were owed.

## 64. The census of "what day is today": seven sites right, three nearly right, twenty-two with no timezone at all — and a schema default hiding the three

**Severity: low today, med the moment somebody sets a trading-day rollover (which the platform's own
doctrine says is the norm). Measured 2026-10-08 22:5x.**

Every place in the API that decides which day a row belongs to, classified by how it answers:

| Kind                                                                                     | Count  | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Right** — merchant timezone, minus `business_day_start`                                | **7**  | `fiscal.repository.ts:243` (+ the period close at `:245-246`), `pos-cash.repository.ts:426` and `:1633`, `kds.repository.ts:1182`, `inventory-costing.repository.ts:209` and `:798`, `pos-inventory.repository.ts:1616` |
| **Nearly right** — merchant timezone, but the calendar day, with no rollover subtraction | **3**  | `dashboard-operations.repository.ts:366` — the Reportes screen's `range=today` window and every range derived from it — and `cash-scan.repository.ts:213`, `:231`                                                       |
| **No timezone** — the server's clock                                                     | **22** | the ten Node `setHours(0,0,0,0)` sites (§4, §63) and the twelve SQL `current_date` sites (§62)                                                                                                                          |

### 64.1 Why the three nearly-right ones look fine

`merchant.merchant.business_day_start` is `time not null default '00:00'`
(`docs/migration/build-v3/20_merchant.sql:198`), and every merchant I can read — the live local one
and all five in the backfilled production clone — carries exactly that. Subtracting zero changes
nothing, so the three sites agree with the seven **by accident of data, not by implementation**.

That matters because the platform's doctrine (quoted in §4) says a café's day ends at the configured
hour, _04:00 by default_. Set one merchant to `04:00` and the Reportes screen starts disagreeing with
the rows it sums: those rows carry a `business_date` the trigger derived **with** the subtraction, so
a sale rung at 02:00 local is booked to the previous trading day — and a `range=today` window built
from the plain local date excludes it. The sale still exists in the ledger and on the shift; it is
the report that cannot see it.

So the ordering of the fixes matters: **the readers have to be right before the data can be.** Flipping
`business_day_start`'s default to the documented 04:00 while those three sites still ignore it would
put every café's report a day off, which is the opposite of what the doctrine is for. (And the
doctrine and the schema already disagree with each other: the document says 04:00, the column says
`'00:00'`.)

### 64.2 The one rule with two answers

`customers.repository.ts:620` computes a customer's daypart and day-of-week with
`placed_at AT TIME ZONE COALESCE(l.timezone, m.timezone)` — the **location's** timezone with the
merchant's as fallback. Everywhere the ledger looks it is the merchant's, with no location override,
and `gate-3c-cash-migration.spec.ts:158` goes as far as asserting the cash repository does **not**
contain that exact `coalesce(location.timezone, merchant.timezone)` expression.

The local data has `merchant.location.timezone` null, so both answers agree today. This is not
obviously a defect — a customer's "evening" happened at the branch they visited, which argues for the
location — it is a decision nobody wrote down, made twice in opposite directions, with a test
forbidding one of them in one file and nothing checking the other.

**Fix.**

1. The one helper §63 asks for covers the three nearly-right sites as well: `merchant.business_date_for(...)`
   in SQL, called by the report window, the two scan windows, and the trigger itself.
2. Decide the location-timezone question in writing — customer profile in the location's zone, or the
   merchant's everywhere — and assert the decision in one place instead of forbidding the expression
   in one file while using it in another.
3. Align the documented default and the column's default, last, and in the same commit as (1).

## 65. The contract makes the _client_ supply the business date — and the dashboard supplies UTC

**Severity: med-high (the stock ledger's day comes from the browser's clock; the platform's own rule
says a client must never supply it). Measured 2026-10-08 23:0x.**

### 65.1 The requirement, in the contract

```ts
// packages/contract/src/pos-inventory.ts:185-203
export const InventoryCommandContext = z.object({
  locationId: Uuid, inventoryLocationId: Uuid, operatorSessionId: Uuid,
  commandId: Uuid, idempotencyKey: Uuid,
  expectedVersion: z.number().int().positive(),
  policyFingerprint: … , approvalId … , approvalFingerprint … ,
  businessDate: MerchantDate,          // ← required, and typed as the merchant's date
}).strict();
const commandShape = InventoryCommandContext.shape;   // spread into every inventory command
```

Every inventory command — adjustment, waste, damage, quarantine, count create/submit/reconcile — is
built from that shape and is `.strict()`, so `businessDate` is **mandatory** and the client is the one
who fills it.

### 65.2 What the dashboard fills it with, in seven places

| Screen                     | Sites                          | Value                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `operations-workspace.jsx` | `:456`, `:522`, `:543`, `:566` | `new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)` |
| `inventory-adjust.jsx`     | `:91`                          | same                                    |
| `inventory-count.jsx`      | `:329`, `:386`                 | same                                    |

`toISOString()` is **UTC**, always. So a browser at 18:00 in a UTC-6 café sends _tomorrow's_ date, and
the window is six hours wide every evening (seven for the terminal's own Mazatlán clock). A platform
admin managing that café from Europe sends a date built from _their_ device, which is wrong at every
hour of the day. A café east of UTC gets the mirror image between local midnight and its offset.

The value is not decorative: `pos-inventory.repository.ts:851` passes `dto.businessDate` straight into
`merchant.append_stock_ledger(...)` as `p_business_date`, so it is the day the stock movement belongs
to — the same column §64's costing day-buckets group by.

### 65.3 The platform says the opposite, and already knows how to do it right

| Fact                                                                                                                                                                   | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The column's own doctrine: "Derived by `merchant.tg_business_date` from `created_at`, the merchant timezone and `business_day_start`. **Never supplied by a client.**" | `docs/migration/build-v3/69_procurement.sql:305` (and the same sentence at `20_merchant.sql:1108-1109`)                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| The server can derive it correctly                                                                                                                                     | `pos-inventory.repository.ts:1613-1623` (`currentBusinessDate`, the rule from §64)                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| And does, for exactly one command                                                                                                                                      | `administrative-command-execution.service.ts:532` injects `businessDate: await this.inventory.currentBusinessDate(...)` for `inventory.production.produce`, with the comment "the command context has no operator session and no business date, so the merchant's own business date is read here" |
| While every other inventory command takes the client's                                                                                                                 | `inventoryDto` spreads `request.parameters` and injects only the target, location, session, ids and approval — never a business date (`:683-698`)                                                                                                                                                 |

So the platform holds both beliefs at once, one command apart, and the contract documents the one the
doctrine forbids.

### 65.4 Fix

1. **Derive it in one place.** `inventoryDto` already builds every inventory DTO; add
   `businessDate: await this.inventory.currentBusinessDate(...)` there, exactly as the production case
   does one branch away, and delete the field from what the client is asked to send. The contract then
   stops requiring a value only the server can know.
2. **If it must stay a request field**, the client has to be given a server-derived value to send —
   today's capabilities payload carries `businessDayStart` but no business _date_, which is why every
   screen invents one. Publishing `businessDate` next to it makes the correct client trivial; leaving
   the field client-built keeps the bug.
3. **Test it the way it breaks.** Submit an adjustment whose `businessDate` is deliberately yesterday,
   or a year ahead, and assert the ledger row carries the merchant's trading day and not the payload's
   — the same date-asserting test §62 and §63 ask for, applied to the inventory door.

the section that proves it. Two of the ten need a person to decide; the rest are code.

## 67. Opening hours: a feature the model advertises and nothing can write, and a window shape that is legal in one place and silently ignored in another

**Severity: low today (both are unreachable through any shipped client), med the day the exceptions
door is built. Measured 2026-10-08 23:3x by running the module.**

`apps/umi-api/src/modules/business-hours/open-hours.ts` is the one place the meaning of
`merchant.open_hours` is written down, and it is careful: absent is not the same as an empty list,
multiple intervals per day are supported, crossing-midnight windows are supported, date exceptions
"replace the weekday entirely", and unknown means closed. Two gaps, both about exceptions.

### 67.1 The advertised capability has no door

The docstring sells date exceptions as one of the two things the old row table could not express — the
example it gives is "Closed on Christmas had nowhere to live at all" — and the spec tests them.
Nothing can create one:

| Layer                                             | State                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The model (`open-hours.ts:53-57`, `:119-127`)     | reads, validates and honours `exceptions`                                                                                                                                     |
| The write DTO (`dto/update-hours.dto.ts:13`)      | `hours?: Record<string, { open: boolean; from: string; to: string }>` — a day map, no exceptions                                                                              |
| The service (`business-hours.service.ts:145-149`) | `fromGrid(hours, existing)` starts from `{ ...existing }`, so exceptions are **preserved but never created**, and its own comment says "one window per day and no exceptions" |
| The dashboard (`screens/hours.jsx`)               | no occurrence of the word `exception`                                                                                                                                         |

So a café can only get a holiday exception by hand-writing the jsonb. The model, the validator and the
test suite all agree the feature exists; the product cannot produce it. That is §28's shape — a figure
that can never render — in a different room: a document field that can never be written.

### 67.2 A crossing window is legal on a weekday and ignored on an exception

Run, not read — compiled the module with the repository's own esbuild and called it:

```
parseOpenHours({ thu: [], exceptions: [{ date: '2026-12-31', open: '20:00', close: '02:00' }] })
  exceptions kept:  [{"date":"2026-12-31","open":"20:00","close":"02:00"}]
  windowsOn(thu, '2026-12-31')  ->  []          the exception is discarded
  isOpenAt(..., 21:00, '2026-12-31')  ->  false  the cafe reads CLOSED on the night it declared open

same exception, with thu: [08:00-20:00]
  isOpenAt(..., 12:00)  ->  true
  isOpenAt(..., 21:00)  ->  false               the declared hours, exactly inverted
```

The cause is one clause: `windowsOn` (`open-hours.ts:142`) honours an exception only when
`close > open`, while the weekday path accepts `close < open` as a crossing window — `parseOpenHours`
rejects only `open === close`, `crossesMidnight` exists for exactly this, and the spec tests a
crossing **weekday** window ("stays open after midnight on a window that crosses it"). The same
`{open, close}` pair is therefore legal in one place and silently discarded in the other, and the
discard **falls through to the weekday** — the answer is not "closed", it is "whatever that weekday
says", which can be the opposite.

The one test that touches a bad exception uses `open: 'noon'` — a non-time value — and asserts that
falling through is deliberate. The crossing case is neither tested nor mentioned, so this reads as an
oversight rather than a decision: someone wrote `close > open` to catch malformed input and
accidentally excluded a shape the rest of the file supports.

**Reachability, to be fair about severity.** Nothing can create an exception today (§67.1), so this
cannot fire in production yet. It fires the moment the exceptions door is built — which the module's
own docstring argues for — and the readers are the WhatsApp ordering window
(`conversations/ordering-window.service.ts:199-202`) and the cash scan's open/closed test
(`cash/cash-scan.repository.ts:506`). New Year's Eve is the most likely overnight exception a café
will ever enter.

### 67.3 Fix

1. **`close > open` becomes `close !== open`** in `windowsOn`, and let `crossesMidnight` and
   `activeWindowAt` do the work they already do for weekdays — `activeWindowAt` gives a window that
   started yesterday a negative opening, which is exactly the exception case too.
2. **Add a spec case for a crossing exception**, and for the afternoon-to-early-morning holiday a café
   actually has, so the shape cannot regress.
3. **Give exceptions a door, or close the claim.** Either add `exceptions` to the DTO and the grid
   round-trip, or say in the docstring that they are SQL-only for now. A field the UI cannot write
   while four documents advertise it is the kind of gap a customer finds on Christmas Day.

---

## 68. "No sale" asks the manager to sign a fingerprint the two sides compute from different fields

**Severity: med (a money control that cannot be approved on a shift that has moved terminals — and
neither side has a test that compares the two strings). Read and cross-checked 2026-10-08 23:5x.**

Opening the drawer without a sale needs a manager PIN. The till asks the manager to authorize a
_fingerprint_ of the action, and the server recomputes the same fingerprint from its own copy of the
request and refuses with `APPROVAL_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH` if they differ. Both sides build it by
joining fields with `:` and hashing, and here is what each one joins:

| #   | The till (`cash_controller.dart:850-856`) | The API (`pos-cash.repository.ts:2195-2205`) |
| --- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | `_merchantId`                             | `merchantId`                                 |
| 2   | `_locationId`                             | `dto.locationId`                             |
| 3   | `shift['id']`                             | `dto.shiftId`                                |
| 4   | `reasonCode`                              | `dto.reasonCode`                             |
| 5   | **`shift['responsibleOperatorId']`**      | **`authorization.operatorId`**               |
| 6   | **`shift['deviceId']`**                   | **`authorization.deviceId`**                 |

The first four agree. The last two are computed from different objects, and the difference is not
cosmetic: `authorization.operatorId` and `authorization.deviceId` come from the live operator session
(`pos-cash.repository.ts:253-254`: `os.user_id AS "operatorId"`, `os.device_id AS "deviceId"`), while
`shift['deviceId']` is the terminal that **opened** the shift — a column the schema keeps separate
from `holding_device_id` precisely because the two can differ.

**When they agree, and when they do not.** They agree whenever the person asking is the shift's
responsible operator and the asking terminal is the one that opened it — the ordinary case, which is
why this has never surfaced. They diverge as soon as a shift continues on a different device, and the
platform has flows built for exactly that:

| Flow               | What it does                                                                             | Source                                                                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `adopt`            | a terminal takes its own shift back after its stored identity changed — the web POS case | `pos-cash.service.ts:546-575`                                               |
| `reclaim_register` | frees a register whose holding terminal is gone and lets this device keep working        | `catalog_surface.dart:3070-3076` calls it from the till's checkout recovery |

On such a shift the till keeps sending field 6 as the dead terminal, the server reads its own session
device, the fingerprints differ, and **no manager PIN can approve the drawer**: the PIN is verified
successfully and then the fingerprint comparison fails, so the operator is told the approval did not
work and the message says nothing about why.

**The movement scheme proves this is an oversight, not a choice.** "Paid in / paid out / safe drop"
uses the same design, and there the two sides are identical field for field — nine fields, including
the `note ?? ''` convention (server `pos-cash.repository.ts:631-643`, till `cash_controller.dart:507-520`).
So the mirroring discipline exists and was applied once; `no_sale` missed it.

**And nothing tests either one.** The API's unit spec mocks the repository
(`pos-cash.service.spec.ts:306`), so the server's string is never computed under test; the till's spec
asserts only that the value it asked the manager to sign is the value it sends
(`cash_center_test.dart:1480-1496`). No test compares the two strings, and the one difference that
matters is invisible to both suites.

**Fix.**

1. **Pick the drawer, not the asker, on both sides.** The action is about the shift's drawer; the
   asking identity is already enforced by the session and the permission check, so both sides should
   join the shift's own `responsible_operator_id` and `holding_device_id` (the till's instinct is
   right; it just used the opening device where the holding one is the live fact).
2. **Or document the pair and use it in both places** — including the operator — with a comment that
   says which fields are the shift's and which are the session's, so the next reviewer can check.
3. **Test the agreement, not each side.** One test that drives a "No sale" approval against a shift
   whose `device_id` differs from its `holding_device_id` and asserts it is accepted; it fails today
   and would have failed when the two strings were written.

**Boundary of this evidence, stated:** I read both computations, traced both sources to their SQL, and
cross-checked the sibling scheme that does agree. I did not drive `reclaim → No sale → manager PIN`
end to end on hardware, because the native window is held by another session's test — that run is the
last step, and it is one scripted flow.

## 69. Approval fingerprints are computed in the wrong place — in both directions

**Severity: med (an internal control whose strength depends on the client, plus §68's trap). Read
2026-10-08 23:5x.**

§68 found one fingerprint that the till and the server compute from different fields. Auditing the
whole family shows the deeper problem: the same field means two incompatible things depending on the
module, and neither meaning is the one the control needs.

### 69.1 Three designs for one word

| Module                                                                                        | Who computes the fingerprint                                                                                                                              | Does the server verify it against the action?                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cash: movement, no-sale, count, resolve, close, recover (`pos-cash.repository.ts`, ten sites) | **the server recomputes** from its own copy of the request and compares                                                                                   | **yes** — and the client must reproduce the string exactly, which §68 shows it does not always do |
| Inventory (dashboard)                                                                         | the **server** computes it during the _preview_ and returns it; the client echoes it back (`inventory-adjust.jsx:118-127`, `inventory-count.jsx:346-355`) | yes, by construction — the client never builds it                                                 |
| Sale exceptions (refunds and voids)                                                           | **the client computes it**: `sha256(jsonEncode({commandId, previewId, previewFingerprint, saleId}))` (`exception_controller.dart:246-256`)                | **no** — see below                                                                                |

### 69.2 What the exception path actually binds

The elevation that a manager's PIN creates stores the string the caller sent, verbatim:

```sql
INSERT INTO runtime.elevation_grant
  (…, permission_key, method, approved_by, expires_at, command_fingerprint)
VALUES (…, $7, 'manager_approval', $1, clock_timestamp() + interval '5 minutes', $8)
```

(`pos-entry.repository.ts:520-560`; `$8` is `input.commandFingerprint`.) At commit, the exception path
looks that elevation up by the same string and never recomputes it
(`pos-exception.repository.ts:797-824`: `e.permission_key='sale.refund.approve' AND
e.command_fingerprint=$5 … FOR UPDATE OF e`, then a single-use `consumed_at` update). The _preview_ is
separately pinned — the commit passes `previewId` and `previewFingerprint` and the lock verifies them
— but nothing ties the **elevation** to that preview.

So the amount the manager approved is enforced only by the client's honesty in hashing the preview it
is about to commit. A client that keeps the string it used for a small refund and commits a larger
one of the same sale satisfies every server-side check: same permission, same session, unexpired,
unused, and a fingerprint the server has no way to recompute.

**How much this matters, stated fairly:** it takes the operator's own hand, since the manager's PIN is
typed on the till's screen and the operator holds the device; and the shipped till does the honest
thing. It is not an outside attack — it is the loss of the second pair of eyes the approval exists
for, which is the whole point of a manager PIN on a refund. There is no test either side of it: the
API's spec mocks the repository, and the till's spec asserts only self-consistency (§68).

### 69.3 The fix is one design, not three

**Let the server own the binding, and let clients echo it.** The inventory path already does exactly
that — the preview returns `commandFingerprint` and the screen sends it back — and it cannot drift
because no client computes anything.

1. For sale exceptions: bind the elevation to the **preview** the server created. Either store the
   preview's id (or the server's own `preview.fingerprint`) on the elevation row and verify it at
   commit, or have the preview response carry a server-computed `commandFingerprint` that the client
   echoes — the pattern the inventory screens use. Then the amount is not negotiable after the
   manager's yes.
2. For cash: keep the recomputation — it is the stronger half — but compute it from **the shift's**
   fields on both sides, as §68 says, so a shift that moved terminals does not lose its drawer.
3. Then delete every client-side hash from the till. After (1) and (2) there is nothing left for a
   client to compute, which is the state where §68's class of bug stops existing rather than being
   found one instance at a time.

## 76. The migration family, run at last: its own recipe builds a target it cannot pass, and fourteen of its failures say nothing about the API

**Severity: med (instrument on the cutover path — this is the only end-to-end read sweep the P7
rehearsal has, and CI never runs it). Measured 2026-10-08 22:20–22:25 local, first time in this hunt
that the four-file family has been executed.**

§16 proved the family _can_ be green when its target is right (P4 rehearsal: `rls` 10/10,
`pooler-isolation` 5/5). This is the same family against the clones actually on this workstation, and
the work it took to read its output is the finding: every red mark below is the _target's_, not the
API's, and nothing in the family says so.

```
Test Files  3 failed | 1 passed (4)
     Tests  2 failed | 13 passed | 10 skipped (25)      ← before the documented harness grants
After re-applying test/integration/harness-roles.sql and setting JWT_ACCESS_SECRET:
  smoke.integration.ts  151 GET routes · 68 answered (<400) · 61 declared · 23 UNEXPECTED
  identity-normalization.integration.ts  8 tests, 1 failed (expected 1016 to be 864)
```

### 76.1 The recipe names one runner; the family then depends on four more

`vitest.integration.config.ts`'s prereq block — the only recipe the family carries — says:

```
1. Build the DB:  PGPORT=5233 docs/migration/build-v3/backfill/00_run_backfill.sh
2. Provision the login roles ONCE:  psql … -f apps/umi-api/test/integration/harness-roles.sql
```

`00_run_backfill.sh` is the half of the chain that _deliberately stops short_, in the words of the
sibling script that completes it (`backfill/01_run_post_backfill.sh`, header): it
"deliberately stops at 53_location_switch_grants, so its output lands on ledger `build-v3-48`", and
"the files after it were then applied by hand, which is how the QA database and the workstation
database ended up at different points with nobody able to say which." Neither the config's prereq
block, nor `harness-roles.sql`, names `01_run_post_backfill.sh` or `migrations/001…011`.

The declared version the app under test carries is `EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION=build-v3-79`
(`apps/umi-api/.env:18`), and the ledger each database actually holds is:

| Database                                         | `runtime.schema_migration`, highest | `/health` |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | --------- |
| `umi_local` (the one the till and dashboard use) | `build-v3-79`                       | 200       |
| `umi_backfill_v3`                                | `build-v3-77`                       | **503**   |
| `umi_backfill_hunt`                              | `build-v3-78`                       | **503**   |

That is the whole of the two `503 /health`, `503 /health/ready` lines in the smoke's unexpected list,
and the index confirms it is the API behaving correctly: the body says
`"expectedSchemaVersion":"build-v3-79"` next to `"state":"Unready"`. **Nothing in the family asserts
the ledger of its own target**, so a target 1–2 steps short reports as two undeclared route
failures.

### 76.2 The fourteen 500s are four columns the clone does not have — and the columns map exactly to its ledger

The smoke records a status and nothing else, so the cause was read with a throwaway probe that boots
the same `AppModule` against the same clone with `{ logger: ['error'] }` and prints the bodies. The
exception filter's own line carries the cause (it is written for exactly this reason,
`all-exceptions.filter.ts:54-66`):

| Route                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `DatabaseError` detail                   | Column's home                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/api/H/admin/reward-config`, `/api/merchants/M/cash/reward-config` (×2)                                                                                                                                         | `column "kind" does not exist`           | `merchant.loyalty_reward.kind`, `20_merchant.sql:774`                                                   |
| `/api/H/admin/customers`, `/api/H/admin/export`, `/api/merchants/M/cash/customers`, `/api/merchants/M/cash/members`, `/api/merchants/M/customers/:id`, `/api/merchants/M/customers/:id/cash`, `/api/H/card` (×7) | `column r.kind does not exist`           | same column, read through `shared/loyalty/reward-config.sql.ts:16,22,33` and `card-state.sql.ts:76-104` |
| `/api/H/admin/stats`, `/api/merchants/M/cash/stats` (×2)                                                                                                                                                         | `column c.rewards_earned does not exist` | `79_cycle_anchor.sql`                                                                                   |
| `/api/H/admin/analytics`, `/api/merchants/M/cash/analytics` (×2)                                                                                                                                                 | `column r.reverted_at does not exist`    | `79_cycle_anchor.sql`                                                                                   |
| `/api/H/admin/customers/:id`                                                                                                                                                                                     | `column cu.device does not exist`        | `78_customer_pass_metadata.sql`                                                                         |

Every one of those columns exists on `umi_local` — where the same routes answer **200** in the live
log (`/cash/stats` ×150, `/cash/analytics` ×151, `/cash/reward-config` ×423, `/cash/customers?page=1…`
200). So the API is not broken; the target is old, and the column set of each clone is exactly its
ledger position: `customer.device` is present on the 78 clone and absent on the 77 clone,
`rewards_earned`/`reverted_at` (both 79) are absent on both.

Worth stating because it changes the priority: of the `/api/:handle/admin/*` spellings in the table,
**none** appears even once in 6 MB of live requests (`admin/stats`, `admin/analytics`,
`admin/customers`, `admin/customers/:id`, `admin/export`, `admin/reward-config` — 0 hits each, while
their `/api/merchants/:id/cash/*` twins carry 150–423 each, and the other `/admin/*` routes such as
`admin/settings` do get called). So this smoke is the only instrument in the tree that exercises the
umi-cash spellings, and on a stale target it reports them broken — evidence about the harness, not
about a route anybody reaches.

The `kind` column is the sharper half, because no ledger step repairs it: `20_merchant.sql` creates it,
`backfill_loyalty.sql:101-103` inserts into it (so the file pair on disk today could not have produced
these tables), and **no file after 20 adds it** — a database built before that create keeps the old
`loyalty_reward` forever, and `runtime.schema_migration` records no hash to notice (§75). That is §75's
argument, one level down: there the editable file was a forward migration, here it is the base chain,
and its only remedy is a full rebuild nobody is told to do.

### 76.3 The two ways the instrument hides what it finds, and one that lets a local file decide

1. **`logger: false`.** `smoke.integration.ts:369-372` boots the app with logging off, so the
   exception filter's `500 request_failed … detail=` line never reaches the run's output and the suite
   prints `500 <url>` alone. One `{ logger: ['error'] }` produced all five column names in a single
   pass. The family's most valuable output — "which route cannot answer, and why" — is one option
   away and has never been switched on.
2. **`readinessExceptions()` is decided by a gitignored file.** It returns `[]` when
   `process.env.EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION` is set (`smoke.integration.ts:138-146`), on the assumption
   that a deployment which states its version is necessarily at it. The app under test loads
   `apps/umi-api/.env` through `ConfigModule`, which sets it to `build-v3-79` — so in _this_ checkout
   the two 503s can never be declared, and the same database produces a different verdict on a machine
   whose `.env` omits the line. The honest form compares the target's ledger to the declared version
   and expects 200 or 503 from that comparison, rather than from whether a variable exists.

### 76.4 Two smaller things the same run measured

The other nine lines of the smoke's "23 unexpected", each checked so the account of 151 routes adds
up: **2** are the readiness pair (76.3.2, the API is right); **1** is
`403 /operations/cash-policy`, which is right — that route asks for `merchant.manage`
(`dashboard-operations.service.ts:105`) and the sweep's cookie is a platform administrator with no
membership in that café, while the owner's own live session reads it 200 (`/operations/cash-policy`
×5 in the live log); **2** are `409` on the Mercado Pago reads, which are deliberate typed refusals
the console reads by code (`MP_POINT_CREDENTIAL_ABSENT` / store required) rather than undeclared
breakage; **2** are `404` on `/recipes/:id/explosion` and `/stock-lots/:id/recall` for an id the sweep
invented — the right answer to the call made, and the declared list simply has no entry for them
(same species as the two 404 entries it _does_ carry); **1** is
`400 /table-order-credentials` without its location context; and **1** is the `/card` 500 already in
76.2's table. So 14 of 23 are the target's staleness, 2 are the harness's own expectation logic, and
7 are correct refusals the exception list never learned.

- **`rls.integration.ts` pins a module list that breaks on the repo's own POS seed.** The assertion
  names `['cash','conversaflow','dashboard','kds']` for Kalala Café; the clone answers
  `cash:true conversaflow:true dashboard:true kds:true pos:true`. Only
  `scripts/umi-pos-local-access-seed.sh` grants `pos` (§16.2: local-only, refuses to run without
  `UMI_POS_DEV_SEED_CONFIRM=disposable`), which is exactly why a clone used for POS work carries it.
  The pin is a snapshot of a database _before_ that seed; it should read the entitlement set from the
  seed's own contract, or say in the test that the target must not have been seeded.
- **`JwtService.signAccess` can mint a token its own `verifyAccess` refuses.** `verifyAccess` requires
  `typeof payload.email === 'string'` (`jwt.service.ts:128-136`), while `signAccess` passes
  `claims.email` through unchecked (`:63-72`). A user row with a blank/NULL email — **1 of the 10 in
  the backfilled clone** — therefore gets a token that is born `401 invalid_token`, with no DB lookup
  involved. It cost me a false lead (see 76.5), and it means "email" is a de-facto NOT NULL the schema
  does not declare.

### 76.5 Withdrawn, recorded so the next reader does not chase it

- **"The API served fourteen 500s and logged nothing at all."** False. The absence of error lines is
  the harness's `logger: false`; with logging on, every 500 has its cause in the log.
- **"The umi-cash read surface is broken."** False as stated: it answers 200 on head (`umi_local`).
  The real defect is the unpinned target and the unattributable report, which is how this section
  reads. My first probe also reported nineteen 401s that I briefly took for a guard problem; they were
  my fixture signing a token for a user with a blank email (76.4), not the API refusing a good one.

### 76.6 Fix, smallest first

1. Give the family a target assertion: read `runtime.schema_migration`'s head and compare it to the
   app's `EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION` before any test runs; fail once, with the two numbers and the
   recipe, instead of 25 scattered verdicts.
2. Put the whole recipe in the config's prereq block: `00_run_backfill.sh` →
   `01_run_post_backfill.sh` → `migrations/001…011` → `harness-roles.sql`, and have the runners write
   the head they reached into `runtime.schema_migration` (the hash §75 asks for) so a stale target is
   detectable rather than inferred from five column names.
3. Turn the smoke's error log on (`logger: ['error']`) and print the `detail` beside each unexpected
   URL; a run that cannot say why a route 500s is not yet an instrument.
4. Derive the readiness expectation from the target's ledger (76.3.2), and unpin the two snapshot
   counts the family still carries (§16.1, §76.4).

## 77. Phone normalization: the length rule closed one door, and the function behind all the others keeps an undialable number as valid-looking E.164 — ten carried customers already hold one

**Severity: med (identity: an undialable number is stored as a deliverable one, and the customer it
belongs to cannot be found by it). Measured 2026-10-08 22:4x local on `umi_local` (head) and on the
carried clone `umi_backfill_v3`, with `umi.e164` probed directly.**

The repo's own doctrine is the sharpest statement of why this matters, and it is already in the tree
(`packages/contract/src/phone.ts:13-21`): a wrong-length number is not rejected by `umi.e164`, it
"falls through to the generic '11..15 digits, keep as international' branch and is stored as a
valid-looking E.164 that reaches nobody… A fabricated E.164 is worse than a rejected one: it is
syntactically deliverable, so it can route to a real person who never signed up." The fix for that was
`nationalDigitsAreValid`, and this section is what its three doors do not cover.

### 77.1 One rule, three doors — and the function behind the rest has no rule

`nationalDigitsAreValid` is called in exactly three places: the POS member-registration DTO
(`register.dto.ts:46`), the contract's `RegisterMemberRequest` (`schemas.ts:323`) and the table-order
QR form (`table-order.ts:145`). The function every _other_ writer funnels through is
`merchant.normalize_identity` → `umi.e164` (`00_foundation.sql:111-136`), and it applies a
country-length rule on one side only:

| Input (probed on `umi_local`)             | `umi.e164`        | Dialable?              |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| `+5266748626` — `+52` + 8 national digits | **NULL**          | no — correctly refused |
| `+52667018516` — `+52` + 9                | `+52667018516`    | **no — kept**          |
| `+5266716222762` — `+52` + 11             | `+5266716222762`  | **no — kept**          |
| `+52556672675598` — `+52` + 12            | `+52556672675598` | **no — kept**          |
| `0000000000`                              | `+520000000000`   | no — kept              |

The verdict is decided by raw string length, not by dialability: a string that begins with a country
code the function _knows_ (`52`, `521`, `1`) and then carries the wrong national length is treated as
an unknown foreign number by the `length(dg) between 11 and 15 then '+' || dg` branch. That is
internally impossible — the country code fixes the length — so the branch is never right for those
inputs.

### 77.2 The population: ten customers in the carried data, all primary, all unreachable

```
select cu.name, m.handle, cm.display_value, c.normalized_value, <digit length>
  from merchant.contact c
  join core.contact_methods cm on cm.id = c.id
  join merchant.customer cu on cu.id = c.customer_id
  join merchant.merchant m on m.id = c.merchant_id
 where c.normalized_value ~ '^\+52'
   and length(regexp_replace(c.normalized_value,'[^0-9]','','g')) <> 12;
```

| Customer                    | Café         | Stored number     | Digits |
| --------------------------- | ------------ | ----------------- | ------ |
| Alma Beatriz Arellano Lopez | elgranribera | `+52667018516`    | 11     |
| Analy Ojeda                 | kalalacafe   | `+52667708255`    | 11     |
| azaza                       | elgranribera | `+52787878787`    | 11     |
| Gema Hernandez              | elgranribera | `+5266716222762`  | 13     |
| Jacqueline Soto             | kalalacafe   | `+5266718054238`  | 13     |
| Oscar                       | elgranribera | `+5266272548178`  | 13     |
| David Beltran               | elgranribera | `+52667376794848` | 14     |
| Kristel Ortiz               | elgranribera | `+52556672675598` | 14     |
| Majo Astorga                | elgranribera | `+52526673439415` | 14     |
| ROSA MARIA OSUNA ACOSTA     | kalalacafe   | `+52526671808141` | 14     |

**10 of the 1014 non-null phone contacts (1.0%)**, every one `is_primary = true`, and all ten pass
through `umi.e164` unchanged today (probed: `passes_through = t` for all ten). Their `display_value`
in the coexisting legacy snapshot is byte-identical to the stored normalized value, so the migration
carried them faithfully — the defect is that the function which now owns this door would accept them
again, not that it created them.

Two consequences, both checked in code rather than assumed:

1. **The customer cannot be found by their own number.** The POS lookup normalizes what the barista
   types and matches exactly — `findPersonCard` (`cash-write.repository.ts:361-378`) computes
   `merchant.normalize_phone($1)` and then `WHERE ct.normalized_value = $2`. `+5266716222762` is
   nobody's number, so typing the café's real 10 digits for Gema returns `null`, and the same is true
   of the identity resolver's spine (`identity.resolver.ts:132-134`, match on `normalized_value`).
   The O-3 raw fallback does not save these rows either: it compares the _trimmed raw string_, and
   these raw strings are already in `+52…` form, so a customer writing `66716222762` matches nothing.
   The observable next step for the resolver is `createCustomer` — i.e. a **second** person for the
   same human, with the card, stamps and wallet pass left on the first. One of the ten already has two
   customers under that name in the same café (`Alma Beatriz Arellano Lopez`: 2 rows), which is
   consistent with that path but is not proof of it — names repeat, and the hunt did not drive a
   duplicate to ground.
2. **A fabricated number is deliverable.** `+52` + 12 digits is a well-formed Mexican number with a
   real area code (`556…`, `526…`), so any campaign, WhatsApp reply or SMS pointed at these rows can
   reach a stranger — the harm `phone.ts` names.

### 77.3 Two input spellings the branches get provably wrong (latent: 0 rows today)

- **`00` is read as a national trunk zero.** `00_foundation.sql:131` is
  `when left(dg,1) = '0' and length(dg) > 10 then '+52' || right(dg,10)` — but in LatAm `00` is the
  _international_ access prefix. Probed: `001 480 401 6182` → `+524804016182` (a US number becomes a
  Mexican one, area code 480 → 631-style MX), and `00 34 600 123 456` → `+524600123456` (a Spanish
  number becomes Mexican). The old fatal function's defect was "decide the country after stripping
  the `+`"; this is the same decision made after stripping `00`.
- **An extension is glued onto the number.** Probed: `+52 667 151 8408 ext 12` → `+52667151840812`
  and `667 151 8408 x12` → `+667151840812` (the second loses its country entirely and becomes a
  foreign-looking number). Both are the "fabricated but deliverable" shape.

Measured population of those two shapes in the carry: **0 of 1016** rows (`like '00%'`: 0; extension
patterns: 0). So they are forward risk, not existing damage — which is the honest reason this section
is `med` and not `high`.

### 77.4 One pinned rule whose cost is now measurable

§77.2's sibling case: `16315551181` (a NANP number written without a `+`) is stored as
`+526315551181` — a **Mexican** number — in two carried contact rows of `kalalacafe`. That is the
documented, _test-pinned_ choice (`identity-normalization.integration.ts:100-110`: "No '+' means
national input, so a leading 1 is Mexico's legacy mobile prefix, NOT country code 1"), and it is not a
defect to call. It is the cost of an ambiguity that cannot be resolved from the string alone, and the
carry shows one live instance of paying it: the US person is stored under a Mexican number, so their
number reaches a stranger and their own number never finds them.

### 77.5 Small drift found on the way

The same customer appears under two different strings. `00_foundation.sql:107` and
`identity-normalization.integration.ts:113` both describe "Mayela's `+5266748626`", but the test's
comment writes `+525266748626` — and probed, that string is **not** NULL, it is
`+525266748626` (12 digits, `+52` + 10, so a perfectly dialable Mexican number). A reader who copies
the comment's example learns the opposite of the rule the assertion enforces.

### 77.6 Fix, smallest first

1. In `umi.e164`, make the `+` branch refuse a known country code with the wrong national length
   instead of falling through to the `11..15` catch-all: `+52`/`+521` ⇒ exactly 10 national digits,
   `+1` ⇒ exactly 10. That is the one condition that turns all ten rows above into honest NULLs at
   write time, and it needs no new table.
2. Decide in writing what a NULL means for those ten _existing_ rows: re-ask the customer for the
   number (the settings screen already edits contacts) or record them as raw-only, as O-3 did for
   Mayela — silently leaving them primary keeps the duplicate-minting door open.
3. Handle `00` before the trunk-zero branch (`left(dg,2) = '00'` ⇒ treat the remainder as an
   international number) and stop at `ext`/`x` before stripping non-digits, so an extension cannot
   become part of the number.
4. Port the length rule into the one place every writer passes through: `merchant.normalize_identity`
   can call a strict variant, with the lookup paths keeping the permissive one — the doctrine in
   `phone.ts:27-31` already says lookups must stay lenient so a customer recorded wrongly can still
   redeem, and that distinction is exactly what the current code cannot express.
