## 90. The stale-dispatch sweeper cannot see device-originated print commands, so a print that stalled mid-dispatch never becomes "unknown outcome"

**Severity: med (a print the operator asked for silently never happens, and the one transition the
product has for exactly this state is filtered out). Measured 2026-10-08 23:3x local on `umi_local`
(17 hardware commands).**

### 90.1 Two ways a command exists, one sweeper

`merchant.hardware_command` has two creation paths and two delivery paths:

|                                                                     | Created by                                                                                                             | Delivered by                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Device-originated** (the till printing its own receipt / reprint) | `POST /hardware/commands` → `repo.createCommand` (`pos-hardware.repository.ts:689`) → `administrative_command_id` NULL | the same device reports its own transitions (`POST commands/:commandId/transition`)  |
| **Administrative** (the dashboard asks a device to print)           | `repo.createAdministrativeCommand` (`:161`) → the column carries the command id                                        | the device polls `GET commands/remote/claim` → `claimAdministrativeCommand` (`:291`) |

Before it claims, the poll runs a **reclaim sweep** for commands a device abandoned mid-dispatch:

```sql
… AND c.originating_pos_device_id = $3
  AND c.administrative_command_id IS NOT NULL     -- ← :307
  AND e.status = 'dispatching'
  AND e.occurred_at < clock_timestamp() - interval '2 minutes'
→ INSERT event 'unknown' / failure_code 'unknown_outcome' / {"statusMessage":"verify_physical_result"}
```

That predicate has nothing to do with staleness — it is provenance. So the sweep can only ever rescue
**administrative** commands, while the commands most likely to stall are the ones the device itself
created, because those are the ones nobody else can finish.

### 90.2 The four rows it should have rescued, measured

| Command              | State 30 h later  | `administrative_command_id` | Created          |
| -------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `print_test_page`    | **`dispatching`** | NULL                        | 2026-10-07 23:08 |
| `controlled_reprint` | `pending`         | NULL                        | 2026-10-07 23:55 |
| `controlled_reprint` | `pending`         | NULL                        | 2026-10-07 23:59 |
| `controlled_reprint` | `pending`         | NULL                        | 2026-10-08 00:17 |

All 17 commands in the database carry a NULL `administrative_command_id`, and 13 of them completed
normally (`pending → dispatching → succeeded`), so the paths above are the live ones. The first row is
the proof of the defect: it has been `dispatching` for ~30 hours, and the sweep that exists for exactly
that state skips it because of its provenance. The product's own idea of what to do — mark it
`unknown_outcome` with the instruction _verify the physical result_ — never runs.

The three `pending` ones are a second, unfilled hole: **nothing ages a `pending` command at all.** The
operator pressed reprint, the row was created, the device never picked it up, and no path — no timeout,
no surface, no operator message — ever says the receipt did not print. This is §15's class again
(a screen promising an action it cannot take) one layer below the UI: the state machines keep a state
nothing leaves.

### 90.3 Fix

1. Remove `administrative_command_id IS NOT NULL` from the reclaim sweep (`:307`): an abandoned
   dispatch is abandoned regardless of who created the command.
2. Add the pending-age rule the `pending` rows need — either the same `unknown_outcome` treatment after
   a bound, or an explicit `failed` with the reason the device never took it.
3. Run the sweep on a clock rather than only as a preamble to a claim (a device that never polls is
   precisely the device whose commands need sweeping), and surface the result to the operator: a
   reprint that did not print is a fact the person at the counter has to know.
4. Assert it with one test: create a device-originated command, never transition it, advance the clock,
   and expect the stale state to resolve rather than sit.

---

## 91. The password-reset token is consumed read-then-write, old links are never invalidated, and there is no unique index — three of them measured against the live database 6 to 1

**Severity: high (account recovery). Measured 2026-10-08 23:4x local; found while checking whether a
July audit's prescription had landed.**

### 91.1 The same codebase has the guarded form and does not use it here

MFA one-time codes are consumed the right way, with the comment saying why:

```ts
// Consume the code. The `consumed_at IS NULL` predicate is the single-use guarantee:
`UPDATE runtime.otp SET consumed_at = now() WHERE id = $1::uuid AND consumed_at IS NULL`   (auth.repository.ts:558-565)
```

The password-reset path is a read, a check in TypeScript, and an unconditional write:

```
findResetToken(tokenHash)   →  SELECT … WHERE token_hash = $1 LIMIT 1        (no lock, no used_at filter)
if (record.usedAt) throw …                                                    (auth.service.ts:591)
updatePassword(record.userId, …)                                              (:598)
markResetTokenUsed(record.id) →  UPDATE … SET used_at = now() WHERE id = $1   (:1108 — no guard)
revokeDashboardSessionsForUser(record.userId, 'credential_changed')           (:600)
```

Two requests holding the same link — a double click, a retry, two tabs, or an attacker racing the owner —
both pass `findResetToken`, both pass the `usedAt` check, and both set a password. The last write wins, and
nothing reports that a second redemption happened.

### 91.2 What the live database says about siblings

```
select count(*) rows, count(distinct token_hash) hashes,
       count(*) filter (where used_at is null) live, count(distinct user_id) users
  from runtime.password_reset_token;
→ 9 rows · 9 hashes · 6 live · 1 user
```

**One user has six simultaneously live reset links.** Issuing a reset never invalidates the previous one
(`insertResetToken` is a bare INSERT, `auth.repository.ts:1064-1070`, and nothing deletes or expires
siblings), and consuming one marks exactly the row the `LIMIT 1` picked. So the sentence a reset flow
implies — "the link you were sent earlier is now dead" — is false for up to N−1 of them, and any link
that leaked stays usable until its own `expires_at`. `revokeDashboardSessionsForUser` closes the sessions,
which is the right instinct applied to the wrong artifact.

### 91.3 And the index the audit asked for is not there

`\d runtime.password_reset_token` shows a primary key on `id` and **no unique index on `token_hash`**. The
July audit prescribed exactly this pair of fixes:

> "make reset-token consumption a single atomic `UPDATE … WHERE used_at IS NULL RETURNING` plus a UNIQUE
> index (kills the TOCTOU)"
> — `docs/migration/build-v3/security-audit-2026-07-12.raw.json`

Neither half landed. Without the unique index, a duplicated `token_hash` would make the `LIMIT 1` lookup
arbitrary — one row consumed, a second still redeemable — which is the same class the predicate is meant
to remove.

### 91.4 Fix (one statement, one index, one invalidation)

1. Consume atomically and return the owner in the same statement:
   `UPDATE runtime.password_reset_token SET used_at = now()
  WHERE token_hash = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
  RETURNING user_id` — the row lock the update takes is the mutual exclusion the read-then-write lacks,
   and a second concurrent caller gets zero rows and the same honest "link already used" answer.
2. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON runtime.password_reset_token (token_hash)`.
3. Invalidate the user's other outstanding tokens when one is used (or when a new one is issued), so the
   count above can never be 6 again.
4. Test it as a race, not as a sequence: two concurrent redemptions of one token, exactly one password
   written.

---

## 92. The rest of the one-time-credential family is guarded — and the offline landing leaves a column that answers its own question wrong

**Severity: none (three verifications) + low (one dead column that reports false alarms). Measured
2026-10-08 23:5x local on `umi_build_v3_ci` and `umi_rehearsal_20261006`.**

### 92.1 Three lenses spent clean, by the same standard §91 failed

| Check                              | Evidence                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| KDS pairing PIN is single-use      | `claimPairing` (`kds.repository.ts:818-827`) is the guarded form: `UPDATE runtime.pairing SET status='used', used_at=now() … WHERE id=$1 AND status='approved' AND used_at IS NULL RETURNING id` — and approval itself adds `AND expires_at > now()` (`:745`) |
| Inbound webhook dedup is atomic    | `INSERT INTO runtime.inbound_event … ON CONFLICT (provider, provider_event_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING id` (`queue.repository.ts:79-83`) — no read-then-write, and the unique key is the vendor's event id                                                       |
| An offline sale lands exactly once | `merchant.offline_provisional_mapping`: **6 mappings in CI and 3 in the rehearsal clone**, each provisional with exactly **1** official sale, no official sale reused by two provisionals (`count(distinct official_sale_id)` equals the row count on both)   |

So the pattern §91 found in the password reset — read, check, unconditional write — is not the house
style; it is one path that missed the pattern the other three follow.

### 92.2 The trap: `offline_replay_command.official_id` is never written

```
select count(*) rows,
       count(*) filter (where accepted_at is not null) accepted,
       count(*) filter (where accepted_at is not null and official_id is null) accepted_without_official
  from merchant.offline_replay_command;
→ CI: 10 rows · 10 accepted · 10 accepted_without_official
→ rehearsal: 5 · 5 · 5
```

Read at face value that says "every offline sale was accepted and **none** landed", which is exactly the
worst possible story for this table and is **false**: the same rows carry
`result = {"status":"accepted","officialId":"88e55178-…"}` — the answer is inside the JSON — and the
relation itself lives in `merchant.offline_provisional_mapping` (`provisional_id → official_sale_id`).
The column exists for the question and nothing writes it.

This is recorded because it caught _this_ hunt: the first measurement above read as 10-of-10 unlanded, a
second query reported "4 duplicated provisional ids", and both were artefacts of the same column — the
duplicates were the four `operational.ack` rows whose `provisional_id` is NULL (grouping counts NULLs as
a value; `count(distinct …)` does not). The truth only appeared on the third query, against a different
table. A future reader should start from `offline_provisional_mapping`.

**Fix:** either write `official_id` in the same transaction that writes the mapping, or drop the column
and let the mapping be the single answer — and point the offline runbook at the mapping so the next audit
does not have to disprove the column first.

---

## 93. Three cash-policy switches are decorative — and one of them cannot be honoured by any code, because the schema forbids it

**Severity: med (an owner can configure behaviour that does not exist; one of the three contradicts a
UNIQUE index). Measured 2026-10-08 23:5x local with an exhaustive grep plus the live catalogue.**

`merchant.cash_shift_policy` carries a dozen switches that travel to the till inside
`CashShiftPolicy`. Four of them are consulted by a decision. **Three are read from the database, carried
in the object, and never used:**

```
registerAssignmentRequired   3 hits:  283 (type)   302 (SELECT)   331 (default)     ← no branch
oneShiftPerOperator          3 hits:  284 (type)   303 (SELECT)   332 (default)     ← no branch
offlineCashShiftAllowed      3 hits:  297 (type)   315 (SELECT)   345 (default)     ← no branch

handoffAllowed               5 hits:  292 310 340 1778 2102                        ← :2102 refuses, :1778 gates
noSaleDrawerAllowed          4 hits:  296 314 344 2194                             ← :2194 throws NO_SALE_DRAWER_DISABLED
```

(Counts are `rg` over `apps/umi-api/src` excluding specs; every hit is listed. All in
`pos-cash.repository.ts`.)

So an owner who sets `offlineCashShiftAllowed = false` has configured nothing: no branch anywhere reads
the value, and the till's offline path (the journal and replay §92 measured) is governed by something
else. The same holds for `registerAssignmentRequired = false` — the assignment requirement lives in the
open-shift code, not in the policy that advertises it.

### 93.1 The third one is worse than unread: it contradicts the schema

`oneShiftPerOperator` says an operator may run more than one shift. The database says otherwise:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX cash_shift_one_active_operator ON merchant.cash_shift
  USING btree (merchant_id, responsible_operator_id)
  WHERE status = ANY (ARRAY['opening','open','suspended','handoff_pending',
                            'counting','reconciliation_required','closing']);
```

(Read from the live catalogue, not the DDL.) Every non-terminal status is covered, so a second active
shift for one operator is **rejected by the index** no matter what the policy says. The flag cannot be
implemented without changing the constraint first — which makes it the strongest form of this defect: not
"nobody wrote the branch", but "the branch could not succeed if it existed".

### 93.2 Stale documentation found on the way (recorded so it is not re-reported)

The superset inventory still says of `closeApprovalThreshold`: _"Exists. The comparison is wrong today
(finding 5.1)."_ The comparison is **fixed**: `pos-cash.repository.ts:1167-1176` gates on the absolute
variance against `policy.closeApprovalThreshold.minorUnits` and carries a comment citing "Deep-design
finding 5.1" and the Toast/Square rule. The design document's line is stale; the code is right. (The same
inventory lists `blindCountRequired`/`countMethod` as "never read", which the till now reads — §15's
screen work.)

### 93.3 Fix

1. For each of the three, choose: implement it (a branch where the policy is consulted) or delete it from
   the policy object and the table. A switch that reads as a control and does nothing is worse than no
   switch, because an owner will rely on it.
2. `oneShiftPerOperator` specifically: the policy must lose to the constraint. Either delete the flag,
   or drop the partial index and enforce the rule in code where the policy can reach it — but not both,
   because they currently disagree.
3. Add the test that makes the class impossible: for every boolean in `CashShiftPolicy`, flip it and
   assert an observable behavioural difference. A boolean with no such test is a boolean for the next
   audit to find.

## 94. The configuration census: 106 declared keys, and the ones nothing reads — including a switch an operator is told to flip

**Severity: med (operational: a documented switch that changes nothing, and a comment that tells a
reviewer the opposite of what the module does). Method measured 2026-10-09 00:0x local.**

### 94.1 The census, and the false positives it produced

`config.schema.ts` declares **106 keys**, every one validated at boot. Grepping each key's bare
identifier across `apps/umi-api/src` (specs and the schema file excluded, which catches
`config.get('K')`, `process.env.K`, destructuring and `cfg.K`) leaves these with **zero real reads**:

```
DATABASE_URL_READONLY      OBJECT_STORAGE_{ENABLED,BUCKET,ENDPOINT,REGION,ACCESS_KEY,SECRET_KEY}
OBSERVABILITY_SCHEMA       GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY       ZETTLE_CLIENT_ID       KDS_STATUS_NOTIFY_ENABLED
```

**Withdrawn from that list before it became a finding:** `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` and
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`. The sweep flagged them (no app code reads them) and they are _correct_:
the process starts with `--require @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node/register`
(`package.json` `start`/`start:worker`), and the OTLP exporter reads those standard variables itself.
Recorded so the next sweep does not re-report them.

### 94.2 `DATABASE_URL_READONLY` is referenced by nothing at all

Not by code, not by a compose file, not by a doc — the only mention in the repository is the schema line
that declares it _"`umi_readonly` (analytics)"_. The role exists in the database, the config has the
slot, and no pool is ever opened for it, so the analytics path has no read-only connection to use and
nothing says so.

### 94.3 `KDS_STATUS_NOTIFY_ENABLED` is documented twice and read by nothing

The schema describes it in detail — "When a KDS transition/partial-cancel runs, emit a
`twilio.status_notification`/`twilio.cancel_notification` outbox row. OFF by default: while the iPad
still hits the Supabase edge functions, the legacy `kds.transition_ticket` RPC already enqueues these —
so enabling here before the iPad is repointed would double-send" — and the deployment runbook repeats it
with an action: _"set `KDS_STATUS_NOTIFY_ENABLED=true`"_ as part of a rollback.

In this repository the flag has **no reader**, and the feature it names has **no producer**: the
consumer half is registered (`outbox-routes.ts:25-31` routes both event types, `outbound.processor.ts:59`
handles them) and nothing anywhere inserts an outbox row of those types. Two readings, and the
deployment doc must say which is true: either the producer lives in the Supabase edge function (then the
flag belongs to that process and this repo's copy is a decoy), or the producer was never written and the
customer is never told the order is ready. Either way an operator flipping the switch as instructed sees
no change in behaviour.

### 94.4 `CASH_WRITE_ENABLED` is dead by design — and a stale comment still sells the gate

The schema is explicit: `CASH_WRITE_ENABLED: booleanFromEnv.default(false), // retained; cash writes are
live`. But `cash.controller.ts:46-47` still says _"Customer-facing wallet/ledger writes are NOT here —
see cash-write.controller (**inert, unmounted unless `CASH_WRITE_ENABLED`**)"_, while
`cash.module.ts:34-42` lists `CashWriteController` in `controllers` with no condition, and the controller
itself documents its live routes (`topup`, `purchase`, `gift-cards`) behind AuthGuard +
MerchantAccessGuard + EntitlementGuard + RolesGuard + `@RequireProduct('cash')`.

So the mount is the truth and the comment is a lie to whoever reads it for a deployment review — the
precise class of stale claim §26 and §93 also found. The routes are guarded, so this is a documentation
defect rather than an exposure; but "this surface is unmounted in production unless a flag is set" is a
sentence an operator will act on.

### 94.5 Fix

1. Every flag: wire it or delete it, and delete its documentation in the same commit. For the four in
   94.1 that still have a purpose (object storage, Maps, Zettle client) that means implementing the
   consumer or removing the key from the schema so an operator cannot set it.
2. For `KDS_STATUS_NOTIFY_ENABLED`, name the **process** that reads it (this API, or the edge function) in
   both places; a switch whose owner is unnamed is a switch nobody can verify.
3. Fix the `cash.controller.ts` comment to say what the module does: the write controller is mounted and
   guarded; the flag is retained history.
4. Same rule as §93, applied to env: no flag ships without a test that sets it and asserts a difference.

---

## 95. The outbox registry has five routes and this repository has one producer: one of the orphans is a documented feature with four shells and no body

**Severity: low (dead capability + a doc line that promises it; the failure direction is safe).
Measured 2026-10-09 00:1x local by diffing the registry against the producers.**

### 95.1 The two sets

`outbox-routes.ts:20-40` registers five event types, and the relay's own docstring says "until these exist
the relay defers every row (no-route)". Producers in `apps/umi-api/src`: **one** —
`turn-commit.repository.ts:43` inside `commitTurnReply`, whose `eventType` is `twilio.reply`
(`turn.service.ts:254`). So four of the five registered routes have no producer in this repo:

| Registered route                                           | Producer here                   | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `twilio.reply`                                             | `commitTurnReply` ✅            | wired                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `twilio.status_notification`, `twilio.cancel_notification` | none                            | the schema comment says the legacy Supabase RPC enqueues them while the iPad is un-repointed — external producer, same ambiguity §94.3 records for its switch                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `whatsapp.lifecycle`                                       | none — and it does not need one | the lifecycle dispatcher enqueues **directly**, durably: `claimSend` first, then a deterministic `jobId`, and if the enqueue throws it **rolls the claim back** so the next cron tick retries (`lifecycle.service.ts:155-172`). The route is redundant, not broken; recording it because "producer enqueues directly" looks like a lost-notification bug and here it is not |
| `twilio.location_pin`                                      | **none anywhere**               | see below                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

### 95.2 The one that is consumer-only end to end

The location pin exists in four places and is reachable from none of them:

- the relay route (`outbox-routes.ts:33-36`),
- the processor case that validates `to/from/lat/lng` and sends it (`outbound.processor.ts:36-55`),
- the adapter method `sendLocationPin` (`twilio.adapter.ts:49-71`) — called by exactly one caller in the
  tree, the processor itself,
- and a **documented tool**: `apps/umi-api/docs/vps-setup.md:215` lists
  `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY=<optional — the location-pin tool degrades to text>` — the same key §94 measured
  as read by nothing at all.

Nothing produces the job, and no tool shares a location. So the deployment doc advertises a capability
whose only implementation is the receiving half; an operator who sets the Maps key to enable it gets
nothing, for the same reason as §94.2 and §94.3.

### 95.3 The safe direction, stated because it is the good half

A producer whose route is **missing** does not lose the event: `relayOne` logs
`no outbox route for event_type=… ; deferring Ns` and calls `deferOutbox` (`outbox-relay.service.ts:113-119`)
— it accumulates rather than disappearing, and it never marks itself delivered. That is the right failure
for a notification: a queue that grows visibly beats a customer message that silently never sent.

### 95.4 Fix

1. For the location pin: write the producer the doc describes, or delete the route, the processor case,
   the adapter method and the doc line together. Four shells are worse than none because they make the
   feature look half-built rather than absent.
2. For the register-with-no-producer pattern in general: log or assert at startup which registered routes
   have no producer in this build, so a route table cannot outlive the feature it was written for —
   the same discipline as §94's "no flag without a test that flips it".
3. For the two KDS notification routes, name the external producer in the schema comment (which process
   and which repository) so the next reader does not have to decide whether the feature is missing.

## 96. The integration chain is documented as open — verified still open, with the consequence measured: a new café's assistant has zero embeddings

**Severity: none new (the repo already records this gap twice) + one measurement that was not on record.
Measured 2026-10-09 00:2x local.**

**Credit first, because this is not a discovery:** the September research already says it —
_"Zettle: exists only as a catalog product-sync job … **No scheduler enqueues `zettle.sync`**
(comment-only in `queues.ts:7`)"_ — and the June addendum records that the _legacy_ `zettle-sync-daily`
cron failed with `ZETTLE_API_KEY not configured`. So this section is a confirmation plus the part nobody
had measured.

### 96.1 The chain, as it stands today

```
zettle.sync      ← nothing enqueues it (integrations.processor.ts:32 only guards on the name)
  ↓ enqueued by integrations.processor.ts:78
product.embed    ← nothing else enqueues it (enrichment.processor.ts:152 re-chains it)
  ↓ enqueued by enrichment.processor.ts:174
embed.backfill   ← nothing else enqueues it
```

Three job names, two queues (`integrations`, `enrichment`), two processors wired with retry policies
(`job-options.ts:74-76`) — and **no entry point anywhere in the repository**. `queues.ts:7` still
describes the queue as a Phase-3 intention in a comment. The `ZETTLE_CLIENT_ID` §94 found read by nothing
is one of the unfinished pieces of the same integration, which is why that census and this chain are
worth reading together.

### 96.2 What it costs, measured

| Database                                                                               | products | product_embedding | message_embedding | knowledge_embedding |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------------------- |
| `umi_local` (a `00_run.sh` + migrations build — the local stack's database)            | 51       | **0**             | **0**             | 0                   |
| `umi_rehearsal_20261006` (the production-shaped clone the legacy backfill ran against) | 195      | **136**           | **1438**          | 0                   |

The vector half of the conversation search is populated **only where the legacy path ran**. A café brought
up on the current build — ONCA's 51 products are in `umi_local` — has no embeddings at all, so
`runtime.product_embedding`, `runtime.message_embedding` and the cosine search built on them have nothing
to search, and the assistant falls back to text matching (`ILIKE`), which the migration notes describe as
the waterfall's second stage. No crash, no error — and the feature those pgvector tables exist for is
inert for exactly the tenants who never had a legacy backfill: the new ones.

### 96.3 What would close it

1. One trigger is enough for the whole chain: a scheduler (or an admin route) that enqueues `zettle.sync`
   for a merchant, or a first `embed.backfill` job for cafés with no Zettle account. The downstream half
   is implemented and tested.
2. Until then, say it where it will be read: the deployment doc and the merchant-provisioning runbook
   should state that embeddings are populated only by the backfill, so "the assistant searched and found
   nothing" is not diagnosed as a search bug.
3. The §94 rule applies to the two keys this chain needs: an unread `ZETTLE_CLIENT_ID` and an unread
   `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` are the shape of a feature left half-wired.

### 96.4 The same gap seen from the engine's side: no turn has ever been created

The queue's downstream is `runtime.conversation_turn` — the debounce/hold machinery that merges rapid
customer messages into one turn (`status pending|processing|completed|failed|superseded`, partial index on
the two active ones, `hold_until`/`released_at`). It holds **0 rows in all three databases**
(`umi_rehearsal_20261006`, `umi_local`, `umi_build_v3_ci`) while the production-shaped clone carries
**1475 real messages** from the legacy backfill. So no message has ever been turned into a turn by this
build: the "stuck turn" question cannot even be asked here, and it corroborates §96 from the other side —
the engine's tables exist, its processors are wired, and nothing has ever reached them.

## 97. Lenses spent on the conversation engine and the queue topology (recorded so they are not re-run)

**Severity: none (verification). Measured 2026-10-09 00:3x local.**

- **The queue topology is complete.** `queues.ts` declares seven queues (`system`, `turns`, `enrichment`,
  `outbound`, `integrations`, `lifecycle`, `tender`) and there are exactly **seven `@Processor`
  declarations**, one per queue — and every queue has a producer except the §96 chain
  (`integrations`/`enrichment`, whose downstream is wired and whose entry point is missing). The
  `tender` queue's own docstring is worth keeping in mind when adding one: two processors on a queue
  _compete_ rather than cooperate, and the comment records the incident where a tender notification was
  swallowed by the wrong consumer.
- **The message table's shape holds where real data exists** (1475 rows in the production-shaped clone):
  `occurred_at` is `NOT NULL` and no row has a null time, which matters because the triage queue orders by
  `m.occurred_at DESC` — in Postgres a `DESC` sort puts **NULLs first**, so a single null would have made
  a message with no timestamp look like "the newest word" and mis-report who is waiting. The constraint
  closes it.
- **The sender vocabulary in real data is exactly two values**: `customer` 755, `bot` 720, no `staff` and
  no `system`. `body` is nullable in the schema and both readers that surface it coerce with `|| ''`
  (`customers.service.ts` maps `lastMessage: row.last_message || ''`), so a body-less message renders as
  empty rather than `null` on screen.

## 98. The stock ledger and its projection: two instruments green, and — unlike §88 — the equality is structural, not a snapshot

**Severity: none (verification). Measured 2026-10-09 00:4x local on `umi_build_v3_ci` (112 ledger rows,
24 items) and `umi_rehearsal_20261006` (39 rows, 13 items).**

### 98.1 Both instruments, green in both databases

```
running sum of effect_on_hand per (inventory_location_id, inventory_item_id), ordered by sequence:
  CI          112 rows · 0 negative · worst running 0
  rehearsal    39 rows · 0 negative · worst running 0

cached projection vs derived ledger (merchant.stock_balance vs SUM(effect_*)):
  CI           24 comparisons · 0 on_hand disagreements · 0 reserved disagreements
  rehearsal    13 comparisons · 0 · 0
```

So stock can never be consumed below zero in the data that exists, and the cached projection is faithful
to the ledger that produced it — the same two results §85 found for stored value.

### 98.2 The derived-of-derived fields hold too

`stock_balance` also carries `available` and `ledger_sequence`, both computed from the same row — the
usual place for a second generation of drift:

- `available = on_hand − reserved` in **24 of 24** rows (CI) and **13 of 13** (rehearsal).
- `ledger_sequence` equals the maximum ledger `sequence` for that `(location, item)` in every row —
  **0 stale, 0 ahead** — so the projection's own "as of" marker is exact, not just plausible.

### 98.3 Why it holds: one door, one transaction, one lock

No trigger maintains the projection (the only trigger on the ledger is `stock_ledger_append_only`), and
`stock_balance` is read in six places across five modules — including the till's catalog
(`pos-catalog.repository.ts:107,135,230,252`), where availability gates whether a product can be sold. So
the projection is application-maintained, which is where drift usually starts. Here it does not, and the
reason is structural:

- there is exactly **one door**: `merchant.append_stock_ledger(…)` locks the balance row
  (`select * into v_balance from merchant.stock_balance … for update`), inserts the ledger entry and
  **updates `stock_balance` in the same transaction** (`:55-67`, `:136`, `:167`);
- **no code inserts into `stock_ledger_entry` directly** — a grep for `INSERT INTO
merchant.stock_ledger_entry` over `apps/umi-api/src` returns nothing, and every caller found
  (procurement, pos-checkout, inventory-authoring) goes through the function;
- the ledger itself is append-only by trigger, and `rebuild_stock_balance` exists as the repair path if
  the projection is ever distrusted.

### 98.4 The contrast that makes the three areas legible

| Area                     | Equality today                                                        | Why                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stored value (§85)       | 0 negative running rows, 392 rows                                     | the spend path takes `FOR UPDATE` before comparing                              |
| **Stock (this section)** | **0 negative, and cache == ledger in every row**                      | **one door, one transaction, one lock, append-only ledger, rebuild function**   |
| Loyalty loop (§88)       | visits and balances equal — but only because the backfill copied them | **nothing joins the two ledgers**: no trigger, no dual-write, no reconciliation |

Three questions of the same shape, three different levels of guarantee, and the report now says which is
which: two are enforced, one is a snapshot waiting for its first post-cutover writer.

## 99. The security audit table's own doctrine says it exists for denials — and the operator PIN's lockout writes nothing

**Severity: med-high (the durable record an incident responder needs has no failures in it, and one
class leaves no trace anywhere). Measured 2026-10-09 01:0x local on `umi_local` and its API log.**

### 99.1 The doctrine, in the codebase's own words

`modules/auth/mfa.service.ts:193-197`, above the MFA denial write:

> "The database, not stdout. `runtime.security_audit_event` exists for denials, lockouts and credential
> failures; a log line on the VPS is not queryable, is not alertable, and rotation eventually discards
> it."

and MFA follows it: `eventType: 'mfa.verify_failed'`, `outcome: 'denied'`,
`reasonCode: 'wrong_code' | 'code_burned'`, with the attempt count in `metadata`.

### 99.2 What the table actually holds

```
select event_type, outcome, count(*) from runtime.security_audit_event group by 1,2;
→ operator.session_started       success  51
  operator.locked                success  15
  device.enrollment_created      success   8
  device.enrollment_claimed      success   5
  device.enrollment_approved     success   5
  device.credential_delivered    success   5
  device.enrollment_completed    success   5
  operator.ended                 success   3
  device.enrollment_claim_denied denied    1
```

**98 rows, nine event types, one denial** — and that denial is a device claim, not a credential. There is
**no credential failure of any kind in the entire history of this database**, while the same database holds
`runtime.password_reset_token` (9 rows), `runtime.otp`, and a device whose `pin_failed_attempts` §15.1
watched go from 0 to 1 when a wrong operator PIN was typed on the real till.

### 99.3 The three classes that are detected and not recorded

| Class                                            | Detected by                                                                                               | Where it lands                                           | Durable?                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wrong operator PIN, and the lockout it causes    | `pos-entry.repository.ts:375-376` — `pin_failed_attempts = least(…+1, 10)`, `pin_locked_until` set from 5 | **a counter on `merchant.device`**                       | no — it is capped, and the next successful PIN resets it |
| Rate-limit refusal                               | `operational.interceptor` / `ip-rate-limit.guard` → `429 request_refused`                                 | stdout `warn` only: **1089 lines** in this one local log | no                                                       |
| Webhook signature rejection (Mercado Pago Point) | `point-webhook.controller.ts` → `mercado_pago_point_webhook_rejected`                                     | stdout `warn` (1 line here)                              | no                                                       |

The PIN case is the sharpest: a credential attack on a till produces **no log line either** (`rg
'PIN_INVALID|pin_failed'` over the local API log returns nothing) — the only trace was the counter this
hunt happened to read. So "which terminal was attacked, when, and how many times" is not answerable from
anything that survives a restart, which is precisely the argument the MFA comment makes.

### 99.4 Fix

1. Write the event where the code already knows: in the PIN failure path and on the lockout, in the same
   shape MFA uses (`eventType: 'elevation.pin_failed'`, `outcome: 'denied'`,
   `reasonCode: 'wrong_pin' | 'locked'`, attempts in `metadata`) — the caller already has the device id,
   the location and the correlation id.
2. Same treatment for the two logging-only classes: a refusal the guard computes is a denial the table
   should hold. (For the rate limiter, aggregate per bucket rather than one row per request, or the table
   inherits the 1089-row shape of the log.)
3. Add the test that makes the log trustworthy: for each denial class the system can produce, trigger it
   in an integration suite and expect a row. A security log with no failures in it is indistinguishable
   from a security log that does not work — and this database has 98 rows and zero.

---

## 100. Three vocabularies for one printed receipt, and the receipts screen filters by a state the database cannot produce

**Severity: med (a dead filter and an invisible failure on the screen whose job is to show failed
receipts). Measured 2026-10-09 01:1x local: the DB CHECK lists, the repository's own SELECT, and the
screen's filter code.**

### 100.1 The three vocabularies

| Source                                                | Values                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `hardware_command_event.status` (DB CHECK)            | `pending`, `dispatching`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `retryable`, `cancelled`, `unknown`                     |
| `hardware_print_job_event.status` (DB CHECK)          | `queued`, `printing`, `printed`, `retryable_failure`, `terminal_failure`, `cancelled`, `unknown_outcome` |
| The receipts screen (`recibos.jsx:14-19`, `:465-467`) | `printed`, `queued`/`printing`, `not_printed`, **`failed`**                                              |

Two of them are declared in the contract as separate lists (`pos-hardware.ts:114-115` and `:302-303`) and
as separate constraints in the database; **only `cancelled` is spelled the same in the first two.** The
third is the screen's own, and between the second and the third there is no mapping at all:

```sql
-- dashboard-operations.repository.ts:116,121 — the receipts domain
coalesce(j.status,'not_printed') AS status
  … LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT … coalesce(e.status,'queued') AS status
                         FROM merchant.hardware_print_job p …) j ON true
```

The API passes the raw print-job status through. So the screen receives seven possible values and filters
with four.

### 100.2 The live symptom: "Fallidos" can never match

```
{ id: 'failed', label: msg`Fallidos`, match: (s) => s === 'failed' }          // recibos.jsx:18
const failed = items.filter((i) => i.status === 'failed').length;            // :467
```

`failed` is **not in the print-job vocabulary** — the CHECK allows `terminal_failure` and
`retryable_failure`, and no code maps either onto `failed`. So:

- the **Fallidos chip filters to nothing and its counter is always 0**, and
- a receipt whose print **failed terminally** — i.e. the customer walked away without a receipt, the one
  case this screen exists to catch — matches **no chip at all**: not `printed`, not `queued|printing`, not
  `not_printed` (its job exists), not `failed`.

`cancelled` and `unknown_outcome` are uncovered the same way. The screen is otherwise careful — it lists
the four states it expects and counts them — which is why the gap is invisible: the numbers add up to
less than the list.

### 100.3 Fix

1. Map in one place: either the repository translates the seven job states onto the screen's vocabulary
   (`terminal_failure`/`retryable_failure` → `failed`, `cancelled`/`unknown_outcome` → their own), or the
   contract publishes the mapping and the screen's `FILTERS` is typed against it.
2. Type both maps so a new state is a compile error rather than a missing chip — the same fix §70 and
   §70.1 ask for in the dashboard's other two status maps.
3. Add the assertion to the receipts domain's own check: **the states the screen can filter on must be a
   superset of the states the query can return**, which is a one-line comparison of two lists and would
   have caught this before the first terminal failure.

## 101. The variance reason has nine values in the contract and five in the only picker — and the four unreachable ones are the diagnosable ones

**Severity: med (the audit record is wrong exactly where it could be right). Measured 2026-10-09 01:2x
local: the contract enum, the picker's items, and a grep for the four values across every app.**

### 101.1 The two lists

The contract declares the vocabulary and the API validates against it
(`packages/contract/src/pos-cash.ts:63-73`, used by three request schemas at `:523`, `:536`, `:550`):

```
no_variance · counting_error · change_error · unrecorded_paid_in · unrecorded_paid_out ·
missing_safe_drop · cash_handling_error · unknown_operational_difference · other_approved_reason
```

The till's dropdown — the only screen that records a variance reason — offers **five**
(`apps/umi-pos/lib/features/cash/cash_surface.dart:2764-2781`):

```
no_variance · counting_error · change_error · cash_handling_error · unknown_operational_difference
```

And the four that are missing are missing everywhere: a tree-wide grep for
`unrecorded_paid_in|unrecorded_paid_out|missing_safe_drop|other_approved_reason` returns hits only in
`packages/contract/src/pos-cash.ts` (and its generated copies) plus one unrelated exception enum — **no
screen, no service, no test**. They are declared, accepted by the API, and unreachable from the product.

### 101.2 Why this is worse than a short list

The four unreachable values are the ones that _name a cause_:

- `unrecorded_paid_in` / `unrecorded_paid_out` — money moved through the drawer and nobody booked it;
- `missing_safe_drop` — the drop that explains the shortage;
- `other_approved_reason` — the schema's own designed catch-all, whose name says an approval exists.

An operator whose drawer is short because of an unrecorded safe drop has no way to say so: the only
choices left that fit are `cash_handling_error` or `unknown_operational_difference`. So the
"Motivo de la diferencia" record reads _unknown_ for the cause the system is most able to name — and the
report that exists to show the owner where the money goes accumulates one vague label instead of three
specific ones. The two remaining slots in the picker (`counting_error`, `change_error`) are real, which
is what makes the gap look deliberate rather than unfinished.

### 101.3 The contrast that makes this specific, not general

Cash **movement** reasons are free text by design: the till asks for a sentence and turns it into a code
with `reason.replaceAll(RegExp(r'\s+'), '_').toLowerCase()` (`cash_surface.dart:2466-2467`), so the
system is not shy about reasons. The five-value list is specific to the **variance** picker — the one
place where the vocabulary _is_ enumerated, and where four of the nine are unreachable.

### 101.4 Fix

1. Add the four options to the dropdown — the labels write themselves ("Ingreso no registrado", "Retiro
   no registrado", "Caja fuerte omitida", "Otro motivo aprobado") — or delete the four from the enum and
   its three request schemas if the doctrine is that the till may not choose them.
2. Add the write-direction twin of §100's rule: **every value of the vocabulary a picker writes must
   appear in the picker's list**. Both assertions are one-line set comparisons, and together they close
   the read and write directions of this class.

## 102. The vocabulary sweep, mechanised: 167 enumerated sets, 29 with a value no app can produce — and two that are not placeholders

**Severity: low-med (dead vocabulary that reads like capability). Method 2026-10-09 01:3x local.**

### 102.1 The instrument

§101 was one hand-picked vocabulary. This is all of them: read every single-column `CHECK (x = ANY
(ARRAY[…] ))` from the live catalogue (167 in `merchant`, `runtime` excluded where the sets are internal),
extract the values, and grep the three app trees (`apps/umi-api/src`, `apps/umi-pos/lib`,
`apps/umi-dashboard/src`, generated Dart and specs excluded) for each literal. A value with **zero app
references** is a value no product code can produce or consume.

29 of the 167 have at least one. The ones whose names end in **`_foundation`** are deliberate
placeholders — the codebase marks reserved-for-later values that way (`transfer_in_foundation`,
`cover_open_foundation`, `points_expired_foundation`, `print_kitchen_ticket_foundation`,
`profiling_foundation`, `terms_acceptance_foundation`, …) — and they are not defects; the convention is
worth keeping precisely because it makes this sweep readable. The interesting entries are the ones
without that suffix:

| Vocabulary                                               | Values no app references                                             | Reading                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pos_checkout_draft.state`                               | **`payment_rejected`**                                               | verified below                                            |
| `cash_reconciliation.outcome`                            | `recount_required`, `posting_pending`, `ambiguous_cash_effect`       | `recount_required` verified below                         |
| `cash_count_attempt.state`                               | `recount_required`                                                   | the same fact, a second dedicated column, also unused     |
| `loyalty_points_ledger.entry_type`                       | `points_earn_pending/committed/cancelled/reversed`                   | §96's inert chain, seen from the vocabulary               |
| `customer_consent_history.consent_type`                  | `marketing_email`, `marketing_sms`, `loyalty_enrollment`, … (5 of 6) | consistent with both consent tables holding 0 rows        |
| `table_reservation.status`                               | `no_show`                                                            | a real operational event with no writer                   |
| `loyalty_gift_card.status`                               | `depleted`                                                           | a card that empties has no status for it                  |
| `product_location_availability.status`                   | `out_of_assortment`                                                  | a third availability state nothing sets                   |
| `contact.verification_status`                            | `suppressed`, `provider_unavailable`                                 | both are states a messaging provider produces in practice |
| `loyalty_reward.{type,reward_type,combinability_policy}` | `spend_cashback`, five `reward_type`s, `explicit_stack`              | the reward ladder is narrower in code than in schema      |
| `hardware_command_event.failure_code`                    | `hardware_not_assigned`, `location_mismatch`, `register_mismatch`    | three plausible device refusals no code emits or maps     |

### 102.2 The two verified instances

**`payment_rejected`** is declared in `packages/contract/src/pos-checkout.ts:22` as one of the ten
`CheckoutState` values, is generated into both clients' types, and appears **nowhere in any app tree** —
the API never sets it and the till never handles it. The decline path in this codebase is expressed
twice already (`PAYMENT_DECLINED` as a failure code, `declined` as an attempt status), so this is a
third spelling nothing uses. One more detail while it is in view: the stale-draft sweep excludes
`('completed','receipt_available','payment_unknown')` (`pos-checkout.repository.ts:414`) — **it does not
exclude `payment_rejected`**, so if anything ever set that state the recovery sweep would keep treating
the draft as live.

**`recount_required`, twice.** `requestRecount` (`pos-cash.repository.ts:875`) moves the shift's status
(`reconciliation_required → counting`, §15) and writes an audit event — and writes **neither**
`cash_count_attempt.state = 'recount_required'` nor `cash_reconciliation.outcome = 'recount_required'`,
the two columns whose vocabularies provide that exact value. So the recount is recorded (the audit event
is real — §15 counted it), but a query against either of the two columns that name it **cannot see a
recount at all**. The reader who trusts `cash_reconciliation.outcome` gets a history with no recounts in
it.

### 102.3 Fix

1. For each entry above, choose: wire it, rename it with the `_foundation` convention (which is the
   codebase's own way of saying "reserved, not implemented"), or delete it. The schedule matters more
   than the choice: a vocabulary value is a promise, and today four of them are promises nobody can keep.
2. Add the sweep as a check, with the convention as the escape hatch: **every value of every enumerated
   set is referenced by app code, or its name ends in `_foundation`**. It is one script and this section
   is its first output.
3. For `payment_rejected` specifically: delete it from `CheckoutState` (the decline path already has two
   names), or add it to the stale-draft exclusion list and the till's state handling in the same commit.

## 103. Sessions: the documented invariant holds, and seven rows sit "live" with no expiry — fail-closed, unfixable, unpruned

**Severity: low (hygiene; the authentication paths fail closed, so nothing is exposed). Measured
2026-10-09 01:4x local on `umi_local` (149 rows) and `umi_rehearsal_20261006` (15).**

### 103.1 The census

```
umi_local:        82 rows revoked but still unexpired · 66 rows live (revoked_at IS NULL) · 1 row with expires_at NULL
rehearsal clone:  …                                               · …                                 · 6 rows with expires_at NULL
```

149 sessions for one human plus a handful of devices, and 82 revoked rows that stay until they expire —
nothing prunes the table, which is normal until it is not.

### 103.2 The invariant the code documents, checked

`cash/customer-session.service.ts:147` states the pairing as a fact of the schema: _"`is_active = (revoked_at
is null)`"_. Measured across both databases: **0 violations in 164 rows**, and specifically 0 rows that are
`is_active` with a `revoked_at` (which would be authenticatable by any predicate that checks only
`is_active`) and 0 rows inactive without a revocation. The pairing is real, not aspirational.

### 103.3 The seven rows that report live and can never authenticate

`runtime.session.expires_at` is **nullable** — nothing in the schema forbids a session without an expiry —
and 7 rows across the two databases have it NULL (1 live, 6 in the clone). Every authentication predicate
in the tree is a strict comparison:

```
auth.repository.ts:379,395      … WHERE s.id=$1 AND s.is_active AND s.expires_at>now()
pos-entry.repository.ts:199,467,533   … AND expires_at>now() / >clock_timestamp()
```

`NULL > now()` is NULL, not true, so those rows are **never selected**: the failure mode is closed, and the
one in `umi_local` is a dead row rather than an eternal session. What makes it worth recording is the
_disagreement between two true statements_: the row reports `is_active = t, revoked_at = NULL` — i.e. any
census of live sessions counts it — while no code path can ever use it. A "how many sessions are open?"
query written from the second truth will be wrong, and the row will never be pruned or revoked by anything.

Worth noting beside it: the July audit prescribed a `runtime.resolve_session` definer function in this
database; the live catalogue holds only `invalidate_operator_sessions_for_rbac` and
`revoke_device_sessions`. So every session check is hand-written application SQL — which is exactly how a
nullable column keeps a null for a day.

### 103.4 Fix

1. `expires_at` becomes `NOT NULL` (with a CHECK and a backfill for the existing rows): no path honours a
   null, so the schema should not allow one.
2. A housekeeping job that revokes/expires rows past `expires_at` and deletes revoked rows past a
   retention window — 82 already linger in one dev database.
3. One definition of "live": a view — `revoked_at IS NULL AND is_active AND expires_at > now()` — so a
   census and an authentication path cannot disagree about the same row.

---

## 104. The platform boundary — the highest-privilege predicate in the product — verified single-sourced and correct

**Severity: none (verification). Measured 2026-10-09 01:5x local.**

### 104.1 One constant, four call sites

`PLATFORM_GRANT_CTE` (`modules/auth/rbac.sql.ts:31-43`) is the predicate that decides whether a login sees
and acts on **every** café. Its own header records why it exists as a constant: it was "copy-pasted
verbatim across `findMerchantsForUser`, `findMembershipAccess`, and `MerchantsRepository.merchantsForUser`;
three independent copies risk silently diverging." Today it is interpolated in four places —
`merchants.repository.ts:249` (the `/me/merchants` list), `auth.repository.ts:912` (membership access),
`:995`, and `:941` inside `platformRole()`, which is what `PlatformAdminGuard` calls — so the guard and the
list **cannot** disagree about who is a platform operator. That is the check that mattered most in this
area, and it passes.

### 104.2 The four conditions, and what each one prevents

```sql
SELECT (SELECT r.key FROM umi.user_role ur JOIN umi.role r ON r.id = ur.role_id
         WHERE ur.user_id = $1::uuid AND r.is_platform
           AND ur.revoked_at IS NULL
           AND (ur.expires_at IS NULL OR ur.expires_at > now())
         ORDER BY CASE r.key WHEN 'super_admin' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END LIMIT 1) AS platform_role
```

- `r.is_platform` — the grant is a platform one, not a café role (the header notes `umi.user_role` now
  holds only platform grants);
- `ur.revoked_at IS NULL` — a **revoked** operator is not an operator (the failure that would have been
  catastrophic and is not there);
- the expiry clause — a time-boxed grant stops working when it runs out;
- the ordering — `super_admin` beats `developer`, which is the whole reason the predicate returns a role
  key rather than a boolean (the header records that a boolean "could only ever mean super_admin", which
  is why `developer` granted nothing for months).

And the write side is narrower on purpose: `PlatformAdminGuard` admits **`super_admin` only**, with the
doctrine written above it — "`developer` has cross-merchant REACH and read-only AUTHORITY … Admitting any
platform grant here would let a debugging login create cafés."

### 104.3 The client half is not a dead field

The console gates on `merchantState?.platformRole !== 'super_admin'` (`cafes.jsx:355`) — a client-side
check, which is fine because the server gates too. That field is real: the contract declares it
(`schemas.ts:81`, `z.enum(['super_admin','developer']).nullable()`), the login/refresh envelope carries it
(`auth.service.ts:242,361`), and the server **narrows** it with `narrowPlatformRole` — mapping anything
outside the two contract values to `null` — with the reasoning stated: "a client gating a platform screen
on an enum it does not know fails open". Fail-closed, typed, and matching on both sides.

### 104.4 The census, and the one thing still untested

`umi_local` defines **2** platform roles and holds exactly **1** live grant — `super_admin`. So the
`developer` role (cross-merchant reach, read-only authority) has **no holder in this database**: the
doctrine is correct in code and untested by data. Driving it once — a `developer` login reading another
café successfully and being refused `POST /merchants` and `POST /api/platform/wallet/push` — would make
the read-only half a measurement instead of a comment. (Informational, not a defect: the guard's 403 body
names the caller their own platform role, `role: role ?? 'none'`.)

---

## 105. The RLS sweep, mechanised: 150 tenant tables, 7 without RLS — and the module that looks like a hole is a documented exception

**Severity: none (verification) + one withdrawn lead. Measured 2026-10-09 02:0x local on `umi_local`.**

### 105.1 Every table with a tenant column, checked

The query asks the catalogue, not the DDL: every ordinary table in `merchant`/`runtime` that carries a
`merchant_id` or `tenant_id` column, and its `relrowsecurity` / `relforcerowsecurity` / policy count.

```
tenant tables 150 · RLS enabled 143 · RLS forced 143 · no RLS 7 · RLS with zero policies 0
```

**143 of 150 have RLS enabled _and_ forced, and every one of those has at least one policy** — 0 tables
in the "enabled but unguarded" state that reads as protection and is not. The 7 without RLS are all in
`runtime`: `dead_letter`, `device_enrollment_request`, `inbound_event`, `outbox_event`, `pairing`,
`platform_elevation`, `session`.

### 105.2 The 7 are sealed by grants instead, and the grants are exact

`runtime` is the "sealed machinery" schema the July audit describes — no RLS, ever, on purpose. That is
safe only if the RLS-confined request role cannot reach it, so the grants are the real check, and they are
clean: `has_table_privilege` says **false** for `api` on SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for all seven,
while `worker` holds INSERT on each. Every request-path read or write therefore fails closed at the role
level, and the audit's own residual note — that `api` might keep INSERT-only on `runtime.outbox_event` —
was **not** taken: even that is revoked, and `turn-commit.repository.ts:43` enqueues through the worker
transaction instead. Stricter than prescribed, and verified.

### 105.3 The pool doctrine, and the census that shows who follows it

`PgService.query()` runs on the **worker** pool (`pg.service.ts:353-354`, BYPASSRLS), and its docstring
enumerates the legitimate uses: "work that RESOLVES which merchant a request belongs to (merchant-by-handle
at login, inbound WhatsApp number → merchant), work that is genuinely cross-merchant (outbox draining,
cron enumerating active merchants, reconciliation), and the sealed auth substrate." Counting the two
idioms per module:

```
dashboard-operations 0 privileged · customers 0 · pos-cash 0 · procurement 0
inventory-authoring 0 · pos-catalog 0        conversations 8 · kds 9
```

The six modules that always know their merchant use the RLS-scoped path exclusively; the two that use the
privileged one are the two the doctrine names — device/token resolution, and the unauthenticated WhatsApp
ingress.

### 105.4 Withdrawn: the 14 unscoped tenant statements in `conversations/*` are the documented exception

The sweep first flagged something that looked like a hole: 14 privileged-pool statements in
`conversations/*.repository.ts` touch tenant tables with **no `merchant_id` predicate** —
`messages.repository.ts:45,76,95,128` and `memory.repository.ts:80,122` (all `merchant.message`),
`conversations.repository.ts:168,175` (`UPDATE merchant.conversation … WHERE id=$1`), and
`conversation-turns.repository.ts:77,110`. On a BYPASSRLS pool the only filter is an id, which is exactly
the shape a cross-tenant bug takes.

It is not one, and the files say so in their headers: `messages.repository.ts:13-15` — _"Runs on the worker
pool (unauthenticated WhatsApp path). The insert uses plain `query` (autocommit) — NOT a transaction — so a
unique-violation on a duplicate `provider_message_id` doesn't poison an open transaction"_ — and
`conversation-turns.repository.ts:9-10` — _"Worker pool — the WhatsApp path is unauthenticated."_ An
unauthenticated ingress has no tenant to scope by: there is no session to trust and no GUC to set, so RLS
cannot apply, and the id is derived server-side through the inbound-number → merchant → conversation
chain. Recorded so the count is not re-raised as a finding — these 14 are the third category of the
doctrine, written down where they live.

## 106. The till honours "this product is unavailable at this location" and nothing in the product can say so

**Severity: med (an operational feature the till is built to obey and no operator can drive; §67's class,
in the catalogue). Measured 2026-10-09 02:1x local: every reference in the tree, with correct flags.**

### 106.1 Every reference to `merchant.product_location_availability`

```
docs/migration/build-v3/20_merchant.sql:1005,1022     the table and its comment
docs/migration/build-v3/90_rls.sql:361                its RLS policy entry
scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:337,347                  a shell seed writes two rows
apps/umi-api/src/modules/table-order/table-order.integration.ts:398   a test fixture writes one
apps/umi-api/src/modules/pos-catalog/pos-catalog.repository.ts:127    read (LEFT JOIN)
apps/umi-api/src/modules/pos-cart/pos-cart.repository.ts:181          read (LEFT JOIN)
```

That is the whole set. No controller, no service, no dashboard screen, no till action, and **no dynamic
SQL** (`rg 'merchant\.\$\{'` over the API returns nothing, so the table name is never interpolated). The
contract's only availability route is a **read**: `pos.inventoryAvailability`, `method: 'GET'`, permission
`inventory.read` (`route-table.ts:2966-2973`). So the only things in this repository that have ever
populated the table are a demo seed and a test.

### 106.2 The read side is complete, which is what makes it a defect

The till does not ignore the column — it maps every status carefully
(`pos-catalog.repository.ts:99-116`):

```sql
CASE WHEN a.status NOT IN ('enabled','future_availability') THEN a.status
     WHEN a.status = 'future_availability' AND a.available_from > now() THEN 'future_availability'
     … ELSE … 'temporarily_unavailable' … END AS availability
```

so `disabled`, `temporarily_unavailable`, `out_of_assortment` and a dated `future_availability` all reach
the catalogue and the cart, and the CHECK that ties `future_availability` to `available_from` is the shape
of a feature that was designed to be used.

### 106.3 Measured: nobody has used it

| database                                      | rows                                             |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `umi_local` (the café the local stack serves) | **none**                                         |
| `umi_build_v3_ci`                             | 3 × `temporarily_unavailable` (the test fixture) |
| `umi_rehearsal_20261006`                      | 1 × `temporarily_unavailable` (seed or fixture)  |

So the café that this workstation has been driving cannot 86 a product: "se acabó el croissant" has no
button, no route and no row — the only ways are `psql` or the demo seed. The till would hide the product
correctly the moment a row existed, which is exactly the asymmetry §67 recorded for opening-hour
exceptions ("a feature the model advertises and nothing can write"), and it is the same shadow §102's
vocabulary sweep saw when `out_of_assortment` came up unreferenced.

### 106.4 Fix

1. Build the write path the rest of the design already assumes: a POS action ("no disponible" / 86 for
   this location, with the four reasons the CHECK enumerates) plus the admin route that sets a dated
   `future_availability`; the CHECK gives the form its validation for free.
2. Or delete the table, its RLS entry and both readers — a read-only availability table is a promise the
   product does not keep, and it costs a join on the catalogue's hot path.
3. Whichever way, assert it: the availability status a reader can render must be settable by some writer,
   which is §101's set-comparison rule applied to catalogue state instead of to a picker.

---

## 107. The generalisation of §106: six tables the product reads and only a shell script, a fixture or a migration ever writes — including the checkout policy the pilot certified

**Severity: high (menu variants and four policy tables are seed-only; the certified features that depend on
them are unreachable for any café not created by the demo seed). Measured 2026-10-09 02:2x local.**

### 107.1 The sweep, and how it was refined

§106 was one table found by hand. This is all 145 base tables in `merchant`, counted for readers
(`FROM`/`JOIN`) and writers (`INSERT INTO`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE FROM`) in `apps/umi-api/src` with specs and
integration fixtures excluded:

```
145 tables → 23 with readers and zero app writers
           → 16 explained: a DB function writes them (append_stock_ledger, commit_customer_value,
             append_loyalty_points, append_gift_card_fact, transition_hardware_command, …)
           →  7 left: no app writer AND no function whose body mentions the table
```

The 16 are the codebase's _preferred_ pattern (one door, §98): my grep was blind to function-based writes,
and the refinement (grep `pg_proc.prosrc`) cleared them. §106's `product_location_availability` was in the
7; the other six are below, and they are not all the same kind of gap.

### 107.2 Who writes them

| table                           | readers | rows in `umi_local` | the only writers                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `product_variant`               | 7       | 24                  | `scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:360`, `migrations/002_onca_onboarding.sql:424`                                         |
| `product_media`                 | 2       | **0**               | `scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:671`                                                                                   |
| `inventory_policy`              | 15      | **0**               | `scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:467`, `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:754`                                                |
| `pos_checkout_policy`           | 1       | **0**               | `scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:117`                                                                                   |
| `pos_exception_policy`          | 1       | **0**               | `scripts/umi-pos-demo-seed.sh:148`, `scripts/umi-pos-gate5a-live-fixture.sql:277`, `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:232` |
| `pos_offline_cash_policy`       | 1       | **0**               | `scripts/umi-pos-gate5a-live-fixture.sql:534`                                                                        |
| `product_location_availability` | 2       | 0                   | §106 (`umi-pos-demo-seed.sh`)                                                                                        |

**The "product" column is empty for every one of them**: no controller, service, dashboard screen or till
action writes any of these six. The writers are a demo shell script, two test/fixture scripts and one
onboarding migration.

### 107.3 What that costs, per table

- **`pos_checkout_policy` — the sharpest case.** It is empty in **all three** databases (`umi_local`,
  `umi_build_v3_ci`, `umi_rehearsal_20261006`), and the reader fails closed to a named default
  (`pos-checkout.repository.ts:171-179`): `version: 'default-deny'`, `manualTerminalEnabled: false`,
  `mixedTenderEnabled: false`, `maximumTenderLines: 1`. So the effective configuration of every deployment
  is: **no split payment, no manual terminal** — the two features the pilot's own certification exercises
  (`certify_mixed_tender`, and the `external_terminal` tenders in the gate data) and which no screen can
  turn on. A café that was not created by `umi-pos-demo-seed.sh` cannot have them.
- **`inventory_policy` — 15 readers, no door.** Negative-stock policy, reservation and low-stock thresholds
  are read all over the inventory module; without a row the module runs on its defaults, and an owner
  cannot change them.
- **`pos_exception_policy` / `pos_offline_cash_policy`** — refunds/voids and offline cash are governed by
  policies whose rows exist only where a fixture put them (CI 1 and 4, rehearsal 1 and 1) and are absent
  from the live local database.
- **`product_variant` — 7 readers, 24 seeded rows, no runtime path.** The till's catalogue and cart resolve
  variants (`pos-cart.repository.ts:180`: `v.id=$4 AND v.product_id=p.id AND v.active`) and
  `table-order.service.ts:437` lists products _through_ their variants, so sizing ("Grande / Chico") is a
  first-class part of the menu — and **nothing can add a variant to a product**. A café's menu can only
  contain variants that arrived from a seed or a migration.
- **`product_media` — 0 rows anywhere, no runtime path**: product images are read by the catalogue and can
  never be attached.

### 107.4 Why this is not "unfinished placeholders"

The distinction matters for the fix. These are not `_foundation`-style reserved values (§102): the readers
are complete, the tables have RLS entries and check constraints, the till renders every status they can
hold, and two of the features (mixed tender, manual terminal) are _certified_ by Gate 5A. The missing half
is the write path — which is exactly what makes the certification misleading: it proves behaviour on a
database a shell script provisioned, not on one the product can produce.

### 107.5 Fix

1. Give each table its door, in the order of what a café actually needs: variants and media in the menu
   authoring screen (they are menu, not policy), the four policies in the settings surface that already
   owns their sibling (`cash_shift_policy` has an owner switch — §93), and product availability in the POS
   (§106).
2. Or retire the ones with no plan: drop the table, its RLS entry and its readers, so the catalogue's hot
   path stops joining a table that can only ever be empty.
3. And make the sweep a check, because this class is invisible from either side alone: **a table with
   readers, no writer in the product, and no writing function must be classified in one place as either
   legacy-carried (with the carrier named) or missing-a-door.** Six of the seven above are the second kind.

### 107.6 The other two money policies, checked: all three fail closed, which is what makes the seed the only door

§107.3 quoted the checkout policy's `default-deny`. The same question was asked of the other two, and all
three answer safely when the row is missing — which removes the risk I was looking for and _sharpens_ the
finding:

| policy table              | rows in `umi_local` | behaviour with no row                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pos_checkout_policy`     | 0                   | `version:'default-deny'`, `mixedTenderEnabled:false`, `manualTerminalEnabled:false`, `maximumTenderLines:1` (`pos-checkout.repository.ts:171-179`)                                                                                                       |
| `pos_exception_policy`    | 0                   | `version:'default-deny'`, `refundsEnabled:false`, `voidsEnabled:false`, both windows `0`, `requireDifferentApprover:true` (`pos-exception.repository.ts:1878-1892`)                                                                                      |
| `pos_offline_cash_policy` | 0                   | the reader returns `null` (`:133`) and its only caller maps that to disabled: `configured?.allowedDeviceClasses.includes(…) ?? false` and `enabled = Boolean(configured?.enabled && configured.expiresAt > now() && …)` (`pos-offline.service.ts:62-76`) |

The columns fail closed too: `pos_offline_cash_policy.enabled` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT false`,
`allowed_device_classes` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT {pos_terminal}`, `expires_at` and `currency` are `NOT NULL`
— so even a half-written policy row denies by default, and the `?.includes` cannot throw on a null array.

Composed, the sentence a café actually experiences: **without the seed scripts, mixed tender, manual
terminal, refunds, voids and offline cash are all off, and no screen in the product can turn any of them
on** — and those are precisely the behaviours Gate 5A certifies. The safety is real; the reachability is
the defect.

_Withdrawn sub-lead:_ "the offline policy returns `null` with no default, so a caller might read it as
unlimited" — its single caller fails closed, as quoted above.
