`comms`, `loyalty`, `observability`, `queue`. The v3 revoke is
`revoke all on all tables in schema umi, merchant, runtime, kds from public;` (`docs/migration/build-v3/90_rls.sql:48`):
an enumeration of four schemas, one object class. Anything the chain did not create, and any class the line does not
name, keeps the stock defaults — and one of those defaults is a live phone normalizer with a fatal branch.

### 139.1 What lives there

The restored clone (`umi_backfill_hunt`, the September dump carried forward) has **32 relations** in `core` and `ops`
that a chain-built database does not have at all: `core.users` (9 rows), `core.sessions` (228), `core.tenant_memberships`
(12), `core.people` (1005), `core.contact_methods` (1016), `core.password_reset_tokens`, `core.integration_tokens`,
`core.tenants` (5), `ops.orders` (53), `ops.order_items` (76), `ops.order_events` (211), `ops.payments`, `ops.refunds`,
and `ops.v_kds_tickets` (a view). `umi_local` reports `ERROR: schema "core" does not exist`. So in one database these
tables and functions are the customer and credential record of five cafés, and in the other they are nothing — which is
why every statement about "the schema" needs to name which database it means.

### 139.2 The grant set, measured per object class

| Object class                                   | Chain-built (`umi_local`)                                           | Restored clone (`umi_backfill_hunt`)                                                                   | Line that decides it                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `core` / `ops` schemas                         | do not exist                                                        | `core nspacl = {postgres=UC, worker=U, api=U}`, `ops = {postgres=UC, api=U}`                           | inherited from the v2 grant `grant usage on schema core, ops, … to umi_app` (`apps/umi-api/db/roles/002_api_grants.sql:21`), never re-named or re-scoped by v3 |
| `core` / `ops` tables                          | —                                                                   | `api` holds **nothing** (all four privileges false on all 31 tables)                                   | §137's index row stands for this class: the legacy tables grant `api` nothing                                                                                  |
| `core` / `ops` functions                       | —                                                                   | **11 of 11 carry `proacl = NULL`**, i.e. the stock `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC`; `api` and `worker` both true | no `revoke … on function` and no `all functions in schema core` appears anywhere in the tree                                                                   |
| `extensions` functions                         | `api` has schema `USAGE` (`api=U`), so **387 of 387** are reachable | `api` has **no** `USAGE` on `extensions`, so all 387 are unreachable despite the same `proacl = NULL`  | `build-v3/00_foundation.sql:78` grants the USAGE to `api`, and the dump predates it                                                                            |
| product schemas (`merchant`, `umi`, `runtime`) | 91 + 5 + 2 functions                                                | same                                                                                                   | 0 carry a NULL ACL — the per-schema revoke works where the chain enumerates                                                                                    |
| `public`                                       | 1 function (`tg_touch_updated_at`, `proacl = NULL`)                 | same                                                                                                   | trigger function; not callable directly                                                                                                                        |

Two facts fall out. First, the revoke's shape is _per-schema enumeration_, so its correctness is a function of the
enumeration being complete — and it is not, on the database that has the extra schemas. Second, `proacl = NULL` is not
the same as reachable: `has_function_privilege` answers about the function, while `has_schema_privilege` decides whether
the call can be made at all. Probed with a throwaway role created inside the transaction (`create role hunt_probe
nologin`): `EXECUTE` true on `core.resolve_contact`, `core.can_access_tenant` and `core.normalize_phone`, `USAGE` on
`core` **false** — and the call then fails with `ERROR: permission denied for schema core`. The schema USAGE is the real
gate, which is exactly why `api` holding it is the finding.

### 139.3 The write, probed rather than inferred

`core.resolve_contact(uuid, text, text, text, text, text)` is `SECURITY DEFINER`, owner `postgres`, with
`SET search_path TO 'core', 'pg_temp'` — the hardening is right. It **writes**: it inserts into `core.people` and
`core.contact_methods`, in the tenant named by its first argument, with no membership check anywhere in the body.

```
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL ROLE api_login;
  has_table_privilege('core.people','INSERT')  ->  f          -- the direct privilege is absent
  core.resolve_contact('<tenant>','email','hunt-probe@example.invalid','probe','hunt','probe-1')
    ->  5b5a2e7b-f2c7-4036-af14-7073061e0489                  -- and the row is created anyway
RESET ROLE;
  count(*) from core.contact_methods where display_value='hunt-probe@example.invalid'  ->  1
ROLLBACK;
  count(*) …  ->  0
```

So the privilege that matters is not the table grant at all: it is `EXECUTE` on a definer function that owns a write the
request-path role is otherwise denied. The same shape is in the umi-cash call site
(`apps/umi-cash/src/lib/identity.ts:36`) — but that file is a **frozen June import** of the old app (last touched
2026-06-20, §153.2), so the door exists wherever the legacy schemas do while no current product path walks through it. `core.can_access_tenant` is
the other definer: `stable`, owner `postgres`, reading `core.tenant_memberships` for `core.current_user_id()`, which
makes it an oracle for "does the user named in the GUC belong to tenant X" — false whenever the GUC is unset, so the
leak is bounded to the caller's own scope. Noted, not inflated.

### 139.4 `api` does not denote one grant set

The repository declares a much wider shape than either database has. `apps/umi-api/db/roles/002_api_grants.sql` — the
Phase-2 cutover file, whose header says the grants were "verified end-to-end against a canonical schema replica" — gives
`umi_app` `select, insert, update, delete on all tables in schema core, ops, comms, loyalty`
(`:31`), `select on all tables in schema observability`, `usage, select on all sequences` and
`execute on all functions in schema core, loyalty, ops, comms` (`:52`), plus
`alter default privileges in schema core, ops, comms, loyalty grant … to umi_app` (`:57-58`) so future tables inherit it.
`004_buildv3_login_roles.sql` then creates `api_login login in role api`, and `build-v3/00_foundation.sql:12` creates
`api` as a fresh group role. The name is the same; the grant set behind it is not. Three shapes share one word:

|                               | `core`/`ops` tables             | `core`/`ops` functions   | `core`/`ops` schema USAGE for the request role |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| chain-built                   | absent                          | absent                   | absent (schema absent)                         |
| restored clone                | **nothing** to `api`            | stock `PUBLIC` `EXECUTE` | **granted**                                    |
| declared / production Phase-2 | **full DML** to `umi_app`→`api` | stock `PUBLIC` `EXECUTE` | **granted**                                    |

The declared shape is the one to size, and it can be simulated inside a rolled-back transaction: `grant select, insert,
update, delete on all tables in schema core, ops to api_login`, then `SET LOCAL ROLE api_login`. The legacy tables turn
out to be well defended _as tables_ — `relrowsecurity = t` **and** `relforcerowsecurity = t` on `core.users`,
`core.sessions`, `core.password_reset_tokens`, `core.integration_tokens`, `core.tenant_memberships`, `ops.orders`,
`ops.payments`, `ops.refunds` (unlike the `merchant` tables §137 found with `force = f`), and the policy predicate is
two-sided: `row_tenant_id = core.current_tenant_id() and core.can_access_tenant(core.current_tenant_id())`. With no GUC
set the read is 0 rows — fail-closed, as designed. With the two scope GUCs set to a **real pair the caller can read out
of the data it already holds** — `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '<tenant>'; SET LOCAL app.user_id = '<user>';` — the same
role reads `core.users` = 1 row and `core.sessions` = **5 rows**, and `core.password_reset_tokens` = 0 for that tenant.
The boundary is therefore "whatever the app asserts, plus one membership row for the asserted user" — nothing binds the
asserted user to the authenticated session, which is the same conclusion the 2026-07-12 audit reached for the
`umi`/`runtime` substrate and the same one §137/§138 reach by another route.

### 139.5 The high-severity half: two normalizers, one of them fatal

The legacy surface is not only a privilege question. `core.normalize_phone` is live, and its `+1` branch is wrong. Both
normalizers are installed in the same clone, so they can be compared on identical input in one query:

```
core.normalize_phone('+1 480 401 6182')   ->  +524804016182      -- a US number rewritten as a Mexican one
umi.e164('+1 480 401 6182')               ->  +14804016182       -- correct
core.normalize_phone('0034600123456')     ->  +524600123456      -- int'l prefix '00' truncated into MX
umi.e164('0034600123456')                 ->  +34600123456       -- correct
core.normalize_phone('0 34 600 123 456')  ->  +524600123456      -- two spellings, one fake number
umi.e164('+34 600123456')                 ->  +34600123456       -- the real one stays separate
```

The mechanism is a missing `had_plus`: both implementations do `left(d,1)='0' and length>10 -> '+52'||right(d,10)`, and
the legacy one also does `length=11 and left='1' -> '+52'||right(d,10)` — which is why country code 1 is _structurally_
unreachable there. The chain's replacement (`umi.e164`, `docs/migration/build-v3/00_foundation.sql:105-135`) fixes both
by deciding on `had_plus` before stripping digits, and its comment says so in as many words: the old branch "strips the
`+` BEFORE deciding the country, so a real NANP number (+1 480 401 6182) is rewritten into a Mexican number that belongs
to nobody." The consequences are two, and both are live:

1. **A wrong number is stored as a customer's identity anchor.** umi-cash normalizes through the DB
   (`apps/umi-cash/src/lib/identity.ts:17-19`), then resolves the contact through `core.resolve_contact` (`:36`), which
   writes `core.contact_methods.normalized_value`. Its `findPersonByPhone` (`:47-52`) matches on that same value, so the
   record is self-consistent — and points at a stranger's phone. Any WhatsApp or SMS the product sends to that customer
   reaches a third party. Measured: `core.contact_methods` holds 1016 normalized rows and **0** of them start with
   `+1`, while `merchant.contact` in the same database holds **8** — the new model kept what the normalizer recognized,
   the legacy model rewrote all of them.
2. **The same human gets two identities, or one identity absorbs another.** `0034600123456` and `0 34 600 123 456`
   collapse into one key while `+34 600123456` stays apart, so dedup both over-merges and under-merges depending on how
   the number was typed.

The chain knew: `docs/migration/2026-07-21-core-resolve-contact-normalized-phone.sql` is the patch that gave
`core.people.normalized_phone` a writer and reports "169 of 572 people" null. But the API side has this backwards —
`apps/umi-api/src/modules/identity/identity.resolver.ts:248` calls its normalizer "identical to the backfill's
`core.normalize_phone`" while the line beneath it (`:256`) calls `merchant.normalize_identity`, the **fixed** one. The
comment describes the broken function as the source of truth, so a future reader "restoring parity" would reintroduce
the fatality.

### 139.6 Two sequences nothing owns

`merchant.order_event_sequence_seq` and `merchant.kitchen_event_sequence_seq` exist in **both** databases, and neither is
created by anything in the tree: `rg 'create sequence' docs/migration/` returns one unrelated hit in a Supabase dump,
`0` columns carry a `nextval` default on them, and no file in `apps/` references either name. They are leftovers of a
`serial`-era column. Their ACLs differ: `NULL` (owner-only) in `umi_local`, `{postgres=rwU, api=rU, worker=rU}` in the
clone. So the restored database hands the request role `USAGE` on two objects the product never created and never uses —
the same class of surplus as §137, at the smallest possible scale.

### 139.7 Fix

The revoke should be written by class and by absence, not by enumeration, and the legacy surface should be either
adopted or retired explicitly:

1. `revoke all on schema core, ops, comms, loyalty, observability, queue, legacy, _migration, grow from public, api,
worker, readonly;` — then grant back the USAGE each role actually needs. A schema that the chain does not create
   cannot be enumerated safely, so the revoke has to be idempotent and re-run on the `pg_restore` path
   (`00_run_backfill.sh` already re-applies `90_rls.sql`; add this line to that file so it rides along).
2. `revoke execute on all functions in schema core, ops, comms, loyalty from public, api, worker, readonly;` — the
   `PUBLIC` default is the reason 11 of 11 legacy functions are open. Then `grant execute` per function, as §138.5 does
   per signature.
3. Turn the fingerprint into an assertion with the two halves §139.2 separates: for every schema the request role cannot
   see, `has_schema_privilege('api', s, 'USAGE')` is false; and for every function in a schema it _can_ see,
   `has_function_privilege('api', oid, 'EXECUTE')` is checked per OID. A check that only counts tables would pass on
   this database, and a check written on `proname` would pass on §138's pair.
4. Decide the normalizer question once: point the last legacy caller at `merchant.normalize_identity`/`umi.e164`, or
   backport `had_plus` into `core.normalize_phone`. Two live implementations of one identity key in one database is the
   §114/§117/§132 lens again, and this time the divergence has already reached customer rows.
5. Correct the comment at `identity.resolver.ts:248`. The code is right; the sentence beside it names the wrong
   function as canonical.

## 140. The guard the till trusts is not the guard the server applies: a shift in `counting` has no resume path on either side, and four of the attempts were audited as successes

The operator's report was "I cannot resume the shift". The till is not lying and the API is not refusing: the resume
**is** admitted and **is** accepted, and the shift does not move. The database says so, the audit table says so, and the
client has a second, unreachable path of its own.

### 140.1 The live state

`merchant.cash_shift` in `umi_local` holds exactly one row: `a45f4711-cde1-4a7f-b7b1-34e17bde6a13`, register
`5aedd2e0-dc2a-4d78-a240-7ec0105a1518` (CAJA-1), `status = counting`, `version = 30`, `ledger_sequence = 8`; the
register is `counting`, `version = 25`, `current_shift_id` pointing at that shift. The audit trail explains how it got
there: opened 2026-10-07 23:19:24 (`cash.shift_opened`), suspended 2026-10-08 07:00:22 (`cash.shift_suspended`), count
submitted 07:03:54 with `outcomeCode = approval_required` (`cash.count_submitted`), **recount requested 07:04:46**
(`cash.recount_requested`) — and `requestRecount` sets `status='counting'`
(`pos-cash.repository.ts:876/909`), where it has sat since.

### 140.2 The clause that admits and then cancels itself

`transition(…, target='open')` (`pos-cash.repository.ts:1949-1992`) builds `source` as
`['open','suspended','handoff_pending','counting','reconciliation_required','closing']`, so the `WHERE … status=ANY($8)`
matches a shift in `counting`. The `SET` then undoes it:

```sql
SET status=CASE
      WHEN $7='open' AND status IN ('counting','reconciliation_required','closing')
        THEN status          -- the status it already had
      ELSE $7
    END
```

`UPDATE 1` is not an error, so the repository returns the row and the controller answers success. Probed with the
repository's own statement inside a transaction: the row comes back `status = counting`, `version = 31`, and the
`ROLLBACK` proves nothing else was attempted. The domain table agrees with the client, not with the server:
`transitions.counting = ['reconciliation_required','blocked']` (`cash-domain.ts:162`) — resuming is not an edge, and the
function that says so (`canTransitionShift`) has no production caller (§116).

### 140.3 The client refuses before the server can

Both resume paths in the till gate on the status the server just ignored:

| Path                              | Gate                                                                          | Source                                                   |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| automatic, at app start           | `recoveryState == 'operator_mismatch'` **and** `shift['status'] == 'open'`    | `cash_controller.dart:343-352` (`_shouldResumeOwnShift`) |
| the PIN pad, at the point of sale | `recoveryState == 'shift_suspended'` **and** `shift['status'] == 'suspended'` | `cash_controller.dart:118-135` (`canResumePausedShift`)  |

For a shift in `counting` neither is true, so `_shouldResumeOwnShift` returns false, `recoverOwnShift()` returns `null`
without a message, and the catalog falls back to the menu (`catalog_surface.dart:3084-3087`). The Caja screen's own
"Reanudar turno" button has no such guard — it calls `suspendOrResume(suspend: false)`
(`cash_surface.dart:1368`, `cash_controller.dart:533-552`), which is the only path that reaches the no-op above. So the
screen offers the one action that cannot work, and the two actions that would (count, cancel count) are hidden because
the server advertised `resume` instead: the snapshot's branch order is `!sessionMatches → ['resume']` _before_ any status
branch (`pos-cash.repository.ts:1896-1912`), so a stale operator session on a `counting` shift is told "resume" while
the shift's own state says "count".

### 140.4 Four false successes in the audit table

`cash.shift_open` is the event the resume path appends (`cash.service.ts:416`, `eventType: \`cash.shift_${target}\``).
After the recount at 07:04:46, the audit table holds four of them with `outcome = 'success'`:

| When (UTC)          | Event             | Outcome | The shift        |
| ------------------- | ----------------- | ------- | ---------------- |
| 2026-10-08 23:33:43 | `cash.shift_open` | success | still `counting` |
| 2026-10-09 01:42:21 | `cash.shift_open` | success | still `counting` |
| 2026-10-09 03:11:08 | `cash.shift_open` | success | still `counting` |
| 2026-10-09 07:42:43 | `cash.shift_open` | success | still `counting` |

This is the hunt's first finding where the audit trail itself is wrong: the table the design leans on for
"who did what to the money" records four successful opens of a shift that never opened. §99 was about denials that go
unrecorded; this is the mirror image, a success that did not happen. A tamper-evident hash chain over a false statement
is still a false statement.

### 140.5 The refusal that arrives as a 500

When the row does not match — a stale `expectedShiftVersion`, or a device or operator that no longer holds the shift —
the same method throws a bare `Error`:

```ts
if (!rows[0]) throw new Error('INVALID_SHIFT_TRANSITION');   // pos-cash.repository.ts:1992
```

`INVALID_SHIFT_TRANSITION` is caught by nothing: `rg` finds it once, at its throw site. `AllExceptionsFilter`
(`all-exceptions.filter.ts:42-51`) only reads a code out of an `HttpException`, so a plain `Error` becomes
`500 { code: 'INTERNAL_ERROR', message: 'Internal server error' }` (`:147`) with the real reason left in the server log.
So the honest refusal is the one shape the till cannot show, and §118's class — a code that exists in the schema but no
client can see — has a live instance rather than a catalogue one.

### 140.6 What the operator can actually do, measured

`counting` has exactly one exit (`submitCount` → `reconciliation_required`, `:758/819`), and the only path back to
`open` is `cancelCount`, which demands `status='reconciliation_required'` (`:941`). A shift stranded in `counting`
therefore cannot be cancelled — it has to accept a second count first. The guards that would allow the cancel
afterwards all hold on this row: no `merchant.cash_variance_resolution` row, no `merchant.cash_reconciliation` row, and
the count's recorded `ledger_sequence = 8` still equals the shift's. The alternatives are the manager path (`recover`,
which refuses the shift's own responsible operator with `SHIFT_NOT_ORPHANED`, `:2438`) and opening a new shift, which
the partial index `cash_shift_one_unresolved_register` forbids while this one exists in a state outside
`(closed, blocked, recovered)` — so the register is locked, not just the shift.

### 140.7 Fix

1. Make the transition table authoritative where the writes happen: call `canTransitionShift(current.status, 'open')`
   inside the lock and throw a **typed** refusal. Either the clause admits a state and moves it, or it refuses; the
   `CASE` that returns the status it already had has to go. Once `counting` is not admitted, §140.4's false events stop
   being written.
2. Derive `allowedActions` from the status, not from the session state alone. A `counting` shift whose stored session is
   stale should offer `count`/`cancel_count`, not `resume`; the branch order in the snapshot is the whole bug.
3. Give the till a path out of `counting`: either let `cancelCount` accept `counting` as well (its ledger and resolution
   guards already prove the money has not moved), or let the client submit-and-cancel in one step. Today the operator
   must invent a second count to get their drawer back.
4. Register the shift codes in the error map — `INVALID_SHIFT_TRANSITION`, `STALE_COUNT`, `CASH_POLICY_DENIED`,
   `SHIFT_NOT_RECOVERABLE`, `SHIFT_NOT_CLOSABLE`, `RECOUNT_NOT_AVAILABLE`, `COUNT_NOT_CANCELLABLE`,
   `VARIANCE_ALREADY_RESOLVED`, `APPROVAL_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH`, `SHIFT_NOT_ORPHANED` — as 409s with their own codes, so
   a refusal reads as a refusal and not as a server fault.
5. Never audit a state change that did not happen: append `cash.shift_open` after the returned row proves the move, or
   record the no-op under its own event type.

## 141. The legacy surface measured whole: what the request role can reach, the eighteen tables that carry no policy, and an abandoned trace of customer conversations that the declared grant hands to the app role

§139 measured `core`/`ops` because those were the schemas with functions. The revoke's shape is an enumeration of
schemas **and** classes, so the question that finishes the axis is the whole set: every legacy schema, both databases,
and all four object classes. Doing it turns up a second, unrelated store of personal data that no current code path
writes and none reads.

### 141.1 The sweep

Every non-system schema on both databases, with what the request role actually holds (`api_login` is a member of `api`,
so its privileges are `api`'s):

| Schema          | Exists in a chain build | `api` schema `USAGE` (clone)                 | Tables | `api` table grants (clone) | RLS on | RLS **forced**       |
| --------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------- | ------ | -------------------- |
| `merchant`      | yes                     | yes                                          | 145    | per §137                   | 145    | 145 (**all**)        |
| `umi`           | yes                     | yes                                          | 22     | per §137                   | 5      | 5 (**all of the 5**) |
| `runtime`       | yes                     | yes                                          | 27     | 27 of 27 (**§137**)        | 9      | 9                    |
| `kds`           | yes                     | no                                           | 0      | —                          | —      | —                    |
| `extensions`    | yes                     | **no** in the clone / yes in the chain build | 0      | —                          | —      | —                    |
| `core`          | **no**                  | **yes**                                      | 17     | 0                          | 17     | 17                   |
| `ops`           | **no**                  | **yes**                                      | 14     | 0                          | 14     | 14                   |
| `loyalty`       | **no**                  | **yes**                                      | 17     | 0                          | 17     | 17                   |
| `grow`          | **no**                  | **yes**                                      | 4      | 0                          | **0**  | 0                    |
| `comms`         | **no**                  | no                                           | 9      | 0                          | 9      | 9                    |
| `device`        | **no**                  | no                                           | 4      | 0                          | 4      | 4                    |
| `kitchen`       | **no**                  | no                                           | 3      | 0                          | 3      | 3                    |
| `observability` | **no**                  | **no**                                       | 8      | 0                          | **0**  | 0                    |
| `queue`         | **no**                  | **no**                                       | 6      | 0                          | **0**  | 0                    |

Two results, and they pull in opposite directions. The good one: **not a single legacy table grants `api` anything** —
so §137's sentence is right for the class it measured, and the six schemas with forced RLS are defended twice over.
The bad one: the schema USAGE and the function EXECUTE are not part of that sentence, and four schemas grant `api`
USAGE (`core`, `ops`, `loyalty`, `grow`) while 11 of the 11 functions behind them sit at the `PUBLIC` default (§139.2).
`pg_default_acl` is **empty** on this clone, so there are no standing defaults here either — the declared file's
`alter default privileges` never ran against this shape. Correcting §137's "the legacy schemas grant `api` nothing in
either" by class, then: **tables true, schemas false for four of them, functions false for `core` and `ops`** — and
`extensions` is the mirror image, 387 functions at the `PUBLIC` default and reachable in the chain build where
`api` holds the USAGE, unreachable in the clone where it does not.

### 141.2 What is stored there

The reason the class matters is what the unreachable tables hold, and how much of it is real customer value:

| Schema          | The rows (clone)                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `loyalty`       | 997 `accounts`, 1010 `cards`, 357 `balances`, 1007 `pass_devices`, 967 `passes`, 390 `points_ledger`, 49 `wallet_transactions`, 161 `earned/spent redemptions`, 2554 `visit_events`, 165 `otp_verifications`, plus a 1-row `gift_card_ledger` |
| `comms`         | 1475 `messages`, 3449 `conversation_turns`, 12 `conversations` — the customer conversations                                                                                                                                                   |
| `observability` | 818 `security_events`, 3022 `edge_logs`, 5279 `pipeline_spans`, 521 `ai_runs`, 20 `audit_log`                                                                                                                                                 |
| `queue`         | 2860 `jobs`, 2763 `job_attempts`, 465 `outbox_events`, 446 `inbound_events`, 3 `dead_letters`                                                                                                                                                 |
| `core` / `ops`  | the identity and order record of §139.1                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

### 141.3 Eighteen tables with no policy at all

`grow` (4), `observability` (8) and `queue` (6) carry `relrowsecurity = f` on every table — no policy, no force, no
tenant predicate of any kind. They are sealed **only** by the absence of grants: `api` holds no table privilege on any
of them in this shape, and it lacks schema USAGE on `observability` and `queue` besides, which is why the control read
below fails with `permission denied for schema observability`. That is a real seal and it should be said plainly. It is
also a single-line seal: the repository's own Phase-2 file hands `umi_app` `select on all tables in schema
observability` (`002_api_grants.sql:32`), and on a database created before the v3 role rename `api` **is** `umi_app`
(§139.4). One granted line separates the request role from 818 records of customer phone numbers and message text.

### 141.4 The read, probed

Inside a transaction, with the declared grant applied and rolled back:

```
BEGIN; SAVEPOINT control;
SET LOCAL ROLE api_login;  SELECT count(*) FROM observability.security_events;
  -> ERROR: permission denied for schema observability        -- sealed by USAGE, exactly as §139.2 predicted
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT control;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA observability TO api_login;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA observability TO api_login;
SET LOCAL ROLE api_login;
  current_user = api_login
  security_events = 818   distinct tenant_id = 0   with a phone = 818
  edge_logs       = 3022
  pipeline_spans  = 5279
  audit_log       = 20
ROLLBACK;
```

No row-security policy stands in the way because there is none on those tables, and no GUC has to be set because the
predicate that would read one does not exist. The count of distinct tenants is **zero** for a different reason, and it
is the more serious half.

### 141.5 The discriminator that was never written

`security_events` has a `tenant_id` column, and so do `edge_logs` and the rest. Measured `count(*)` against
`count(tenant_id)`: `security_events` **818 of 818 NULL**, `edge_logs` **3022 of 3022 NULL**,
`pipeline_spans` 5279 rows with 260 NULL, while `queue.*`, `grow.subscriptions`, `observability.ai_runs` and
`observability.audit_log` are fully populated. So the two tables that carry the personal data are precisely the two
that cannot be attributed to a tenant — the writers never set the column, which means a policy added today would
either hide every row (a two-sided `rls_tenant_check(NULL)` is false) or have to be written on something weaker than
the tenant. Retroactive isolation is not available for these rows; only deletion or a by-hand mapping is.

And nothing owns them. `rg 'observability\.(security_events|edge_logs|audit_log|pipeline_spans)' apps/` returns **no
file**; the 818 rows are all `turn_integrity_*` traces written between 2026-02-19 and 2026-05-06 (event, phone, and up
to 450 characters of `input_text` — the customer's own message), 50 of the 3022 edge logs carry an `error_stack`. This
is a forensic store of customer conversations, abandoned in place, with no writer to notice it and no reader to
protect it. The §99 lens applies to the new model's audit table; nobody has been looking at this one at all.

### 141.6 Fix

1. Retire the store, don't police it: `security_events` and `edge_logs` are debug traces with no reader
   (`apps/` is empty of call sites) and a NULL discriminator. Drop the rows, or export and drop, and say so in the
   migration notes — an unpoliced PII table that no code touches is a liability with no upside. `pipeline_spans` and
   `ai_runs` are attributable, so they can be kept behind RLS if anything still wants them.
2. Before that, close the one-line door: remove `grant select on all tables in schema observability to umi_app` from
   `002_api_grants.sql`, or scope it to the one table the Customer-360 read actually names
   (`observability.data_quality_findings`, per the file's own comment at `:32`). A blanket grant over a schema with
   RLS disabled is a grant over whatever is added to it later.
3. Turn the sweep into the assertion §137.5 and §139.7 ask for, extended to the classes this section separates: for
   every schema the request role must not see, `has_schema_privilege('api', s, 'USAGE')` **and**
   `has_table_privilege('api', 's.t', 'SELECT')` **and** `has_function_privilege('api', oid, 'EXECUTE')` must be false;
   and for every table in a schema it _can_ see, `relrowsecurity` must be true — 18 tables fail that last clause today,
   which is a number a fingerprint can hold still.
4. If any legacy table is ever given a policy, require the discriminator first: a `check (tenant_id is not null)` on
   the observability tables would have refused all 3840 un-attributable rows at write time instead of leaving them to
   be found by a hunt two releases later.

## 142. The policy-less set, enumerated: 35 tables no policy reaches, a second session store §137 never named — and one lead withdrawn because the token table is hashed, not plaintext

§137 measured the grants on `runtime` and `umi` and §141 swept the legacy schemas. This is the same axis asked the other
way round — not "what is granted" but **"what has no policy at all"** — and it produces both a clean result and a table
§137's enumeration missed.

### 142.1 The count, measured in both shapes (and one of my own cells corrected)

| Schema     | Tables | RLS on | RLS **forced** | **No policy at all** |
| ---------- | ------ | ------ | -------------- | -------------------- |
| `merchant` | 145    | 145    | **145**        | **0**                |
| `umi`      | 22     | 5      | 5              | **17**               |
| `runtime`  | 27     | 9      | 9              | **18**               |

Identical in `umi_local` and `umi_backfill_hunt`. The clean half is worth stating plainly: **the live money schema is
fully policed** — every one of the 145 `merchant` tables has RLS enabled, forced, and at least one policy — which is
what §135's verdict style looks like on a schema nobody expects to pass. The other half is 35 tables in the two auth
and platform schemas that no policy reaches, where the only thing standing between them and the request role is the
grant.

A correction to §141.1 first, because the finding above depended on reading it: I wrote `mixed` in the _forced_ cell for
`merchant` and `umi` from memory of the 2026-07-12 audit's `relforcerowsecurity = f` reading, which the hardened schema
had already fixed. The measurement says 145 of 145 and 5 of 5 — the sentence "the legacy schemas are better defended
than §137's tables because RLS is forced" is right for `merchant` too, and my table said otherwise for two rows. That is
the hunt's own blind spot #7 (a value recalled instead of measured) surviving into a written table, and it is recorded
rather than quietly patched.

### 142.2 All 35, with the thing that seals each one

Measured `has_table_privilege('api_login', …)` per table in both databases:

| Where `api` holds `SELECT` in a chain build            | Count | Tables                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| yes (sealed here by **nothing** but a read-only grant) | 11    | `runtime.product_embedding`; `umi.channel_type`, `umi.feature`, `umi.permission`, `umi.plan`, `umi.plan_feature`, `umi.role`, `umi.role_permission`, `umi.role_template`, `umi.role_template_revision`, `umi.role_template_revision_permission`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| no (sealed by the absence of a grant)                  | 24    | `runtime.session` (164 rows), `runtime.dashboard_session` (82), `runtime.password_reset_token` (9), `runtime.device_enrollment_request` (5), `runtime.device_pairing_session` (4), `runtime.otp`, `runtime.pairing`, `runtime.pass_device`, `runtime.platform_elevation`, `runtime.platform_bootstrap_command`, `runtime.outbox_event`, `runtime.inbound_event`, `runtime.dead_letter`, `runtime.integration_sync`, `runtime.knowledge_embedding`, `runtime.message_embedding`, `runtime.schema_migration`, and `umi.user` (5), `umi.user_role` (1), `umi.access_grant`, `umi.audit_log` (1), `umi.audit_retention_policy`, `umi.prospect`, `umi.prospect_event` |

In the clone the same 35 return **true for SELECT, INSERT and DELETE** — no third state, no partial table. So the
apparatus that contains 35 policy-less tables is one grant set, and its shape is decided by which database you are
looking at (§137).

### 142.3 The one §137 did not name

`runtime.dashboard_session` is a **second session store** and it is not in §137's list:
`startDashboardSession` writes `runtime.session` **and** `runtime.dashboard_session` in one transaction with the _same_
`token_hash` (`auth.repository.ts:714-722`), and the row is what other repositories validate a dashboard caller against
— `pos-entry.repository.ts:333` and `:531`, `administrative-command.repository.ts:20`,
`pos-inventory.repository.ts:189`, `pos-customer-value.repository.ts:2037` (which distinguishes a dashboard session
from a POS session by which of the two columns is set). It holds 82 rows in the live database and **all 82 are
unexpired** (51 flagged `is_active`; the next expiry is 2026-11-08), beside `runtime.session`'s 163 unexpired of 164. It
has no policy, and on the restored shape `api` can select, insert, update and delete it. §137's seven-and-then-26 count was built by
walking the tables it knew were sensitive; the class sweep is what finds the one it did not know about. The same is true
of `umi.user` (5 rows) and `umi.user_role` (1): policy-less, and the latter is the table the 2026-07-12 audit already
called out as the place `worker` can mint platform-wide grants.

### 142.4 A lead I withdrew, because I assumed instead of reading the auth model

The reading I started with was that §137's severity was understated: if the request role can read the token table, the
argument ran, it can present those values as bearer tokens and be whoever they name — a full dashboard and POS
impersonation out of a _read_. That would have made §137 high rather than med, on a table it already named.

It is wrong, and the reason is the auth model, so the fix is unchanged either way. Access tokens are signed JWTs
(`shared/auth/jwt.service.ts`, verified in `auth.service.ts:209/377`), so their value is not in the database at all;
refresh and reset tokens are **opaque secrets stored as `sha256(token)`** and looked up by hash
(`auth.repository.ts:751`, `:770`, `:856`, `:1077`), so the row holds a preimage-free hash that cannot be turned back
into a usable token. Reading the table is therefore not forgery — it is a hash list. What _is_ forgery is the write the
restored database also grants (`arwd`): replacing `token_hash` with the digest of a token the caller holds makes the row
the caller's session, and the same move against `runtime.password_reset_token` (9 live rows) is an account takeover by
reset. So §137's severity stands as written, the read half survives only because the column is hashed, and the finding's
weight sits on the write. Recorded in the same spirit as §119 and §138.4: the first reading was the dramatic one, and
the code says no.

### 142.5 Fix

§137.5's revoke and §139.7's class sweep cover this; three additions come out of the enumeration:

1. Name `runtime.dashboard_session` in the sealed set explicitly, beside `runtime.session` — the privilege fingerprint
   must list the session stores, not the tables someone happened to think of. Same for `umi.user_role` and
   `umi.access_grant`.
2. Assert `relrowsecurity` over the 35: a check that the two auth schemas have no policy-less table carrying a grant is
   one query, and it is the assertion that would have caught this class before §137 measured grants on it.
3. Keep the read/write distinction in the assertion's message. "Can read" and "can forge" are different severities, and
   the fingerprint should say which one a failing table represents — `runtime.session` is `arwd` on the restored shape,
   which is the forgeable half.

## 143. The append-only and tamper-evident substrate, verified end to end: it holds — and the three residues are all about who checks it, not what it does

The audit table sells one guarantee in its comments ("a column that names WHO acted through the café must not be editable
without breaking the chain — that is the one guarantee this table sells"). Six months of §99 and §140 saying _the audit
path is wrong elsewhere_ make it worth asking whether the guarantee itself is real. It is, and the way it is real is
worth writing down, because it is the second artifact in this hunt that passes in full (§135 was the first).

### 143.1 The stack, measured

| Layer                        | Measure                                                                                                                                  | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hash chain, live data        | `lag(event_hash)` vs `previous_hash` per merchant, ordered `occurred_at, id`                                                             | **0 broken links**, 173 rows, exactly **1 genesis** (`previous_hash IS NULL`)                                                                                                                                                          |
| Forking                      | rows sharing a `previous_hash` within a merchant                                                                                         | **0**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Serialization                | `merchant.tg_audit_event_hash()` opens with `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(new.merchant_id::text, 0))`                          | the whole insert is serialized per merchant, so the tail cannot be read twice by two live transactions                                                                                                                                 |
| Hash input                   | every column, each `coalesce`d (the comment explains why: `concat_ws` _skips_ NULLs, so two rows differing only by a NULL would collide) | the digest covers `id, merchant_id, location_id, actor, delegate, command_id, event_type, entity_type, entity_id, outcome, reason_code, public_data, correlation_id, prior, occurred_at`                                               |
| Trigger hygiene              | `SECURITY DEFINER` with `search_path = pg_catalog, extensions`, every reference schema-qualified                                         | hardened against the §139 class of trojan                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| The classic bypass           | `has_table_privilege('api_login'/'worker_login', …, 'TRUNCATE')` on `audit_event`, `financial_event`, `cash_ledger_entry`                | **false for both roles in both databases** — `TRUNCATE` fires no row trigger, and it is closed                                                                                                                                         |
| Immutability under a _grant_ | `api` holds `UPDATE`+`DELETE` on `merchant.cash_ledger_entry` (both databases)                                                           | inert: `cash_ledger_immutable` is `BEFORE DELETE OR UPDATE … EXECUTE merchant.tg_cash_fact_immutable()`, which raises `cash fact is immutable`; the three loyalty ledgers and `stock_ledger_entry` carry `tg_append_only` the same way |
| Can the guard be removed?    | `pg_get_userbyid(relowner)` for `audit_event`, `financial_event`, `cash_ledger_entry`, `loyalty_points_ledger`, `stock_ledger_entry`     | **`postgres` for all five**, so no application role can `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER`                                                                                                                                                |
| Is it checked anywhere?      | `rg previous_hash`                                                                                                                       | `scripts/umi-pos-db-check.sh:184-189` — and that check is exactly the `lag()` comparison run above, plus "the first event of a merchant is genesis"                                                                                    |

This is the shape the literature asks for: the ACL is not the guarantee, the trigger is; the trigger is owned by a role
the application does not have; the lock is taken inside the same transaction as the write; and the ordering the trigger
uses to pick its parent (`occurred_at desc, id desc`) is the ordering the verifier uses to check it. A hash chain whose
writer and verifier disagree about order is a chain that "fails" for the wrong reason — this one agrees.

### 143.2 The three residues

**(a) `internalMetadata` has no writer — and on a restored database its table is readable by the request role.**
`runtime.audit_event_internal` receives `redactObject(event.internalMetadata ?? {})` on every append
(`integrity.repository.ts:229-232`), and `rg internalMetadata` finds exactly two hits: the type
(`integrity.types.ts:35`) and that line. No caller in the tree ever passes the field, and the data agrees: **155 rows,
155 with `metadata = '{}'`**. So it is a declared path with no writer. Both tables pass through the same
`redactObject`/`redactTelemetry` scrubber (which masks by key — `password`, `token`, `pin`, `credential`, `card_number`
… — truncates at 2 000 characters and caps depth), so the split is not redacted-vs-raw: it is _what the UI shows_ versus
_what is kept beside it_. And the sibling is the one `api` can read on the restored shape (`SELECT` true in
`umi_backfill_hunt`, false in `umi_local`, RLS on with one policy in both). The day someone starts using the field,
"internal" will mean "readable by the request role" on one of the two databases.

**(b) The chain's only verifier sits inside the harness §48 measured as unrunnable.** No spec and no application code
mentions `previous_hash`; `rg` over `.github/workflows/` finds no job that invokes any `*-db-check` script. The
invariant "every event links to its predecessor" is therefore asserted in exactly one place — a shell script whose
frozen migration list makes it fail in two seconds (§48), whose repaired form then stops on a stale fixture. An
invariant checked only by a harness that cannot run is, operationally, an invariant that is not checked. The chain is
intact today because the _writer_ is right; nothing would notice if it stopped being.

**(c) The audit cursor is a timestamp without a tiebreaker.** `searchAudit` paginates with
`AND ($2::timestamptz IS NULL OR occurred_at < $2::timestamptz)` while ordering `occurred_at DESC, id DESC`
(`integrity.repository.ts:277`, `:282`). A page boundary that falls between two rows sharing a `occurred_at` drops one,
and the `id` in the `ORDER BY` cannot save it because the cursor never carries an id — the textbook keyset-pagination
defect. Measured on the live table: **0 groups share a `(merchant_id, occurred_at)`** (the trigger stamps
`clock_timestamp()` per row, not the transaction's `now()`), so this is latent, not active. The fix is one clause.

### 143.3 Fix

1. Move the chain check out of the shell harness and into the spec suite that does run: recompute
   `lag(event_hash) over (partition by merchant_id order by occurred_at, id)` and assert 0 mismatches and exactly one
   genesis per merchant. It is the same query the script already contains, and it makes §143.2(b) stop being true
   without touching the writer.
2. Decide `internalMetadata`'s fate: delete the field and the sibling table (no writer, no reader), or write it and seal
   `runtime.audit_event_internal` with the §137 revoke so that "internal" cannot mean "app-readable" on a restored
   database. Leaving a declared-but-unwritten redaction split is the same shape as §107's tables with no door.
3. Make the cursor a pair: `(occurred_at, id) < ($2, $3)` with the id returned by the previous page. One clause, and it
   removes the only way this endpoint can lose a row.

## 144. The migration family, run against a production-shaped clone: three red — two of them the product's own suite confirming §137, one of them the instrument — plus a smoke suite that cannot start

`test:integration:migration` is the family the vitest config describes as "a BACKFILLED clone of production … asks what
the migration produced from real rows", and the workflow says it "belongs to the P7 rehearsal". It has never been run
against the restore-shaped clone this hunt has been measuring. Run there, three of its twenty-five tests are red, and
the split between them is the interesting part: two are the divergence of §137 asserted by the repo's own gate, and one
is the gate itself.

### 144.1 The run

```
$ APP=$(grep -m1 '^DATABASE_URL_APP=' apps/umi-api/.env | cut -d= -f2- | sed 's|/umi_local|/umi_backfill_hunt|')
$ DATABASE_URL_APP="$APP" DATABASE_URL_WORKER="$WRK" \
    npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts \
      src/shared/database/rls.integration.ts src/shared/database/pooler-isolation.integration.ts \
      src/shared/database/identity-normalization.integration.ts src/smoke.integration.ts

 Test Files  3 failed | 1 passed (4)
      Tests  3 failed | 20 passed | 2 skipped (25)
```

| Test                                                                                 | What it asserts                                                                   | What the clone does                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `rls › api pool cannot read credential columns on umi.user`                          | `select password_hash from umi.user limit 1` **rejects** with `permission denied` | the read succeeds — §137 measured `api` on 22 of 22 `umi` tables there                                                   |
| `rls › api pool has zero privilege on the runtime auth substrate`                    | `runtime.password_reset_token` and `runtime.session` **reject**                   | both selects succeed; the empty table returns `count = 0`, which is why the failure reads as a value and not as a denial |
| `identity-normalization › repairs the NANP rows and NULLs only the un-dialable ones` | `total = SNAPSHOT.phoneContacts` = **864**                                        | `total = 1016` — `expected 1016 to be 864`                                                                               |

Twenty tests pass, including all five of `pooler-isolation` (with its "proves the defect this gate exists for" case) and
the two _shape_ assertions in the normalization file — "leaves the repaired rows holding their TRUE numbers" and "NULLs
a row only when the number is nobody's number". So the invariant §139.5 worried about (no rewritten country codes in the
migrated data) is **confirmed** on this clone; only the counts pin fails.

### 144.2 What the two red privilege tests mean

This is §137 in the strongest available form: not a hunt measuring `has_table_privilege`, but the repository's own gate
asserting the seal — `pg.app.connect()`, the raw app pool, no merchant scope involved — and failing on the clone that
was restored from a dump. The gate's verdict and the hunt's measurement agree, and the fix is already known to work:

```
BEGIN;
  api_login SELECT runtime.session                -> t
  api_login SELECT runtime.password_reset_token   -> t
  api_login SELECT umi.user                       -> t
REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA umi, runtime FROM api;
  api_login SELECT runtime.session                -> f
  api_login SELECT runtime.password_reset_token   -> f
  api_login SELECT umi.user                       -> f
ROLLBACK;  -- restores t, so the probe changed nothing
```

One statement flips all three, which is why §137.5 asks for exactly it. The reason the family passed a different
backfill clone (10/10, recorded earlier in this log) is the shape of the clone, not the product: that one was built by
`00_run_backfill.sh`, which re-applies the chain over a restored database, and this one is the platform database as the dump captured it — the product's own tables are created by the chain and sealed (§153)
itself. **The migration gate's colour therefore depends on which clone is rehearsed against, and the workflow makes
that structural — the migration family is deliberately absent from CI** ("it needs a backfilled clone of production,
which CI has not got and must never have. It belongs to the P7 rehearsal",
`.github/workflows/umi-api-ci.yml:249-252`), so the pipeline runs the _pristine_ family and can never see this. The
gate that certifies the cutover target is rehearsed against a database the cutover does not produce.

### 144.3 The count pin, which is the instrument and not the product

`expect(total).toBe(SNAPSHOT.phoneContacts)` with the snapshot re-pinned to `phoneContacts: 864` on 2026-09-01, against
a clone whose dump is newer and whose join returns 1016. The file itself explains the tension — it pins counts to a
named snapshot and the _shape_ structurally so "a newer dump moves the counts without loosening the rule" — but the
count assertion is a hard equality, so the family can only be green against one specific dump. That is the §43/§46/§48/
§89 family of defect (an instrument that cannot run, or measures something other than what it claims) and it is worth
naming here rather than in the abstract, because this is the only suite in the tree that watches the migration target
and a red-for-the-wrong-reason gate is a gate people learn to skip. The honest fix is the one the comment already
describes: assert `changed <= repaired + nulled` with the shape checks doing the real work, and keep the exact counts in
a named, versioned fixture that says which dump it was measured on.

### 144.4 The suite that cannot start

`smoke.integration.ts` is the check that "every route answers, or is a declared exception" — the sweep whose own note
in this log credits it with finding the audit endpoint that answered 500 for any merchant with audit events
(`integrity.repository.ts:285-300`). Its `beforeAll` refuses to run without `APP_QR_SECRET`
(`smoke.integration.ts:356-359`), and the variable is not in `apps/umi-api/.env` — it is _commented out_ in
`.env.example:124` ("≥32 chars; byte-identical to umi-cash") and `.optional()` in the config schema
(`shared/config/config.schema.ts:233`), required only for `staging`/`pilot`/`production` (`:342-360`). So on any machine
that copied the example the suite dies in `beforeAll`, its two tests report as **skipped**, and the summary line reads
"2 skipped" instead of "0 routes swept".

The runtime half of that gap is a user-facing one: with the secret absent, `QrService` throws a bare
`new Error('APP_QR_SECRET is not set')` (`shared/auth/qr.service.ts:59`, `:103`) — an untyped `Error` → the 500 mapping
of §142.5 — on a route that is reachable on a running instance (`shared/auth/qr.service.ts` is consumed by the wallet
pass builders and `modules/cash/cash-card.service.ts`). The boot guard does not catch it locally because local is not a
deployed environment, and the one suite that would have walked the route cannot run without the same value. That is a
closed loop with a gap in it: the check needs the secret, the machine has no secret, and the failure that results is a
500 at a customer's barcode rather than a refusal at boot.

### 144.5 Fix

1. Apply §137.5's revoke on the restore path and re-apply it whenever a dump is restored — the probe above shows one
   statement turns the two red privilege tests green, and the family is the assertion that keeps them green.
2. Add the migration family to the rehearsal runbook as a _required_ step with its target named (a restore-shaped clone,
   not a chain-built one), since CI is not the place for it and therefore something else has to be.
3. Replace the hard count pin with the shape assertions plus a dump-identified fixture (§144.3), so a newer dump does
   not fail the gate for the wrong reason.
4. Ship `APP_QR_SECRET` the way `JWT_SECRET` is shipped — it is present in `apps/umi-api/.env` and read by
   `scripts/local-reset.sh:177`, while `APP_QR_SECRET` appears in no bootstrap at all — and make the QR routes refuse
   with a typed code instead of an untyped `Error` when it is missing, so the smoke suite runs everywhere and the
   customer barcode path degrades loudly instead of answering 500.

## 145. `POST /pos/elevation/pin` mints an elevation for whatever permission the client names, checks nobody for it, records the wrong approver — and no code in the tree can consume it

Every money approval in this product runs through `runtime.elevation_grant`, and there are two doors into that table.
One of them checks the approver's authority in SQL. The other checks a PIN and then writes the permission it was
handed. The second door is reachable by any enrolled operator, requires no permission of its own
(`route-table.ts:2022`: `permission: null`), and produces a grant that nothing in the tree accepts.

### 145.1 The two doors, side by side

The route is `pos.verifyPin` → `POST /api/v1/pos/elevation/pin` (`packages/contract/src/route-table.ts:2014-2024`,
request `VerifyOperatorPinRequest`, response `ElevationGrantView`, `auth: 'operator-session'`,
`permission: null`), implemented at `pos-entry.controller.ts:44-52` → `PosEntryService.verifyPin`
(`pos-entry.service.ts:71-115`) → `PosEntryRepository.grantPinElevation`
(`pos-entry.repository.ts:383-435`).

|                                                              | `grantManagerElevation` (`:437-511`)                                                              | `grantPinElevation` (`:383-435`)                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The credential                                               | a manager's PIN **or** card (`managerCredential`, exactly one)                                    | the caller's own PIN (`pinRecord` joins `s.user_id = $1`, `:243`)                     |
| Who the staff row is                                         | `managerStaffId`, checked to be `active`, in this merchant, and at this location or merchant-wide | `staffId` is passed as `$1` of the INSERT … **and never referenced in the statement** |
| Does the requested permission have to belong to that person? | **yes** — `AND $5 = ANY(umi.resolve_staff_permissions(ms.id))`                                    | **no clause of any kind**                                                             |
| Entitlement                                                  | `EXISTS (… ee.feature_key='pos' AND ee.enabled)`                                                  | none                                                                                  |
| The session the grant lands on                               | the operator session named in the request, matched by `state='active' AND expires_at>now()`       | the caller's own session, unconditionally                                             |
| Approver is not the actor                                    | `WHERE target.user_id <> $1::uuid`                                                                | none — `approved_by = input.userId`, the requester                                    |
| `method` written                                             | `manager_approval` / `manager_card`                                                               | `operator_pin`                                                                        |

So the second door grants `permission_key = <the string the client sent>`, to `<the caller's own session>`, attributed
to `<the caller>`. It also carries a side effect worth naming: the `reset` CTE clears `pin_failed_attempts` and
`pin_locked_until` on the device (`:395-398`) for any successful PIN — so the endpoint is additionally a lockout reset
on the caller's own device.

### 145.2 Nothing can consume it, which is the only reason this is not an escalation

Every authority check against that table in the tree filters the method:

| Consumer                                         | Filter                                                                               | Line                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `consumeApproval` (variance, recover, movements) | `AND method='manager_approval'`                                                      | `pos-cash.repository.ts:3049`                |
| checkout's multi-approval match                  | `AND … method='manager_approval'`                                                    | `pos-checkout.repository.ts:489-491`         |
| refund approval                                  | `AND e.method='manager_approval'`                                                    | `pos-exception.repository.ts:800`            |
| customer-value approvals                         | `AND command_fingerprint=$7 AND method='manager_approval' AND approved_by<>$8::uuid` | `pos-customer-value.repository.ts:2033-2041` |
| inventory approval                               | `AND method='manager_approval'`                                                      | `pos-inventory.repository.ts:1770-1774`      |

(The two other reads of the table, `pos-exception.repository.ts:595` and `:1460`, only look up the approver's _name_ for
display.) `rg operator_pin` finds the writer (`pos-entry.service.ts:111`) and the staff credential columns, and **no
reader that compares it**. The `operator_pin` grant is therefore unconsumable today: the door mints authority that
expires in five minutes unused. Two things follow, and both are why this is a finding rather than a curiosity:

Probed rather than inferred — one `operator_pin` grant for `stored_value.approve`, then the consumers' own `UPDATE`
with and without their clause, inside a transaction that was rolled back:

```
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO runtime.elevation_grant (session_id, merchant_id, location_id, permission_key, method, approved_by, expires_at)
  VALUES (<live session>, <merchant>, <location>, 'stored_value.approve', 'operator_pin', <operator>, now()+interval '5 minutes');
UPDATE … WHERE permission_key='stored_value.approve' AND method='manager_approval' AND expires_at>now() AND consumed_at IS NULL
  -> 0 rows          -- what all five consumers do
UPDATE … WHERE permission_key='stored_value.approve' AND expires_at>now() AND consumed_at IS NULL
  -> 1 row           -- the same statement with the clause dropped
ROLLBACK;            -- 0 rows left behind
```

The only thing between an operator's own PIN and an approval is that clause.

1. **The 5-minute grant and its audit event are false statements.** `grantPinElevation` writes
   `runtime.security_audit_event` with `event_type='elevation.granted'` and
   `metadata = {method:'operator_pin', permission:<client string>}` (`:418-432`). The record asserts a permission was
   granted; whether the person who typed the PIN holds it is never tested, so the record is exactly as true as the
   client is honest. The same column is what a refund UI reads to print "approved by" (`pos-exception.repository.ts:595`
   joins `approved_by`), and here `approved_by` is the requester, not the PIN's staff row — the one piece of information
   the PIN was supposed to add is dropped on the floor.
2. **The inventory says six permissions are controlled by this table, and all six are money.** `customer.merge.approve`,
   `gift_card.activate.approve`, `gift_card.issue.approve`, `loyalty.adjust.approve`, `loyalty.reward.approve`,
   `stored_value.approve` (`config/umipos-permission-inventory.json:614, 698, 749, 1637, 1688, 2028`, all with
   `control: "runtime.elevation_grant"` and profiles `admin/manager/owner[/supervisor]`). The client chooses the
   `permission` string, so the day a consumer checks the table without repeating `method='manager_approval'` — a filter
   copied by hand into five places, which is five chances to forget it in the sixth — an operator's own PIN is enough
   to mint the approval for any of them. The guard is a string, and strings are what §138.4 and §137 taught this hunt to
   distrust.

### 145.3 The in-flight client says the opposite, and throws the grant away

The uncommitted change to `apps/umi-pos/lib/features/cash/cash_repository.dart:316-322` documents the call as:
"The elevation the server returns is what names the permission this PIN proved, so a till cannot use it to unlock
something the operator does not hold." That is the design the code should have and does not: the server echoes the
permission from the request body (`dto.permission` at `pos-entry.service.ts:109`). Two smaller facts in the same diff:
`CashController.resumePausedShiftWithPin` awaits `verifyOperatorPin` and **discards its return value**
(`cash_controller.dart:295-301`), so the grant has no client-side effect either; and the resume it then performs needs no
elevation at all — `PosCashService.transition` authorizes from the operator session
(`pos-cash.service.ts:397-410`, permission `cash.shift.resume`), which means the new PIN pad is a courtesy the server
does not require. A drawer can be reopened by a request that never presents a PIN; §130's "the guard exists and
protects one route" meets its mirror image here, a gate that exists only in the client.

### 145.4 Fix

1. Decide what the route is for. If it is step-up for the caller's own session, then it must check the caller holds the
   named permission: add `AND $5 = ANY(umi.resolve_staff_permissions($1::uuid))` — the clause the sibling has — and set
   `approved_by` to the PIN's `staffId`, which is already in hand.
2. If nothing consumes `operator_pin` grants, delete the route and the insert, or make the method filter structural
   rather than repeated: a single `consume_elevation(...)` helper, or a check constraint/`ENUM` where the reader cannot
   forget the clause that five call sites now copy by hand.
3. Keep the audit honest: only write `elevation.granted` when a check passed, and record the staff row whose credential
   was verified (the parameter is already there and currently unused — `$1` in the INSERT statement).
4. Correct the Dart comment, or make it true by (1). A security claim in a comment that the server does not enforce is
   how §124's "the flag is real, the guard lies" happens a second time.

## 146. Withdrawn: the new cash-policy switch does not cross the location boundary — I read a diff hunk as if it were the code. What survives is that the boundary now rests on one check where the schema wrote two

### 146.1 The claim, and the two lines that killed it

The blind-count switch is the newest thing in the tree (uncommitted): a `GET`/`PATCH` pair on
`/api/merchants/:merchantId/operations/cash-policy` that reads and writes one location's `blind_count_required` and moves
`count_method` with it (`dashboard-operations.repository.ts:847-884`). I read the new service block as far as its helper's
first line —

```ts
const scoped = locationId ?? access.locationId ?? null;   // the request appears to win
if (!scoped) throw new ForbiddenException({ code: 'LOCATION_SCOPE_VIOLATION' });
```

— concluded that a caller limited to branch A could `PATCH` with branch B's id, and wrote the finding up: the same
service guards this exact boundary twice (`:55-57` in `snapshot`, `:173-176` in `saleReceipt`), and here, I said, it was
omitted. It is not omitted. Reading the file instead of the hunk shows the next two lines:

```ts
if (access.locationId && access.locationId !== scoped) {
  throw new ForbiddenException({ code: 'LOCATION_SCOPE_VIOLATION' });
}
```

The guard is the same guard, in the same direction, with the same code. The finding is withdrawn in full: no
cross-location write exists. The claim also became §146.4's own contradiction — the fix I had drafted ("add the check
that `snapshot` and `saleReceipt` carry") is the check that was already there, three lines below where I stopped reading.

### 146.2 The blind spot this adds to the instrument's list

The hunt's own error class #7 is "a value recalled instead of measured". This is #8, and it is worth naming because the
tooling makes it easy: **a diff hunk is not the code.** `git diff` prints three lines of context on each side, and a new
method longer than that arrives cut in half — the beginning with the shape of the thing and the end, with the guard
buried in a part that scrolls past. The check that would have caught this costs one command (`sed -n '140,152p'` on the
file, not on the diff), and the hunt has been applying it everywhere except here, where the code was new and therefore
familiar. It is the same failure as §142.4's withdrawn lead, in a different direction: there the first reading was the
dramatic one and the code said no; here the first reading was the alarming one and the code said no.

### 146.3 What survives, and it is measured

One real property came out of the probe, and it is a defence-in-depth note rather than a bug: **for this endpoint the
service check is the only thing enforcing the location boundary, because the SQL session never arms the policy that was
written for it.**

`merchant.cash_shift_policy` carries a restrictive `location_narrowing` policy —
`umi.current_location() IS NULL OR location_id IS NULL OR location_id = umi.current_location()` — beside two permissive
ones (`merchant_isolation: merchant_id = umi.current_merchant()`, `merchant_location_isolation`: that **and** the
location). The new repository methods call `this.pg.runWithMerchant(merchantId, userId, work)`; the fourth parameter
defaults to null (`pg.service.ts:399-404`), which sets `app.current_location` to `''` (`:418-421`), and
`umi.current_location()` maps that to NULL — so the restrictive clause is satisfied by its first disjunct and the write
is narrowed by nothing but the merchant. Probed on the clone, two policies seeded for Kalala Café's two locations inside
a transaction that was rolled back:

```
SET LOCAL ROLE api_login;  set_config('app.current_merchant', <Kalala>, true);
set_config('app.current_location', '', true);             -- what the endpoint does today
  UPDATE … WHERE location_id = <Congreso>                 -> 1 row written
set_config('app.current_location', <Chapultepec>, true);  -- the location actually in scope
  UPDATE … WHERE location_id = <Congreso>                 -> 0 rows
ROLLBACK;                                                 -- 0 policies left behind
```

One row versus zero on the same statement, decided only by whether the scope is set. Today the service's guard makes
that difference unreachable through the endpoint, so nothing is broken. What the measurement changes is the _count of
things keeping it correct_: the schema author wrote two (the service check and the policy), and the endpoint leaves one
of them unarmed. My own misreading is the argument for arming it — a reader who has the file open in front of them
still missed the guard, and RLS would not have been fooled.

### 146.4 Fix

1. Pass the resolved location through: `runWithMerchant(merchantId, userId, work, locationId)`. One argument, in the two
   new methods, and `location_narrowing` stops being decorative for this table.
2. Give the new spec the two-location fixture anyway — a location-scoped caller and a `PATCH` naming the other location
   — so the guard is asserted by a test rather than by a careful reading. That is the assertion §146.1 shows is worth
   having, even though the code already passes it.

## 147. The new blind-count switch tells four of the nine roles "there is no policy" when the truth is "you may not read it"

The switch the last two sections circle around reads one location's rule and shows it as a pill. The read is gated by
`merchant.manage` (`dashboard-operations.service.ts:105-108`), the screen that shows it is gated by `cash.shift.read`
(`dashboard-operations.policy.ts:116-122`), and the screen renders the refusal as `Sin política`
(`caja-turnos.jsx:1074-1080`). Those three sentences do not compose.

### 147.1 The measurement

`umi.role_permission`, live database:

| Role                                        | may read the shifts (`cash.shift.read`) | may read/set the policy (`merchant.manage`) |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `admin`, `owner`, `super_admin`             | yes                                     | **yes**                                     |
| `manager`, `supervisor`, `cashier`, `staff` | yes                                     | **no**                                      |
| `developer`, `viewer`                       | no                                      | no                                          |

So four roles open Caja y turnos — the screen's only requirement is the shifts read — and every one of them gets a
`403 PERMISSION_DENIED` from `GET /operations/cash-policy` before the policy is ever looked at. The screen's effect
catches that and sets `policy = null` (`caja-turnos.jsx:921-923`), and the null renders as:

```
{policy ? (policy.blindCountRequired ? t`Ciego` : t`Visible · total`) : t`Sin política`}
```

with the checkbox disabled (`disabled={!policy || policySaving}`, `:1040`). The switch is therefore _inert and
unlabelled as such_ for the manager who runs the drawer, and it shows a claim about the database that is not the reason.

### 147.2 Why the label is false, in three different situations

`null` is where four distinct facts collapse:

1. **The API refused** (403) — the case above. The location's rule exists; this reader may not see it.
2. **The read failed** (network, 500, a parse refusal) — same rendering, same sentence.
3. **No merchant or no location in context** — the effect returns early without setting state (`:916`), so the pill
   keeps its initial null and says `Sin política` for a screen that has not asked anybody anything yet.
4. **The location genuinely has no policy row** — the only case the label is written for. The service returns `null`
   with 200 here, and its own comment says the screen "then says so instead of inventing a default"
   (`dashboard-operations.service.ts:92-99`): the four cases are indistinguishable, so the one honest rendering is the
   one used for all four.

For the live database the first case is the _only_ one that occurs for four of the nine roles, and the sentence is
measurably wrong there: ONCA's policy exists (`blind_count_required = f`, `count_method = 'total_only'`, `umi_local`).
A support conversation that starts with "dice _Sin política_" sends someone to seed a row that is already there.

### 147.3 Fix

1. Keep the refusal: `catch (error)` and store `error.code` (`AppException` carries it — `PERMISSION_DENIED`,
   `RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`), then render three states rather than two: _no access_, _could not read_,
